#35660. Bakımın bir coğrafyası var

27.10.2026 - 07:00 | Son Güncellenme: 27.10.2026 - 07:01

Afetlerin ardından ortaya çıkan hizmet boşluklarının yüzde 76’sı ücretsiz bakım emeğiyle kapanıyor. Buna karşılık küresel iklime uyum finansmanının yalnızca yüzde 4’ü afet sonrası sağlık hizmetlerine, yüzde 2’si ise eğitime ayrılıyor. Krizin ardından açığı kapatan emek, finansmanın neredeyse tamamen dışında kalıyor. Oysa bakım yalnızca krizin maliyeti değil, çözümün de parçası. UN Women ile Dünya Bankası’nın ortak politika notuna göre bakım sektöründeki ortalama bir iş, imalat sektöründeki bir işe kıyasla 26 kat daha az sera gazı üretiyor. Bakım hizmetlerine ve politikalarına ayrılacak kaynakla 2035’e kadar 300 milyona yakın insan onuruna yakışır iş yaratılabileceği, bu işlerin çoğunluğundan kadınların yararlanacağı öngörülüyor. Çocuk bakımı politikalarındaki boşlukların kapatılması için harcanan her 1 dolar ise 2035’e kadar küresel gayrisafi yurt içi hasılaya 3,76 dolar olarak geri dönebilir.

BM Genel Kurulu, 2023’te 29 Ekim’i Uluslararası Bakım ve Destek Günü ilan etti. Günün bu yılki teması bakım çalışanlarının koşullarına odaklanıyor. Rakamlar bu çağrının karşılığını gösteriyor:

* Dünyada bakım iş gücü yaklaşık 381 milyon kişi. Bu, toplam istihdamın yüzde 11,5’ine karşılık geliyor. Ücretli bakım çalışanlarının yüzde 65’i kadın ve bu kadınlar çoğunlukla düşük ücretle, uzun saatler boyunca, sosyal güvencesi olmayan ya da kayıt dışı işlerde çalışıyor.

* Bakım emeğinin ekonomik karşılığı çoğu zaman görünmüyor. Oysa bazı ülkelerde bu emeğin değeri gayrisafi yurt içi hasılanın (GSYH) yüzde 40’ına yaklaşıyor.

* Çalışma çağındaki kadınların yüzde 45’i ücretsiz bakım sorumlulukları nedeniyle iş gücünün dışında kalıyor. Erkeklerde bu oran yüzde 5. Altı yaşın altında en az bir çocuğu olan 25-54 yaş arası kadınlarda iş gücüne katılım yüzde 53’e düşerken, erkeklerde yüzde 95 olarak kalıyor.

Bakım yalnızca evin içinde geçmiyor. Evi okula, kreşe, sağlık merkezine ve işyerine bağlayan yolculuklar da bakımın parçası ve bunlar çoğu zaman tek bir gidiş geliş değil, zamana sıkışmış bir dizi yolculuk oluyor. Kentin bu noktaları nasıl bağladığı, bakımın kadınların gününden ne kadar yer kaplayacağını doğrudan belirliyor. Erişim her zaman erişilebilirlik anlamına gelmiyor. Engelli Kadın Derneği’nin UN Women desteğiyle 2024’te yaklaşık bin kişiyle yürüttüğü araştırmaya göre engelli kadınların yüzde 60,3’ü toplu taşımayı kullanırken ve kentte hareket ederken erişilebilirlik engelleriyle karşılaştığını belirtti.

Bu tartışma Antalya’ya da taşınıyor. Geçen yıl Brezilya’nın Belém kentinde kabul edilen Belém Toplumsal Cinsiyet Eylem Planı (2026-2034), BM İklim Değişikliği Çerçeve Sözleşmesi tarihinde bakım emeğini ilk kez açık biçimde bir başlık olarak tanımladı. Plan, ülkelerden iklim değişikliği bağlamında bakım emeğine ilişkin ulusal değerlendirmelerini Mart 2027’ye kadar sunmalarını istiyor. Aynı zirvede kurulan Belém Adil Dönüşüm Mekanizması ise adil dönüşüme Sözleşme içinde ilk kez kurumsal bir adres verdi. 9-20 Kasım’da Antalya’da düzenlenecek COP31’de UN Women çeşitli paydaşlarla birlikte bakım ekonomisini ve politikalarını toplumsal cinsiyet eşitliği perspektifiyle ele alacak.

İklim ve afet politikaları bakım hizmetlerini ve sosyal koruma sistemlerini merkeze almadığı sürece, krizin faturası görünmeden hanelerin içinde ödenmeye devam ediyor. UN Women beş alanda adım atılmasını öneriyor:

* Afet dönemlerinde çocuklara, yaşlılara, hastalara ve engelli kişilere yönelik bakım hizmetleri kesintisiz sürmeli.

* Sağlık, rehabilitasyon ve destek hizmetleri afet ve tahliye planlarının içinde yer almalı.

* Güvenli suya, temiz enerjiye, toplu ulaşıma ve erişilebilir kamu hizmetlerine ayrılan kaynak artırılmalı.

* İklim kaynaklı gelir kayıplarına karşı uyarlanabilir sosyal koruma programları geliştirilmeli.

* Kadınların ücretsiz bakım ve ev içi sorumlulukları için harcadığı zamanı azaltan kamu hizmetleri ve altyapı yaygınlaştırılmalı. Bakım, ailelerin kendi başına üstlenmesi gereken özel bir sorumluluk değil, devletin, iş verenlerin ve toplumun birlikte taşıması gereken kamusal bir yükümlülük. Görünür kılındığı ve paylaşıldığı anda, iklim krizine karşı en güçlü dayanaklardan biri.

Milliyet, küresel medya birliği Media Compact üyesi olduğu Birleşmiş Milletler Kadın Birimi (UN Women) ile iklim krizinin çok boyutlu etkilerini ele alan yazı dizisine devam ediyor. Dizi, 9-20 Kasım tarihlerinde Türkiye’nin ev sahipliğinde Antalya’da düzenlenecek Birleşmiş Milletler İklim Değişikliği Konferansı’na (COP31) kadar sürecek.

Türkiye'den ve Dünya’dan son dakika haberler, köşe yazıları, magazinden siyasete, spordan seyahate bütün konuların tek adresi milliyet.com.tr; Milliyet.com.tr haber içerikleri izin alınmadan, kaynak gösterilerek dahi iktibas edilemez, kanuna aykırı ve izinsiz olarak kopyalanamaz, başka yerde yayınlanamaz.

#35663. Trump, ignoring polls, predicts economy to help Republicans in midterms

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

CORINTH, Mississippi, Oct 26 - US President Donald Trump campaigned on Monday in deeply Republican Mississippi, predicting victory for a Republican Senate candidate based on what he deemed to be a booming US economy, while also repeating his claim that oil prices would soon plummet.

Trump, a Republican, has been on a campaign blitz through normally safe Republican states ahead of the November 3 vote, with party strategists telling Reuters they are on edge about races from Alaska to South Carolina, in part because of voter discontent over how Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have fueled inflation.

Sounding hoarse from his recent series of campaign rallies, Trump remarked, "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day."

Trump is expected to visit Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, Florida and Iowa in the final days of the campaign, with voter concerns over affordability likely to weigh on Republicans, pollsters say.

Trump acknowledged the war in Iran has pushed up oil prices, but said it was a small price to pay to stop Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

"I thought the price of oil was going to go much, much higher," Trump said.

"It's worked out fine and it'll be over soon," Trump said about the war.

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, with public opinion polls suggesting the Democrats will regain control of the House and have a chance to retake the Senate.

A Republican victory would preserve Republican control of Congress, which Trump has enjoyed since returning to the White House after the 2024 election, while a Democratic victory could impede the president and trigger congressional investigations into his administration.

In Mississippi, an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race has given Democrats a rare opening ahead of next week's congressional elections.

Democrats last won a Senate seat in Mississippi in 1982. Trump carried the state by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024, and he won the northeastern Mississippi county he was set to visit on Monday by 68 percentage points.

But several election analysts no longer regard US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s reelection as a sure bet. The Trump-endorsed Republican faces Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney from the Columbus area, and independent Ty Pinkins, a military veteran and attorney who previously ran statewide as a Democrat.

"Cindy's doing great but I've just got to make sure," Trump said. "I can't take a chance."

After listing a series of economic achievements, many of them exaggerations or unverifiable claims, Trump said, "I can't help Cindy Hyde-Smith any better than that."

Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in support of Colom last week, and Democrats have dispatched big-name figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to former presidential primary candidate Pete Buttigieg to campaign alongside the Democratic candidate.

Colom came to Corinth on Monday, posting pictures of himself meeting with voters outside the venue where some 5,500 Trump supporters gathered inside.

"Walking the line outside the Trump rally in Corinth, I was reminded that more unites us than divides us here in Mississippi," Colom said on X. "When I’m elected to the U.S. Senate, I’ll represent every Mississippian — whether you voted for me or not."

Democrats are contesting all three Republican-held House seats in Mississippi, but none is viewed as a likely pickup opportunity. A fourth seat, represented by US Representative Bennie Thompson in a heavily Black district, is considered safe for the Democrats. REUTERS

#35664. Kayhan opens fire on diplomacy, warns Iran risks losing leverage

As Iran hosted senior Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials for security talks on Monday, an influential hardline newspaper editor warned that the diplomatic initiative could undermine Tehran's position and relieve pressure on the United States.

Hossein Shariatmadari, editor of Kayhan daily and a longtime appointee of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, questioned the purpose of the gathering in an article headlined “Tehran summit: Oasis or mirage?”

His criticism extended even to Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and himself a prominent hardliner who opposed the nuclear diplomacy of former President Hassan Rouhani.

Bagheri had presented the meeting as an opportunity to develop a new regional security framework. Shariatmadari dismissed that prospect, arguing that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan were too close to the United States to credibly mediate between Tehran and Washington.

He accused the three countries of supporting US and Israeli military operations against Iran and questioned why Tehran would expect them to abandon their longstanding strategic ties with Washington.

Shariatmadari's central objection concerned Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August, committing themselves to collective defense. With Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensifying, Shariatmadari argued that cooperation with the three countries risked weakening Iran's support for the Yemeni group.

He described Iran, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias and Palestinian armed factions as “one spirit in several bodies,” arguing that confronting any of them amounted to confronting Iran itself.

Shariatmadari questioned whether the visiting delegations intended to pressure Tehran into distancing itself from the Houthis and insisted Iran would never abandon them.

Yet he also portrayed the diplomatic visit as evidence of Iranian strength, arguing that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had brought Washington and its allies close to economic suffocation and forced regional governments to seek relief through Tehran.

His argument exposed a tension in the hardline position: the arrival of foreign delegations was presented as proof that Iran's pressure was succeeding, while negotiations aimed at easing that pressure risked squandering the leverage it had created.

On Saturday, the hardline Paydari Front urged Iran to begin withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and reconsider its defense doctrine. Hardline lawmakers have also sought to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over his dealings with Washington.

These critics are closely tied to Iran's security establishment. Paydari Front leader Sadegh Mahsouli is a former Revolutionary Guards officer, while Shariatmadari represented the late supreme leader at Kayhan for decades.

Their criticism has continued even as President Masoud Pezeshkian and national security chief Mohsen Rezaei welcomed the visiting delegations. The four countries ended Monday's meeting with an agreement to continue discussions on regional peace and security.

The dispute exposes a growing divide within Iran's ruling establishment over what to do with the leverage created by months of confrontation.

Shariatmadari and like-minded hardliners believe that confrontation is working. In their view, diplomacy that requires Tehran to relinquish that leverage risks trading away the very gains it has produced.

An Iraqi court ordered the arrest of a provincial leader on Monday after he threatened road blockades and even separation from Iraq over the closure of a border crossing with Iran, revealing tensions over Baghdad's efforts to curb Tehran’s influence on Iraqi security decisions.

Mustafa Duair, head of the provincial council in Maysan, a southeastern governorate bordering Iran, threatened civil disobedience unless the Al Sheeb crossing was reopened.

Baghdad has cited technical problems for the closure, while Tehran has pointed to US pressure.

The Iran-aligned Badr Organization defended Duair, turning the dispute over a border crossing into a broader challenge to the central government's authority from within Iraq's Shiite political establishment.

In September, Iraqi authorities seized a drone launcher allegedly used to attack Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline. Saudi officials had traced the attack to the province, close to the Iranian border.

Asharq Al-Awsat reported Saturday that Iraqi officials suspected Israel had struck two depots storing Chinese-made portable air-defense systems allegedly supplied by Iran to allied Iraqi militias.

The reported shipments and Israeli involvement remain unconfirmed, but the allegations underscore the risks Baghdad faces when armed factions acquire weapons and pursue military agendas outside state control.

Ammar al-Hakim, a veteran leader with longstanding ties to Tehran, acknowledged sympathy for Iranians facing sanctions but warned in a September interview that Iraq must protect its own citizens from the same penalties.

“The feeling that the Islamic Republic has been treated unjustly under this siege of sanctions is valid and justified. But countries cannot be governed by wishes and emotions,” Hakim said.

On Monday, a spokesman for his Hikma Movement warned that breaking a militia de-escalation agreement could plunge Iraq into a “tunnel of sanctions.”

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has set June 2027 as the deadline for bringing armed factions under state authority, although some Iran-backed groups continue to resist.

He has also replaced several security chiefs since taking office in May. On Monday, Zaidi dismissed intelligence chief Hamid al-Shatri, who was appointed by his predecessor and had himself been considered for prime minister. No official explanation was given for his dismissal.

The push for greater state authority aligns with Washington's longstanding demands that Baghdad curb independent militias.

Zaidi has also sought closer economic and political ties with the United States, with more than $60 billion in commercial agreements and memorandums announced during his July visit to Washington.

But Zaidi still relies on a coalition that includes Iran-aligned parties. He insists Iraq will not become involved in the Iran war and wants Baghdad to act as a mediator, while acknowledging that disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has damaged Iraq's economy.

Iraq’s leaders are emphasizing national authority and economic interests over involvement in Tehran's confrontations, but the reaction to the Maysan border closure shows how difficult asserting that authority over Iran-aligned factions remains.

Hardliners in Tehran are hailing a surge in global oil prices as evidence that pressure on shipping is paying off, even as moderates warn that the same confrontation is inflicting mounting damage on Iran's economy and strengthening the case for a deal with Washington.

Crude prices rose above $116 a barrel on October 24 following reports of two attacks involving supertankers near Oman, prompting hardline newspaper Kayhan to portray the increase as vindication of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy's strategy of asymmetric pressure around the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the headline “Minefields near Musandam Prove Diplomacy Is Obsolete,” Kayhan argued that disruption to shipping and the resulting pressure on global energy markets had strengthened Iran's bargaining position rather than demonstrated the need for compromise.

The newspaper accused moderates and more pragmatic conservatives of “begging for an agreement,” singling out the centrist Sazandegi newspaper, which supports reaching a deal with the United States.

But the same confrontation is taking a growing toll on Iran's economy.

Moderate daily Shargh warned that higher crude prices offer little relief to private-sector manufacturers facing bankruptcy and argued that keeping negotiations with Washington alive is essential to Iran's economic survival.

The economic daily Donya-ye Eghtesad has also highlighted pressure on factories in industrial centers including Isfahan, Tabriz and Arak, reporting an unprecedented wave of corporate bankruptcies as the maritime blockade continues.

The competing assessments expose an increasingly important argument in Tehran: whether the economic disruption caused by the confrontation is leverage to be exploited or damage Iran can no longer afford.

The debate comes as signs of diplomatic movement feed cautious optimism among some Iranian political figures that an agreement with the United States may be becoming more likely than another round of war.

Former deputy parliamentary speaker Ali Motahari gave voice to that view on Monday, saying that for the first time in several weeks, the prospects of an agreement with Washington appeared greater than the likelihood of renewed conflict.

Speaking to reporters in Tehran, Motahari argued that war was becoming less likely because the United States was facing multiple problems and might therefore be prepared to accept some of Iran’s conditions.

Monday’s high-level talks with regional powers have added to that sense. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are in Tehran to meet national security chief Mohsen Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

According to Iranian state outlets, Tehran has reiterated its proposal for reducing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz. Following technical discussions in Doha, it resubmitted a plan to restore shipping through the waterway in stages over seven days.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iranian technical negotiators were examining US counterproposals on procedures for lifting the naval blockade.

Tehran insists the seven-day window will not begin until $24 billion in foreign reserves becomes fully accessible and restrictions on container clearance at Bandar Abbas are lifted.

Iran has also insisted that its seven-point de-escalation plan, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, remain separate from negotiations over uranium enrichment, International Atomic Energy Agency inspections and regional missile defense arrangements.

It remains unclear whether Washington accepts that separation. Tehran's position suggests it is seeking immediate economic relief while avoiding concessions on broader strategic issues.

The divide leaves Tehran confronting an awkward calculation. The disruption around Hormuz may be imposing higher costs on Iran's adversaries just as hardliners intended, but it is also increasing the economic pressure driving others in Tehran toward a deal.

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey opened talks with Iranian authorities in Tehran on Monday, following increased Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed warnings of military action between Tehran and Washington.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will travel to Tehran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing Saudi and Iranian officials.

Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, confirmed the visit.

The initiative was proposed during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials, according to a senior Iranian official.

Iranian media reported that officials told Munir they would not negotiate with Washington until Tehran's demands were met.

The visit marks the first high-level meeting between Iran and all three members of the Mecca defense pact since the escalation of hostilities.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the agreement in August, establishing that a military attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three.

Pakistan has ratified the pact, while ratification remains pending in Turkey's parliament.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to implement their defense commitments and rapidly deploy military personnel and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

The agreement faces its first significant test following increased Houthi attacks on Saudi territory.

Saudi Arabia announced on Sunday that it had intercepted another wave of missiles and drones.

The visit is intended to reduce hostilities and support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister for Public Diplomacy Raed bin Khalid Qarmali said earlier.

Qatari officials also visited Tehran on Sunday for talks with Iranian authorities.

Previous mediation by Qatar and Pakistan helped secure a temporary halt to hostilities, but the agreement collapsed when fighting resumed.

Indirect contacts between Tehran and Washington have continued through both mediators, a process also referenced by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran on Friday.

Iranian officials have warned that any further attack would trigger a stronger response.

The diplomatic meetings come as Saudi Arabia seeks to prevent the conflict from spreading to its critical infrastructure, putting the Mecca defense pact and regional mediation efforts under growing pressure.

Tehran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, Iran’s envoy to Pakistan said Saturday, while an IRGC-affiliated outlet rejected such an exchange and President Donald Trump raised the possibility of strikes as soon as “tomorrow.”

Iran’s ambassador to Islamabad, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran had conveyed through Pakistani mediators that it was prepared to reopen the strait if Washington ended its blockade of Iranian ports, the Associated Press reported.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, Moghadam said Iranian officials had communicated that position during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir. He accused Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade would continue.

Moghadam said Iran remained open to negotiations under a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in June, according to AP’s readout of his remarks.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker that framework, which envisaged restoring shipping through the strait, lifting the blockade and beginning negotiations on a broader deal covering Iran’s nuclear program.

Al Arabiya separately reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources, that Iran had informed Pakistan it was willing to resume negotiations with Washington and reopen the strait in exchange for the blockade being lifted.

But the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an informed source rejecting Al Arabiya’s account as “lies and fantasy” and saying Tehran had made no new proposal to Pakistani mediators.

“Iran fundamentally does not accept any equation of the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the blockade,” the source said, adding that Iran would find ways around the blockade and ultimately break it.

The source said Tehran stood by seven conditions already formally conveyed through mediators. An earlier “seven-day plan” setting out its demands for reopening the strait had been passed to Washington, the source said, adding that insecurity would persist until all Iranian demands were met, including an end to disruption of its ports and shipping.

Tasnim’s denial explicitly targeted Al Arabiya’s report, rather than the ambassador’s remarks reported by AP.

Trump, meanwhile, kept open the possibility of both military action and an agreement, saying he wanted a permanent solution to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” Trump told reporters Saturday. “There’s a possibility I will. There’s also a possibility we’ll have a nice big beautiful agreement.”

He said Iranian leaders wanted a deal but questioned whether they would abide by it.

“They want to make a deal. But the problem is, will they hold the deal?”

Trump argued that ending the military campaign after B-2 bomber strikes in 2025 would have allowed Iran to rebuild its nuclear capabilities and eventually develop a bomb.

“I’ve got to make it permanent. That’s the only reason I’m doing it as long as I’m doing,” he said.

The Hill reported Saturday, citing two sources familiar with the planning, that the US military had prepared options for renewed strikes on Iran after November’s midterm elections.

One source said US Central Command had follow-up strike plans ready pending White House authorization. Another said multiple options were being presented to War Secretary Pete Hegseth and that Trump would keep his options open until a final decision was required.

A Pentagon official told The Hill the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that US naval forces are preparing for possible renewed strikes against Iran, with sailors loading munitions and readying aircraft aboard American warships.

The preparations include the USS George Washington aircraft carrier strike group, as Washington considers further military action against the Islamic Republic.

Pakistan is mediating between Iran and the United States even as it sends troops to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Tehran’s allies, placing Islamabad in the conflicting roles of peace broker and military partner to Iran’s rivals.

On Tuesday, Pakistan's military chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran.

Munir has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, including meetings at the White House.

Islamabad helped broker the June agreement between Washington and Tehran. The truce did not last, but Pakistan has kept its mediation channel open.

Pakistan has taken a direct military role in Saudi Arabia's defense.

Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed approximately 8,000 troops, a squadron of fighter jets and air-defense systems to the kingdom under a bilateral agreement. Saudi Arabia financed the deployment, according to Pakistani officials cited by Reuters.

Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security deepened in August when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, treating an attack against one member as an attack against all.

This week, Islamabad announced that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed ratification, while Turkey's remained pending. The partners have also discussed further military mobilization following attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi territory.

On Wednesday, Pakistan signed another defense agreement, this time with Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia. The Badr agreement, signed in Doha, offers opportunities for industrial cooperation and defense production.

Together with Makkah, the agreements deepen Pakistan's military, diplomatic and economic ties across countries pursuing different regional agendas.

That tension was evident during Munir's Tehran visit. Pakistani government sources told Turkey's state-run Anadolu news agency that the talks focused more on stopping Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia than on reviving US-Iran negotiations.

Munir pressed Iranian leaders to use their influence over the Houthis, citing Pakistan's commitment to defend the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states supply much of Pakistan’s energy, while millions of Pakistani workers live in the region. Defense cooperation brings financial support and industrial opportunities, while diplomacy helps protect relations with competing partners.

Pakistan appears to be carving out an unusual role: mediating between Iran and the United States, helping defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, and joining new regional defense ventures while retaining direct access to Iranian leaders.

But the same network could become harder to manage if regional tensions escalate. The more security commitments Pakistan assumes, the greater the chance that relationships which currently give Islamabad leverage could eventually force it to choose between them.

#35665. 43 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

When the cool winds blow, we pine for apple desserts. You too? Welcome, friend. Whether they’re sweet or tart, cooked down to a sticky paste or gently warmed to keep their crisp bite, apples only need a little butter, some cinnamon sugar, and heat to shine. (And a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurts.)

With classic apple pie, buttery crisps, flaky pastries, and glazed apple fritters, this collection of apple dessert recipes makes the most of the season’s bounty. Some are simple enough for a weeknight; others are baking projects worth clearing an afternoon for.

We like firm apples for baking—favorites include Pink Lady, Honeycrisp, and Braeburn. They hold up well in pies, crisps, and cakes, while mixing sweet and tart apples can add complexity. Our guide to the best apples for baking has more advice on which varieties to choose. For peeling, follow the recipe: leaving the skins on adds color and texture, while removing them gives you a softer, more uniform filling.

Reducing fresh cider and the juices from the apples to a syrupy consistency concentrates their flavor and gives this mile-high pie its juicy, saucy filling. A buttery, flaky crust seals the deal.

This golden brown crumble topping looks impressive, but it’s way easier to make than a complicated lattice. And who wouldn’t want a little extra buttery crunch with their apple pie?

Apple pie and sharp cheddar are one of life’s great sweet-savory combinations. This recipe folds the cheese right into the buttery pastry, so you get a salty tang with every bite.

Before vanilla extract was widely available, says baker Cheryl Day, rose water was one of the most popular flavorings in American baking. This apple pie revives that lovely floral pairing.

A little cream cheese makes the pie dough more malleable so that you can arrange your lattice to perfection without worrying too much about overhandling.

Why choose between apple pie and apple crumble? This Dutch-style pie combines a tender apple filling and flaky bottom crust with a generous layer of cinnamon-spiked streusel.

This make-ahead apple cobbler is great for busy mornings—or for dinner parties, when there are a lot of other things to maneuver in and out of the oven. A dollop of yogurt or softly whipped cream wouldn’t be out of place.

A combination of apples gives this classic crumble the best of both worlds: Some soften into a jammy filling; others keep their shape. On top, buttery crumbs bake into golden, craggy clusters. Serve warm, preferably with vanilla ice cream.

No room in the oven? No problem. This stovetop crisp gets its buttery, golden topping from a separately prepared streusel. It’s a clever way to get the contrast of tender fruit and crunchy crumbs without baking the whole dessert.

Apples run throughout this tender vanilla cake, while a generous cinnamon streusel topping brings buttery crunch to every slice. It’s the kind of cake you can leave on the counter and cut yourself another square of whenever the mood strikes.

Usually, when cake emerges, that signals the party is ending soon. But with six layers of spice cake and an orchard’s worth of apple butter, this apple dessert IS the party.

Caramelized apples meet dark molasses, fresh ginger, and warm spices in this richly flavored cake. The fruit forms a glossy topping when you turn it out of the pan. A little cream alongside is all it needs.

This hand-mixed cake is packed with chopped apples and topped with cinnamon sugar and toasted walnuts. Sour cream keeps the crumb tender, while a splash of apple cider vinegar adds a subtle tang.

This recipe gives traditional apple cake the sticky toffee pudding treatment. A rich, silky toffee sauce makes it especially tempting served warm.

Claire Saffitz’s upside-down apple cake has a dramatic presentation, with glossy, caramelized apple halves nestled into a walnut-rich sponge. Her trick for getting the neatest, prettiest apple halves? Use a melon baller to scoop out the cores.

Sticky-sweet monkey bread transports you right back to childhood. This version doubles down on the nostalgia with the caramel-apple flavors of a county fair.

Grated apples keep this dairy-free olive oil cake moist and tender, while cinnamon, cardamom, ginger, and black pepper bring the spice. It’s equally welcome at dessert or with an afternoon cup of tea.

You need little more than a bowl and baking dish for this tender apple cake. The caramel sauce comes together in a small skillet, making this a decidedly low-fuss way to get your caramel-apple fix.

The secret to this gorgeous cake’s neat rows of apples is the Hasselback method: Thin, parallel cuts let the fruit fan out as it bakes while keeping each quarter intact.

Homemade apple butter brings concentrated fruit flavor to this warmly spiced loaf cake, while a cinnamon crumble adds a little crunch. It’s just the thing to bring to a new neighbor—or keep on the counter for yourself.

A mixture of all-purpose and rye flours gives this apple cake an earthy, nutty flavor and deep copper hue. Hazelnuts double down on the toastiness, making it especially good alongside coffee or tea.

Sumac brings a citrusy fragrance to this apple loaf cake, while spelt flour adds a delicate nuttiness. The unexpected combination adds a little intrigue to a familiar fall bake.

Tarte Tatin is a French classic for good reason: Caramelized apples, buttery pastry, and a dramatic flip at the finish. This version uses frozen puff pastry, saving you the trouble of making dough from scratch.

Tart cranberries turn this Tatin variation a beautiful rosy pink. It’s a Thanksgiving showstopper if you want something other than the usual pumpkin or pecan pie.

This free-form galette wraps a buttery crust around sliced apples, and you can make it your own with warming spices, citrus zest, or a little black pepper. See our extra-flaky pastry dough for the foundation (or use a store-bought crust, we won’t tell).

Apples on the bottom of this tart steam and soften as they bake, while the fruit on top holds its shape. The result is a beautiful contrast of tender and slightly firmer apples in every bite.

Think apple pie with the fruit turned all the way up. This tart layers apples over an exceptionally flaky crust with a glossy finish that makes it look every bit as good as it tastes.

This French apple tart doubles down on the fruit with thinly sliced apples layered over Calvados-spiked applesauce. A dollop of apple-brandy-flavored whipped cream makes it feel especially dinner-party-worthy.

This traditional German Christmas apple “cake” holds a sweet-tart fruit filling in tender pastry and finishes it with a lemon glaze. Fresh cranberries replace the usual raisins, giving the holiday bake a welcome pop of tartness.

Frozen puff pastry does the heavy lifting in this easy dessert recipe. Add fresh apples and your favorite nut butter, and you’ve got a dessert made largely from things you may already have on hand.

Take a cue from legendary Southern chef Edna Lewis and use dried apples for the filling. Rehydrated in apple cider, they develop a concentrated flavor and rich, jammy texture that works beautifully inside golden fried pastry.

Thinly sliced apples baked with maple syrup, vanilla, and bourbon make a luxurious filling for layers of flaky puff pastry and softly whipped cream.

Store-bought phyllo pastry makes strudel’s delicate, flaky layers possible without the elaborate dough-stretching of traditional versions. Serve warm with coffee or tea and perhaps a spoonful of whipped cream.

These golden fried treats, courtesy of BA Bake Club, have ricotta in the batter for a tender crumb and juicy apple chunks throughout. They’re the perfect treat after an afternoon of apple picking.

Cheez-Its in dessert? Trust us on this one. The crackers give bars a toasty, buttery, salty edge that makes the sweet filling taste even better. Your guests don’t need to know the secret ingredient.

Somewhere between a custard and a pancake, this clafoutis bakes up tender around slices of tart apple. An easy brown sugar toffee sauce adds buttery richness, making it taste more indulgent than its simple preparation suggests.

Pandowdy is fun to say, and it’s even more fun to eat. Top sliced-and-spiced apples with puff pastry shingles, then bake until the crust is golden and the apples soft and bubbling.

Caramelized apples tucked into crisp, buttery phyllo shells make these individual pastries feel especially dinner-party-worthy. They’re excellent on their own, but a scoop of brown sugar–bourbon ice cream takes them over the top.

Whole apples stuffed with an almond, prune, and amaretto filling bake until tender, then get a shower of caramelized almonds. Pour the cream over at the table for a little extra drama.

A thin layer of caramelized sugar on the surface of these apples mimics the crackle of crème brûlée. Finally, a good reason to poach fruit.

Think of these baked apples as individual apple crisps, with tender fruit and a hearty oat topping studded with dried cherries, pecans, and seeds. They’re particularly good warm from the oven, with a little cream or yogurt.

#35668. Princess Anne begins her official visit to Hong Kong in 1971 – from the SCMP archive

On this day 55 years ago, Princess Anne received a warm welcome to British Hong Kong, sailing Victoria Harbour to kick off her royal tour

This article was first published on October 27, 1971.

Princess Anne, radiant in a stylish knee-length beige suit and a matching wide-brimmed hat, flew in yesterday (October 26, 1971) to a warm welcome from the people of Hong Kong.

She begins her official visits today (October 27, 1971) – a public holiday – when thousands of people will be able to see her during her calls at places like the Tung Wah Hospital, the Po Leung Kuk and the ancient Man Mo Temple.

The Princess, who has heard a lot about this “Pearl of the Orient” from her father, will do a little sightseeing, and perhaps a little shopping too in Sheung Wan, a district which boasts a history almost as long as that of the Colony itself.

#35670. Russia, Ukraine begin localised ceasefire to allow for humanitarian operation in Oleshky

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

A drone image shows destroyed vehicles sitting on a street in Oleshky, Kherson Region.

KYIV – Russia and Ukraine have started a localised ceasefire to allow for a humanitarian operation to begin in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, both sides said on Oct 27.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Telegram that it stopped shelling in the direction of the Ukrainian city of Kherson from 4am Moscow time (9am Singapore time) to prepare for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, just across the Dnipro River from Kherson.

Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s Parliament commissioner for human rights, confirmed in a Facebook post that the ceasefire has started at the same time.

“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,” he wrote.

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a localised ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, an arrangement that will enable aid deliveries and allow evacuations from a front-line town suffering acute shortages of food and medicine.

Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine’s southern region of Kherson, opposite the city of Kherson, which is held by Ukrainian forces.

Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since. The White House said earlier in October that US First Lady Melania Trump helped to secure the Oleshky ceasefire.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, a Russian missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Oct 26 killed at least one person and injured 10, including students at a dormitory, with the attacks also killing and injuring people in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.

New explosions were heard on the morning of Oct 27 in Kyiv, a Reuters witness said. REUTERS

#35671. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Doku Kumaş Tasarım Yarışması Gaziantep’te gerçekleştirilen final gecesiyle tamamlandı. Tekstil sektörüne yeni yetenekler kazandırmak ve katma değeri yüksek üretimi teşvik etmek amacıyla düzenlenen yarışmada üç kategoride dereceye giren dokuz tasarımcı ile Sürdürülebilirlik Özel Ödülü’nün sahibi belirlendi. Final defilesinde sergilenen 60 kıyafet, gençlerin özgün tasarımlarını sektörün üretim gücüyle buluşturdu. Güneydoğu Anadolu İhracatçı Birlikleri Koordinatör Başkanı Mete Akcan, küresel tekstil sektöründe rekabetin artık yalnızca üretim kapasitesi ve fiyat üzerinden şekillenmediğini, tasarım, inovasyon ve sürdürülebilirliğin giderek daha fazla önem kazandığını söyledi. ‘Daha ileriye taşıyacağız’ Törende konuşan Akcan, “Burada ortaya çıkan her çalışma, tekstil sektörümüzün yenilikçi ve katma değerli ihracat vizyonunun bir parçası. Gençlerimizin uluslararası pazarlarda fark yaratacak tasarımlara imza atacağına inanıyorum” dedi. Bölge ihracatında tekstilin bu yılın 10 ayında yüzde 10’un üzerinde yükselmesine rağmen üretimde sıkıntılar bulunduğunu belirten Akcan, “Bazı şirketler ihracatını yüzde 50’ye kadar çıkardı. İç piyasa daraldı. Tekstil sektörünün en kötü tarafı konfeksiyon. Ama genelde hammadde üretiyoruz ve tedarik avantajımız sayesinde rekabet ettiğimiz ülkelere de mal satabiliyoruz” dedi. 60 kıyafetlik final defilesi Toplam 2 milyon 950 bin TL ödülün dağıtıldığı yarışmada dokuma, baskı ve örme kategorilerinin her birinde birinciye 400 bin TL, ikinciye 300 bin TL, üçüncüye ise 200 bin TL ödül verildi. Sürdürülebilirlik Özel Ödülü’nü alan tasarımcıya da 250 bin TL verildi. Kategori birincileri, T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığının uygun görmesi ve ilgili mevzuat hükümlerinin karşılanması hâlinde bir yıl süreyle yurt dışında eğitim alma imkânından yararlanabilecek. ‘Mısıra giden pişman’ Mısır’ın iş gücü açısından Türkiye ile karşılaştırıldığında üçte bir düzeyinde maliyetinin olduğunu ifade eden Akcan, “Buna rağmen büyük sıkıntılar yaşanıyor. İş gücü Türkiye’deki gibi verimli değil, sıkıntılar çıkıyor. Ben şahsen Mısır’a üretime gitmem. Gidenlerden de sürekli bir şikayet duyuyoruz” ifadelerini kullandı. ABD-İran savaşının etkilerine değinen Akcan, savaşın herkese olumsuz bir yansıması olduğunu, bu durumun fiyat tutturmayı zorlaştırdığını kaydetti. Petrol fiyatları konusunda Akcan, “O hem enflasyon tarafında bizi yoruyor. Nakliye maliyetleri artıyor, araç bulamıyorsun ya da konteyner bulmakta zorlanıyorsunuz” diye konuştu. Bu yıl bölgeden kuru meyve ihracatında yüzde 22.9’luk bir gerileme olduğu sorusu üzerine Akcan, “Bu kayıp önceki yıl yaşadığımız geniş çahlı don vakasının bir sonucu. Ancak yıl sonuna kadar bir toparanma bekliyoruz” ifadelerini kullandı.

#35674. ZTE up 7% after AI pivot, computing surge drive fivefold increase in third quarter profit

For the first nine months, computing-related revenue surged over 70 per cent, accounting for 38 per cent of total sales

Shares in ZTE rose as much as 7 per cent in Hong Kong on Tuesday morning after the Chinese telecommunications equipment maker posted a nearly fivefold jump in third-quarter profit, driven by rapid expansion in its computing infrastructure and overseas operations.

Net profit attributable to shareholders reached 1.31 billion yuan (US$196.3 million) for the three months ended September 30, up 395 per cent from a year earlier, according to an exchange filing released on Monday evening. Revenue climbed 34 per cent to 38.81 billion yuan over the same period.

#35675. ​Trump enemy and former FBI chief James Comey charged for third time

Updated October 27, 2026 — 9:30am,first published 9:02am

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Washington: The US Department of Justice has charged former FBI director James Comey with leaking national defence information, marking the third time the political enemy of President Donald Trump has been charged in the past 13 months.

The charges, unsealed on Monday (US time), accuse Comey with directing an individual, “through one and more co-conspirators”, to disclose national defence information to a reporter at a national news publication in 2016, while he was FBI director.

Comey already faces charges over an Instagram photograph he posted showing seashells on a beach arranged to spell “86 47”. This was alleged to be a death threat against Trump because “86” in restaurant parlance means to get rid of something. It has also sometimes been appropriated as a mob term.

Last year, Comey was indicted on charges of making false statements to a 2020 Senate hearing and obstructing a congressional investigation. But that case was thrown out by a judge who found that the prosecutor bringing the case, Trump’s former personal lawyer Lindsey Halligan, was illegally appointed.

On Monday, Comey reacted to the latest charges with a video he posted on Instagram. “Well, they’re back – again,” he said.

“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.

“Nothing’s changed with me, I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.

“The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It’s really important that we stand straight, and keep the faith in America.”

Court documents show the charges were filed exactly 10 years after the alleged leak took place – which appears to be the last possible day before the statute of limitations on the offence would expire.

The document was signed by Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, who was appointed to the role by attorney-general Todd Blanche in April. Blanche is another of Trump’s former lawyers.

The Justice Department said it filed a waiverless criminal information to stop the clock on the statute of limitations. That means the defendant, Comey, has not waived their right to be charged by a grand jury. “This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” the department said.

Comey’s lawyer Patrick Fitzgerald said the accusation related to a New York Times article from October 2016 – the circumstances of which have been investigated previously, by two different prosecution teams, and did not result in charges.

“Now, 10 years after the article was published, the government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury,” Fitzgerald said. “It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”

Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer

The charges were unsealed on the same day that a judge in New York ruled Trump’s Justice Department had unlawfully fired Comey’s eldest daughter, Maurene Comey, in July 2025.

The younger Comey was a prosecutor in the Manhattan US Attorney’s office who brought criminal cases against Jeffrey Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs.

She successfully argued that she was sacked because of who her father was, in violation of federal laws prohibiting firing civil servants for political reasons and guaranteeing federal employees due process in employment disputes.

Trump’s hatred of Comey stems from the former FBI director authorising an investigation into alleged links between the president’s 2016 campaign and the Russian government, which Trump routinely refers to as the “Russia, Russia, Russia hoax”.

#35676. Iraq orders arrest of provincial leader amid tensions over Iran ties

An Iraqi court ordered the arrest of a provincial leader on Monday after he threatened road blockades and even separation from Iraq over the closure of a border crossing with Iran, revealing tensions over Baghdad's efforts to curb Tehran’s influence on Iraqi security decisions.

Mustafa Duair, head of the provincial council in Maysan, a southeastern governorate bordering Iran, threatened civil disobedience unless the Al Sheeb crossing was reopened.

Baghdad has cited technical problems for the closure, while Tehran has pointed to US pressure.

The Iran-aligned Badr Organization defended Duair, turning the dispute over a border crossing into a broader challenge to the central government's authority from within Iraq's Shiite political establishment.

In September, Iraqi authorities seized a drone launcher allegedly used to attack Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline. Saudi officials had traced the attack to the province, close to the Iranian border.

Asharq Al-Awsat reported Saturday that Iraqi officials suspected Israel had struck two depots storing Chinese-made portable air-defense systems allegedly supplied by Iran to allied Iraqi militias.

The reported shipments and Israeli involvement remain unconfirmed, but the allegations underscore the risks Baghdad faces when armed factions acquire weapons and pursue military agendas outside state control.

Ammar al-Hakim, a veteran leader with longstanding ties to Tehran, acknowledged sympathy for Iranians facing sanctions but warned in a September interview that Iraq must protect its own citizens from the same penalties.

“The feeling that the Islamic Republic has been treated unjustly under this siege of sanctions is valid and justified. But countries cannot be governed by wishes and emotions,” Hakim said.

On Monday, a spokesman for his Hikma Movement warned that breaking a militia de-escalation agreement could plunge Iraq into a “tunnel of sanctions.”

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has set June 2027 as the deadline for bringing armed factions under state authority, although some Iran-backed groups continue to resist.

He has also replaced several security chiefs since taking office in May. On Monday, Zaidi dismissed intelligence chief Hamid al-Shatri, who was appointed by his predecessor and had himself been considered for prime minister. No official explanation was given for his dismissal.

The push for greater state authority aligns with Washington's longstanding demands that Baghdad curb independent militias.

Zaidi has also sought closer economic and political ties with the United States, with more than $60 billion in commercial agreements and memorandums announced during his July visit to Washington.

But Zaidi still relies on a coalition that includes Iran-aligned parties. He insists Iraq will not become involved in the Iran war and wants Baghdad to act as a mediator, while acknowledging that disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has damaged Iraq's economy.

Iraq’s leaders are emphasizing national authority and economic interests over involvement in Tehran's confrontations, but the reaction to the Maysan border closure shows how difficult asserting that authority over Iran-aligned factions remains.

Hardliners in Tehran are hailing a surge in global oil prices as evidence that pressure on shipping is paying off, even as moderates warn that the same confrontation is inflicting mounting damage on Iran's economy and strengthening the case for a deal with Washington.

Crude prices rose above $116 a barrel on October 24 following reports of two attacks involving supertankers near Oman, prompting hardline newspaper Kayhan to portray the increase as vindication of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy's strategy of asymmetric pressure around the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the headline “Minefields near Musandam Prove Diplomacy Is Obsolete,” Kayhan argued that disruption to shipping and the resulting pressure on global energy markets had strengthened Iran's bargaining position rather than demonstrated the need for compromise.

The newspaper accused moderates and more pragmatic conservatives of “begging for an agreement,” singling out the centrist Sazandegi newspaper, which supports reaching a deal with the United States.

But the same confrontation is taking a growing toll on Iran's economy.

Moderate daily Shargh warned that higher crude prices offer little relief to private-sector manufacturers facing bankruptcy and argued that keeping negotiations with Washington alive is essential to Iran's economic survival.

The economic daily Donya-ye Eghtesad has also highlighted pressure on factories in industrial centers including Isfahan, Tabriz and Arak, reporting an unprecedented wave of corporate bankruptcies as the maritime blockade continues.

The competing assessments expose an increasingly important argument in Tehran: whether the economic disruption caused by the confrontation is leverage to be exploited or damage Iran can no longer afford.

The debate comes as signs of diplomatic movement feed cautious optimism among some Iranian political figures that an agreement with the United States may be becoming more likely than another round of war.

Former deputy parliamentary speaker Ali Motahari gave voice to that view on Monday, saying that for the first time in several weeks, the prospects of an agreement with Washington appeared greater than the likelihood of renewed conflict.

Speaking to reporters in Tehran, Motahari argued that war was becoming less likely because the United States was facing multiple problems and might therefore be prepared to accept some of Iran’s conditions.

Monday’s high-level talks with regional powers have added to that sense. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are in Tehran to meet national security chief Mohsen Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

According to Iranian state outlets, Tehran has reiterated its proposal for reducing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz. Following technical discussions in Doha, it resubmitted a plan to restore shipping through the waterway in stages over seven days.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iranian technical negotiators were examining US counterproposals on procedures for lifting the naval blockade.

Tehran insists the seven-day window will not begin until $24 billion in foreign reserves becomes fully accessible and restrictions on container clearance at Bandar Abbas are lifted.

Iran has also insisted that its seven-point de-escalation plan, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, remain separate from negotiations over uranium enrichment, International Atomic Energy Agency inspections and regional missile defense arrangements.

It remains unclear whether Washington accepts that separation. Tehran's position suggests it is seeking immediate economic relief while avoiding concessions on broader strategic issues.

The divide leaves Tehran confronting an awkward calculation. The disruption around Hormuz may be imposing higher costs on Iran's adversaries just as hardliners intended, but it is also increasing the economic pressure driving others in Tehran toward a deal.

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey opened talks with Iranian authorities in Tehran on Monday, following increased Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed warnings of military action between Tehran and Washington.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will travel to Tehran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing Saudi and Iranian officials.

Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, confirmed the visit.

The initiative was proposed during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials, according to a senior Iranian official.

Iranian media reported that officials told Munir they would not negotiate with Washington until Tehran's demands were met.

The visit marks the first high-level meeting between Iran and all three members of the Mecca defense pact since the escalation of hostilities.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the agreement in August, establishing that a military attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three.

Pakistan has ratified the pact, while ratification remains pending in Turkey's parliament.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to implement their defense commitments and rapidly deploy military personnel and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

The agreement faces its first significant test following increased Houthi attacks on Saudi territory.

Saudi Arabia announced on Sunday that it had intercepted another wave of missiles and drones.

The visit is intended to reduce hostilities and support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister for Public Diplomacy Raed bin Khalid Qarmali said earlier.

Qatari officials also visited Tehran on Sunday for talks with Iranian authorities.

Previous mediation by Qatar and Pakistan helped secure a temporary halt to hostilities, but the agreement collapsed when fighting resumed.

Indirect contacts between Tehran and Washington have continued through both mediators, a process also referenced by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran on Friday.

Iranian officials have warned that any further attack would trigger a stronger response.

The diplomatic meetings come as Saudi Arabia seeks to prevent the conflict from spreading to its critical infrastructure, putting the Mecca defense pact and regional mediation efforts under growing pressure.

Tehran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, Iran’s envoy to Pakistan said Saturday, while an IRGC-affiliated outlet rejected such an exchange and President Donald Trump raised the possibility of strikes as soon as “tomorrow.”

Iran’s ambassador to Islamabad, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran had conveyed through Pakistani mediators that it was prepared to reopen the strait if Washington ended its blockade of Iranian ports, the Associated Press reported.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, Moghadam said Iranian officials had communicated that position during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir. He accused Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade would continue.

Moghadam said Iran remained open to negotiations under a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in June, according to AP’s readout of his remarks.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker that framework, which envisaged restoring shipping through the strait, lifting the blockade and beginning negotiations on a broader deal covering Iran’s nuclear program.

Al Arabiya separately reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources, that Iran had informed Pakistan it was willing to resume negotiations with Washington and reopen the strait in exchange for the blockade being lifted.

But the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an informed source rejecting Al Arabiya’s account as “lies and fantasy” and saying Tehran had made no new proposal to Pakistani mediators.

“Iran fundamentally does not accept any equation of the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the blockade,” the source said, adding that Iran would find ways around the blockade and ultimately break it.

The source said Tehran stood by seven conditions already formally conveyed through mediators. An earlier “seven-day plan” setting out its demands for reopening the strait had been passed to Washington, the source said, adding that insecurity would persist until all Iranian demands were met, including an end to disruption of its ports and shipping.

Tasnim’s denial explicitly targeted Al Arabiya’s report, rather than the ambassador’s remarks reported by AP.

Trump, meanwhile, kept open the possibility of both military action and an agreement, saying he wanted a permanent solution to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” Trump told reporters Saturday. “There’s a possibility I will. There’s also a possibility we’ll have a nice big beautiful agreement.”

He said Iranian leaders wanted a deal but questioned whether they would abide by it.

“They want to make a deal. But the problem is, will they hold the deal?”

Trump argued that ending the military campaign after B-2 bomber strikes in 2025 would have allowed Iran to rebuild its nuclear capabilities and eventually develop a bomb.

“I’ve got to make it permanent. That’s the only reason I’m doing it as long as I’m doing,” he said.

The Hill reported Saturday, citing two sources familiar with the planning, that the US military had prepared options for renewed strikes on Iran after November’s midterm elections.

One source said US Central Command had follow-up strike plans ready pending White House authorization. Another said multiple options were being presented to War Secretary Pete Hegseth and that Trump would keep his options open until a final decision was required.

A Pentagon official told The Hill the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that US naval forces are preparing for possible renewed strikes against Iran, with sailors loading munitions and readying aircraft aboard American warships.

The preparations include the USS George Washington aircraft carrier strike group, as Washington considers further military action against the Islamic Republic.

Pakistan is mediating between Iran and the United States even as it sends troops to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Tehran’s allies, placing Islamabad in the conflicting roles of peace broker and military partner to Iran’s rivals.

On Tuesday, Pakistan's military chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran.

Munir has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, including meetings at the White House.

Islamabad helped broker the June agreement between Washington and Tehran. The truce did not last, but Pakistan has kept its mediation channel open.

Pakistan has taken a direct military role in Saudi Arabia's defense.

Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed approximately 8,000 troops, a squadron of fighter jets and air-defense systems to the kingdom under a bilateral agreement. Saudi Arabia financed the deployment, according to Pakistani officials cited by Reuters.

Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security deepened in August when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, treating an attack against one member as an attack against all.

This week, Islamabad announced that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed ratification, while Turkey's remained pending. The partners have also discussed further military mobilization following attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi territory.

On Wednesday, Pakistan signed another defense agreement, this time with Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia. The Badr agreement, signed in Doha, offers opportunities for industrial cooperation and defense production.

Together with Makkah, the agreements deepen Pakistan's military, diplomatic and economic ties across countries pursuing different regional agendas.

That tension was evident during Munir's Tehran visit. Pakistani government sources told Turkey's state-run Anadolu news agency that the talks focused more on stopping Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia than on reviving US-Iran negotiations.

Munir pressed Iranian leaders to use their influence over the Houthis, citing Pakistan's commitment to defend the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states supply much of Pakistan’s energy, while millions of Pakistani workers live in the region. Defense cooperation brings financial support and industrial opportunities, while diplomacy helps protect relations with competing partners.

Pakistan appears to be carving out an unusual role: mediating between Iran and the United States, helping defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, and joining new regional defense ventures while retaining direct access to Iranian leaders.

But the same network could become harder to manage if regional tensions escalate. The more security commitments Pakistan assumes, the greater the chance that relationships which currently give Islamabad leverage could eventually force it to choose between them.

China regards its relationship with Iran as largely transactional and is not firmly committed to defending the current Iranian government, according to Tong Zhao, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Speaking to Iran International, Zhao said Beijing shares Iran’s “common displeasure” with the United States and Western systems and values Iran’s geographic position for the Belt and Road Initiative.

Yet he described the partnership as driven by energy security, economic interests and longer-term geopolitical calculations rather than ideological solidarity.

“There is some long-term interest in there for sure,” Zhao said. “But it is a transactional relationship.”

China has become Iran's main economic lifeline under US sanctions, buying nearly all of its exported oil, while Tehran has increasingly looked to Beijing alongside Moscow for diplomatic support in the face of Western pressure.

Energy security has provided one of the clearest illustrations of the limits of that partnership.

In a recent meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, both sides publicly underscored that the Strait of Hormuz should remain open without any toll system.

“China is protecting its own economic and energy interest first and foremost,” Zhao said. “We do see China’s position evolving when its own domestic calculations about energy and overall supply chain security change over time.”

The 25-year comprehensive strategic partnership signed by China and Iran in 2021 has also under-delivered. Reports at the time suggested Chinese investment of roughly $400 billion, or about $20 billion annually.

Actual flows have been “at least one order of magnitude smaller,” Zhao said, as Chinese banks and companies have sought to avoid US secondary sanctions.

Zhao said Beijing has come to value nuclear non-proliferation more as its global influence has grown, in part because of its experience with North Korea.

“China doesn’t want Iran to have nuclear weapons, but China eventually is sympathetic to Iran’s cause,” he said. “It thinks that Iran’s need for deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is ultimately driven by American hostile policy.”

Beijing does not see its role as changing Iran’s calculations and has been reluctant to threaten economic or military cutoffs, Zhao said. Instead, it has emphasized that the US and Israel should alter their policies to reduce Tehran’s incentives for nuclear deterrence.

Opposition to externally imposed regime change is a higher priority for Beijing than the nuclear file itself, he said.

“China’s primary security concern is its own regime security, so it doesn’t want to see the norm of allowing foreign countries interfering in other countries’ internal affairs and toppling governments that they don’t like.”

Beijing’s initial criticism of the US-Israeli war against Iran focused heavily on the killing of the supreme leader, which China viewed as a violation of international norms.

But Zhao suggested Beijing's opposition had limits and would depend in part on whether efforts to remove Iran's government violated what China regarded as established international norms.

Beijing has cultivated ties with Saudi Arabia, including joint military exercises and involvement in its missile and nuclear programs, partly as a hedge against uncertainty elsewhere in the region.

China and Russia have meanwhile provided Tehran with diplomatic cover at the UN Security Council, disputing the reimposition of UN sanctions on Iran and most recently opposing efforts to restore international monitoring of their implementation.

Yet China has shown little appetite for becoming a security guarantor for Iran or other regional partners, Zhao said, including through proposals that Iran transfer enriched uranium to Chinese custody.

“China is keenly aware of the potential risks and burdens to play a greater security role,” he said. “Its approach is to develop relations, increasing Chinese influence at the lowest cost.”

That calculation could change as the conflict develops. Zhao said China and Russia could influence its trajectory by supplying air-defense systems or missile-related materials that would help Iran deter or survive future strikes.

But he declined to predict how the confrontation over Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz would ultimately end.

“I generally don’t have good answers about how this war will end in the long run,” Zhao said.

#35679. Otomotivde Bursa’ya 300 milyon dolar daha

Sanayi ve Teknoloji Bakanı Mehmet Fatih Kacır, “Gerek ana sanayide gerekse tedarik zincirinde oluşturduğu katma değer, sağladığı nitelikli istihdam ve ulaştığı ihracat hacmiyle otomotiv sektörümüz, Türk sanayisinin yüz akı olmaya devam ediyor” dedi. Koç Topluluğu ve Stellantis işbirliğiyle Bursa’da hayata geçirilen 300 milyon dolarlık TOFAŞ K9 Projesi’nde üretim başladı. Fabrikadaki törende konuşan Bakan Kacır, projeyle Stellantis çatısındaki markaların hafif ticari araçları ile yolcu taşımacılığına yönelik Combi versiyonlarının Bursa’da üretileceğini söyledi. Kacır, “K9 Projesi, TOFAŞ’a yıllık 100 bin araçlık ilave üretim kapasitesi kazandırırken 1000 çalışma arkadaşımıza da yeni istihdam sunacak” dedi. Üretim sürecine 100’e yakın yerli tedarikçinin katılacağını belirten Kacır, çoklu enerji platformuna uygun kurulan hattın gelecekte elektrikli hafif ticari araçların Bursa’da üretilmesinin önünü açacağını vurguladı. Doblo geri döndü 2000 yılında Bursa’da üretim yolculuğuna başlayan Doblo’nun Stellantis ailesinin diğer modelleriyle birlikte ‘doğduğu topraklara’ döndüğünü ifade eden Kacır, “300 milyon dolarlık yatırımla hayata geçirilen K9 Projesi, TOFAŞ’ın üretim yolculuğunda yeni bir dönemin kapılarını aralıyor” diye konuştu. 41,5 milyar dolarla rekor Otomotiv sektörünün geçen yıl 41.5 milyar dolarlık ihracatla rekor tazelediğini hatırlatan Bakan Kacır, son 23 yılda otomotiv ana ve yan sanayisinin 1 trilyon 600 milyar lira büyüklüğündeki 3 bin 857 projesinin yatırım teşvikleriyle desteklendiğini söyledi. Kacır, elektrikli ve sürücüsüz araçlar, yapay zeka ve yazılım yatırımlarına desteklerin süreceğini belirterek, alınacak tedbirlerle otomotiv pazarının yılda 2 milyonu aşmasını hedeflediklerini kaydetti. Koç Ailesi’ne Gazze teşekkürü TBMM Sanayi, Ticaret, Enerji, Tabii Kaynaklar, Bilgi ve Teknoloji Komisyonu Başkanı ve AK Parti Bursa Milletvekili Mustafa Varank, TOFAŞ Bursa Fabrikası’nda düzenlenen K9 Projesi Üretim Başlangıç Töreni’ne katıldı. Burada bir konuşma yapan Varank, İsrail’in soykırımcı politikalarını eleştirmeleri ve Gazze’ye yönelik insani yardım hassasiyetleri nedeniyle Koç Ailesi’ne teşekkür etti. Koç Holding Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Ömer Koç’un İsrail rejiminin işlediği insanlık dışı suçlarda “ikiyüzlü batı politikaları”nın etkisi olduğunu yönündeki açıklamalarını hatırlatan Varank, “Globalde bu kadar iş yapabilen bir şirket sahibinin siyonist lobiden çekinmeden cesurca bu açıklamaları yapabilmesi takdire şayandır. Ben kendisine çok teşekkür ediyorum” dedi. Varank, Ali Koç’un da hakkını teslim etmesi gerektiğini kaydederek, “Kendisine dedim ki ‘Bize Gazze’ye gönderilecek ambulanslar lazım’. Aynen şu cümleyi kurdu. ‘Devletimizin kaç tane ambulansa ihtiyacı varsa Gazze’ye göndermek için ben hepsini vermeye hazırım. Yeter ki devletimiz bana söylesin.’ Bu iki hakkı bu kürsüden teslim etmem lazım” ifadelerini kullandı. ‘Yeni modeller için görüşüyoruz’ Koç Holding Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Ömer Koç, otomotiv sektöründe kuralların tüm dünyada yeniden yazıldığını belirterek, “Ülkemize çekebildiğimiz her yatırımın son derece kıymetli olduğu kanaatindeyim” dedi.Stellantis’in Türkiye’deki tüm faaliyetlerinin 2025 itibarıyla TOFAŞ’ın yönetimine devredilmesinin ve alınan ortak yatırım kararlarının iki ortağın şirkete inancının en güçlü göstergesi olduğunu ifade eden Ömer Koç, son 5 yılda TOFAŞ’ın yatırımlarının 1 milyar dolara ulaştığını söyledi. Koç, “Bu yatırımın yarısı Ar-Ge ve inovasyon çalışmalarımıza yönelik” dedi. 150 bin üretim hedefi TOFAŞ’ın yarım asırda 7.5 milyon araç ürettiğini hatırlatan Koç, yeni model yatırımlarının da sürdüğünü belirterek, “K0 başarıyla devreye alındı. K9 modelimiz de sizlerin huzuruna çıkacak. 300 milyon dolar yatırım yaptığımız K9 projesi kapsamında yıllık 150 bin üretim hedefleniyor” diye konuştu. K9’un Türkiye’nin Avrupa’daki ticari araç üretim liderliğini güçlendireceğini vurgulayan Koç, “TOFAŞ’ın yetkinliklerini ve kapasitesini azami şekilde kullanıp müşterilerimize daha fazla yerli model sunabilmeyi, böylece memleketimizin cari dengesine de katkı sağlamayı hedefliyoruz” dedi. Koç, yeni yatırımların süreceğinin de sinyalini vererek, “Başka yeni modeller konusunda ortağımızla görüşmeleri sürdürüyoruz” ifadesini kullandı.

#35685. Australia is approaching American levels of anger. Here’s how we defuse the bomb

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
