You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Francis Fukuyama didn’t get annoyed with me for accusing him of being almost unAmerican. Probably the world’s most famous political scientist, he was born in the USA and lives there still. I wasn’t charging him with treacherous loyalties or politics but of an almost unAmerican modesty.

He is, notoriously, the author of The End of History and the Last Man, published 34 years ago and still selling in many languages around the world. The first half of the book’s title has been used by the leaders of the great powers and high school debaters and innumerable others in between. Not to embrace it but, almost universally, to reject it. “It might be the most maligned, unfairly dismissed and misunderstood book of the post-war era,” wrote Paul Sagar of King’s College, London.

Critics denounced the idea that liberal democracy’s triumph over communism could have delivered the ultimate model for society – “the final form of human government”. The concept of the “end of history” was rejected by dictators and democrats alike. Including Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Joe Biden. Margaret Thatcher is supposed to have heard the book’s title and expostulated: “The end of history? The beginning of nonsense.”

Fukuyama has borne all this stoically, patiently. “I have been asked several times a week over the past three decades whether I wished to recant my argument,” he writes in his new book. “None of the individuals asking have read more than the title of my essay or book. In particular, none bothered to read the last five chapters of my book, which dealt with the problem of the Last Man.”

He’s never attacked his critics personally or rushed to defend himself. Famous American public figures are not known for their restraint. But that’s only the beginning of his modesty. He might well have titled his new book I Was Right. Because he has never argued that events, history-making events, would cease. He has never claimed that economic and political liberalism would go unchallenged. Only that events wouldn’t produce a better alternative. For the simple reason that the main locomotive of history is the human struggle for recognition.

Where Marx said it’s all about material gain, Fukuyama says that it’s truly about our craving for recognition of our fundamental dignity. “For most of human history, this led to an unequal contest between masters and slaves, until the advent of the French Revolution, which established the principle of equal recognition as the only rational solution to the human problem,” says Fukuyama.

It’s not a new idea. The ancient Greeks called this innate desire for recognition “thymos”. The phrase “the end of history” itself is taken from the work of a Russian-born philosopher, Alexandre Kojeve, who died in 1968. Funnily enough, Margaret Thatcher mocked Fukuyama’s title but actually shared his conclusion that political and economic liberalism are the best form of human organisation. Biden, too, yet he feared China’s challenge to its survival.

And who is offering a better vision for the organising of society? Right-wing populists are good at demolition but unable to build anything better. “These right-wing populist parties aren’t good at governing and they don’t deliver what they promise,” Fukuyama tells me. “Look at Brexit. They didn’t change the level of immigration one bit.” Trump, of course, is the prime exhibit. Promising no new wars and lower prices, he’s delivered the exact opposite.

And the left has no coherent vision, either. Young Americans are reviving talk of communism: “The word is being thrown around by kids who don’t know what it means.” Progressives in the US, notably the Democratic Socialists of America, have a nonsensical grab-bag of what Fukuyama calls “small bore” ideas like free bus rides and taxing billionaires together with unrealistically radical proposals to “defund the police” and abolish the Senate.

Doesn’t China present an alternative model to liberal democracy? “There are still big questions about both the political and economic sustainability of the China model. If they are still doing well relative to the US in another generation, then I would concede it may be a real alternative, though one that will be hard to universalise.”

Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer

So how to explain today’s wild political thrashings? “The absence of plausible visions for a better future society means that politicians and activists have to whip people into panic over how bad the present it.” A “focus on real reform is boring”. The great struggles of ideology and history had been fought and won, and now people “struggle for the sake of struggle”. “We see this now on both the extreme right and left”.

Fukuyama acknowledges that extreme inequality is a problem that needs redressing. But populist anger, he says, is “driven much more by resentment against a society that does not distribute respect equally”. It demands a redistribution of respect. That doesn’t require a revolution.

Which brings us to the Last Man. His new book is titled In the Realm of the Last Man, a place we’ve been living in for some time now. “The problem,” according to Fukuyama, “is that the peace and prosperity brought about by a liberal order based on equal recognition is not enough for many people. “They do not want to be recognised as the equals of every other person on earth; they want to be recognised as superior in some respect.” Fukuyama nominated Donald Trump as the standout example, even in his original book.

Not content with thymos, Trump demands megadoses of thymos, a condition Fukuyama calls “megalothymia”. He didn’t foresee Trump as president but, as Paul Sagar attests, “he got closer than most” in recognising the personality that would thrive In the Realm of the Last Man. Fukuyama’s modesty is such that, in his new book, he doesn’t remind us of this prescience.

Australia, after a 10-year lag, seems to be approaching American levels of populist anger. Fukuyama, who has travelled a number of times to Australia, offers this as his only advice to us. The mainstream parties, he says, “ought to think about alliances” with One Nation. “That defanged populist parties in Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It’s distasteful but it reduces their impact.” Perhaps that’s why Pauline Hanson rejects the idea of any coalition with the Liberals.

Fukuyama’s suggestion of enfolding the far right is the exact opposite of the German “firewall” policy, under which mainstream parties refuse any coalition with the far-right Alternative for Deutschland.

Fukuyama notes the attack on Australia’s Helen Haines last week, a symptom of “social” media and political anger. He says he fears more violence could follow the US midterm elections next week: “There’s a lot of anger and hidden violence in the way we deal with each other. If the Republicans lose control of Congress, Trump won’t move to the centre and be more reasonable. He will accelerate his threats and the crazy things he wants to do to his enemies. “I am a little worried about this period after the midterms. It’s surprising that there haven’t been more acts of violence and attempted assassinations.”

A final measure of his modesty is his generosity in attributing his success to others, including an Australian intellectual, the late Owen Harries: “Owen played an important part in my life.” As the editor of a Washington journal, Harries spotted Fukuyama’s talent and commissioned him to write the essay that formed the basis for The End of History and the Last Man.

Accused of modesty, Fukuyama just chuckles: “Imagine if I were Donald Trump.” The world is oversupplied with Trumps. Even America’s voters seem to be reaching the same conclusion.

Peter Hartcher is political editor and international editor of The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age.

#35686. In Islamophobic rant, Trump seeks to stir Republican base in Michigan

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Trump’s comments underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch.

PORT HURON, United States – US President Donald Trump turned to Islamophobic stereotypes to motivate Michigan Republicans on Oct 25, claiming at a rally that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, if elected, would bring a wave of jihadis to the country.

“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump told more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron, a working class, waterfront city in a deep-red congressional district about 95km north-east of Detroit.

Trump called El-Sayed, 41, whose family emigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” – a baseless claim.

He then contrasted El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the US, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the US.

“I call him apple pie,” Trump said of Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”

Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch.

And, while he has often used crude and racist language, Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.

But a broader question about Trump’s rally here – which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops – is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president.

His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.

Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory.

While Trump carried Michigan by 2 points in 2024, just 34% of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.

Polls indicate that El-Sayed has a narrow edge over Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.

Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed on Oct 25, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.

Speaking in a town on the Canadian border, Trump did not dwell on his battle with Prime Minister Mark Carney, one of the few world leaders who has directly confronted him on tariffs and other issues, and he did not repeat his frequent call for Canada to give up its independence and become the 51st state.

Instead, he focused on El-Sayed, his religion and his relatives. Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for El-Sayed.

“Any Jewish person who supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy”.

Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.

Trump made the statement after claiming that El-Sayed’s half sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Oct 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis by Hamas fighters.

She posted a video on the first anniversary of the attack that said that “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner”, but did not mention the massacre directly and did not celebrate the violence.

El-Sayed’s campaign told Fox News that he disagreed with her “on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use”.

El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.

But his opponents have raised an open letter he signed in 2012, when he was a medical student.

It was addressed to Mohammed Morsi, then the new Egyptian president, from a party that represents the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood.

It asked him to “purge the media and police” of loyalists to the government that was overturned during the Arab Spring.

El-Sayed has not discussed the letter. But his spokesperson, Cole Wozniak, said, “Abdul remains laser-focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington”.

“Michigan knows Trump is on the ballot on Nov 3,” he added, “and they will vote like it by rejecting Trump’s rubber stamp Mike Rogers and sending Abdul to the Senate.”

Trump deepened his critique as the day went on, saying that someone with El-Sayed’s background “would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane”.

“They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate,” he added.

He also said that El-Sayed should not be given access to classified information.

At his own rally on Oct 25 in Grand Rapids, El-Sayed said the Republican strategy was “to point at me and my name and my faith”.

“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” he said.

In Michigan, Trump also veered into a discussion of Greenland. He insisted, “Oh, you know we did get Greenland”, suggesting that it was now owned by the US.

In fact, Trump was forced to drop that demand and instead signed a new treaty with Denmark, which handles Greenland’s foreign affairs, that envisions opening two new US bases on the island and bars similar arrangements with foreign powers, notably China. But it does not change Denmark’s sovereignty, as Trump initially insisted.

He also drew cheers when he insisted Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and vaguely said the war with Iran would be resolved soon.

But he largely steered clear of discussing how his decision to attack Iran led directly to high gas and diesel prices.

Rogers has sought distance from the war, calling for it to “end quickly”, and from the President’s tariffs on Canadian goods, saying “Canada is not our enemy” in a campaign ad. He has also backed a one-year moratorium on data centres, creating a contrast with Trump’s support for them.

Like other Republicans, Rogers has largely avoided talking about Trump in ads and on the campaign trail.

Speaking at the rally in Port Huron, Rogers again accused El-Sayed of having family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. He said that watching El-Sayed try to tell the truth is like “watching an octopus put his socks on in the morning”. And he said the country “can’t risk his extreme ideology and thinking”.

On NBC News’ Meet The Press on the morning of Oct 25, Rogers did not endorse Trump’s baseless claim that El-Sayed is “a terrorist”, but did not condemn it outright.

“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers said of El-Sayed.

El-Sayed has become a central villain in Republicans’ narrative of the midterms.

In western Iowa on Oct 22, more than 1280km from Port Huron, Trump railed against El- Sayed, drawing some of the loudest applause of the night. He did the same in North Carolina and Ohio last week.

After holding forth on the potential demise of the nation in Michigan on Oct 25, Trump spent five full minutes admiring the body and physicality of Senator Jon Husted, the Republican running for re-election in Ohio, and rapper Nicki Minaj, who traveled with Trump to the rally.

“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj,” Trump said. “Hard to miss it.”

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

#35687. Bessent says Iran economy will contract by more than 25%

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview with Iran International, warned Iranians to stock up on gasoline and heating fuel ahead of expected shortages, predicting the economy would shrink by more than a quarter in the year ending March 2027.

Bessent said Iran was running short of foreign currency, oil production was beginning to falter and the next eight weeks of Washington's Operation Economic Outcast would be “even more intense.”

“I would predict that from March of '26 until March of '27, the economy would contract more than 25 percent, which is more than the Soviet Union contracted after its collapse,” Bessent told Iran International’s Kambiz Tavana on Monday.

The Treasury secretary said the campaign was intended to pressure Iran's leadership rather than its population, while warning of severe fuel shortages this winter.

“My advice to the Iranian people would be: don't pay your taxes because you're not going to get anything back from the government,” Bessent said.

“You should start stocking up on heating fuel. There's going to be a big heating fuel shortage. In terms of gasoline, everyone should fill up their tanks now.”

Asked about the impact on ordinary Iranians, Bessent said humanitarian channels remained open for food and medicine, but the government was running out of dollars to pay for imports.

He also said authorities were printing money, failing to pay salaries and would continue cutting social benefits.

Bessent said economic pressure was exposing disagreements among Iranian politicians, the Revolutionary Guards and the supreme leader. He described some IRGC commanders as isolated from the public and unaware of the extent of the economic deterioration.

Iran's economy has come under mounting pressure from two rounds of war with the United States and Israel, a US naval blockade that has sharply curtailed its oil exports and an expanding sanctions campaign targeting its remaining sources of foreign currency.

“Iran, for the first time, probably since oil was discovered, has no oil on the water,” Bessent said. “There have been no loadings at Kharg Island. Production is starting to falter.”

“We've been going for eight weeks, and I can tell you the next eight weeks is going to get even more intense,” he said.

Bessent said Washington remained prepared to negotiate, but insisted Iran could not have a nuclear weapon and must stop financing regional armed groups.

Diplomatic efforts have intensified in recent days, with Qatari mediators in Tehran on Sunday followed on Monday by senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey seeking to de-escalate tensions and revive negotiations.

Tehran, however, has shown little sign of softening its core demands under mounting economic pressure. Iranian officials insist Washington must meet its conditions, including lifting the naval blockade.

Bessent also appealed directly to people involved in moving Iranian government money overseas, saying some financial intermediaries were already refusing to return funds to Tehran.

Iranian officials commonly refer to such intermediaries as “trustees,” who handle oil revenues and other transactions outside the formal banking system to circumvent sanctions.

“We are seeing the regime go bankrupt,” Bessent said. “So many of the people who are holding money outside of Iran do not want to send it back in.”

He said Iranians inside the country, members of the diaspora and employees of embassies and consulates could provide information to Treasury under its whistleblower program, with rewards of up to 30% of recovered funds.

“We are happy to unsanction individuals who work with us,” he said, adding that cooperating intermediaries could potentially claim 30% of funds they were holding for Tehran.

Bessent said Treasury was also tracking Iran's attempts to move money through cryptocurrency and foreign banks.

“There are numerous banks… We shut the Dubai branches of an Egyptian bank. We closed a Turkish bank, the second-largest Russian bank, VTB. We discovered that their external branches outside of Russia were aiding the regime,” he said.

Bessent rejected suggestions that Iran could wait for the US midterm elections in the hope that Washington's approach would change.

“Nothing will change in terms of President Trump's calculus, in terms of how resolute we are here at Treasury, in terms of the blockade,” he said.

Asked whether the combination of sanctions and a naval blockade had any historical precedent, Bessent said the closest comparison was Washington's campaign against Venezuela, but argued that the measures imposed on Iran went substantially further.

“There's been nothing like this,” he said.

Two retired employees of Iran's national airline died after being forced to abandon medical treatment they could not afford, the semi-official ILNA news agency reported on Monday, citing the head of the airline's retirees' association.

Jalal Hashemi, chairman of the Iran Air Retirees Association, said the deaths occurred over the past two to three weeks amid worsening financial and healthcare problems affecting around 13,000 retirees and pensioners of the airline, also known as Homa.

"The situation has become so catastrophic that in just the past two or three weeks, two of our retired colleagues were forced to abandon treatment because they could not afford hospital expenses, and unfortunately lost their lives," Hashemi told ILNA.

Iranian households face mounting economic hardship after years of inflation, sanctions and economic mismanagement, compounded by two rounds of war with the United States and Israel.

Iran Air retirees have staged repeated protests over pension payments, healthcare coverage and the management of their retirement fund.

In August, retirees gathered outside the airline's headquarters in Tehran to demand improvements to healthcare services and the reinstatement of suspended welfare payments.

Hashemi said Iran Air had paid only two of 12 installments owed to Iran Insurance Company under its insurance contract for the Iranian year ending in March 2026, prompting the insurer to suspend inpatient hospital coverage for retirees.

According to Hashemi, Iran Air retirees receive an average monthly pension of around 270 million rials (about $100), while approximately 5,600 receive minimum pensions of just over 180 million rials (about $66).

He estimated the shortfall in the airline's healthcare insurance fund at 4 trillion rials (about $1.5 million), saying no institution had accepted responsibility for covering the deficit.

Recent reductions in government-subsidized foreign currency for medicine imports, drug price increases and rising out-of-pocket healthcare costs have further strained the fund.

Hashemi also said Iran Air management had suspended a monthly welfare allowance of 60 million rials (about $22), citing financial losses from the war and reduced flights.

Flour shortages have forced bakeries to close in several Iranian cities and pushed up bread prices, with residents and bakers reporting disrupted supplies, falling purchasing power and growing uncertainty over their businesses.

Residents in Tabriz, Karaj, Kerman and Hamedan told Iran International that interruptions and delays in flour deliveries had disrupted independent bakeries and producers of various types of bread.

Several bakeries on a street in Tabriz have shut down, a resident said.

“I asked why, and they told me they weren't receiving flour. They keep promising that the flour quotas will be replenished today or tomorrow, but nothing happens.”

Previous reports have also documented flour shortages and bakery closures, with residents describing bread shortages and interruptions to production caused by electricity outages.

Flour supply disruptions shut bakeries and sandwich shops

Independent bakers have reported that difficulties obtaining flour have forced businesses to suspend operations.

A citizen of Hamedan in western Iran said flour shortages and rising prices had affected not only bakeries producing specialty bread but also sandwich shops.

Flour prices have risen, and suppliers are now saying there is no flour available at all, the resident said.

“Our bakery is closed because we have no flour, and nobody is taking responsibility,” a independent baker told Iran International.

The shortages have coincided with declining purchasing power, leaving bakeries struggling to secure supplies as customers struggle to afford bread.

“They don't have flour to give us, and I swear to God, people don't have money to buy bread either. Our economic situation has become critical,” another baker said.

Iran's flour distribution system distinguishes between subsidized bakeries and independent bakeries, which face different purchasing prices and supply arrangements.

Flour allocations to certain independent bakeries had been reduced, Bagher Khodadadi, head of supervision and inspection at the Khorasan Razavi provincial agriculture department, confirmed on October 21.

Khodadadi said the shortages in flour distribution had been addressed.

Bakeries reducing their operating hours because of flour shortages would be committing a violation and could face enforcement measures, he added.

The flour supply problems have also affected food retailers that depend on bakeries for their products, according to messages.

Two bakeries supplying bread to a supermarket in Kerman said they no longer had enough flour to continue production, the store's owner said.

“Two of the bakers who supply me called and said there was no flour left and they couldn't bake and deliver bread tomorrow. A famine has officially begun.”

A resident of Karaj also described a sharp increase in bread prices.

“I bought two baguettes and they cost 800,000 rials. The price of flour has also tripled.”

Iran International previously reported on October 8 that residents had described unannounced increases in bread prices and flour shortages in several areas.

Bread prices in Tehran province had risen by as much as 100% for certain varieties by June 23.

The increases have added to the financial pressure on households already struggling with declining purchasing power.

Uncertainty over flour quotas and pricing

The disruption has raised further questions about how flour quotas are allocated and priced for independent bakeries and producers of larger and semi-industrial bread varieties.

Flour allocations to these businesses were suspended about two weeks ago, according to another message received by Iran International.

The sender said suppliers had attributed the suspension to the government's failure to announce new flour prices, leaving bakeries uncertain about when deliveries would resume.

The resident also said certain flour mills were selling supplies on the black market without issuing invoices specifying prices.

Comments by provincial grain officials about flour allocations have added to questions over the distribution system and the availability of supplies.

Iranians say they are paying more for slow, unreliable and heavily restricted internet after mobile operators raised data prices by up to 40%, with some reporting that their allowances run out unusually quickly.

Messages sent to Iran International described mounting frustration over the cost of staying connected, from families worried about paying for online classes to users struggling to send even a text message.

“All we have left of life in Iran is passing the time on our phones, and they are taking that away too,” one reader from Baharestan said.

Mobile operators Hamrah-e Aval and Irancell increased their data package prices by up to 40% early on Friday, October 23, according to state media.

One reader said a weekly four-gigabyte package had risen from 330,000 rials ($0.12) to 450,000 rials ($0.17). Another said a monthly six-gigabyte package that cost 530,000 rials ($0.20) three days earlier now cost 740,000 rials ($0.28).

The pressure comes as Iran’s official minimum wage stands at about 166.3 million rials per month, equivalent to roughly $62 at the unofficial-market exchange rate.

Others questioned why prices were rising again after earlier increases before and during the war.

“Didn’t they raise internet prices two months before the 40-day war? Didn’t they raise package prices again during the war, taking advantage of the blackout?” one reader asked, referring to the US-led war that began on February 28. “So what is this latest increase for?”

The higher charges have brought no improvement in service, according to accounts from users across the country.

A reader in the northern province of Mazandaran described Hamrah-e Aval’s connection as moving “at a snail’s pace,” saying Wi-Fi connections in many areas also cut out, even when accessing domestic messaging apps.

In Iranshahr, in southeastern Iran, another reader reported severely degraded ADSL service followed by a complete outage from 8 p.m. on Friday. Another said sending a text message on Telegram was difficult, let alone a photograph or video.

Iran International reported on Friday that users in Semnan, Shiraz, Tabriz, Kerman, Tehran and Tonekabon had complained of sharply slower connections, malfunctioning tools used to bypass internet filtering and difficulty accessing social media.

The Telecommunications Company of Iran has previously attributed some disruptions to “upgrading and optimizing technical infrastructure.”

The complaints come against a backdrop of extensive restrictions on internet access. Freedom House’s 2026 report gave Iran an internet freedom score of nine out of 100, down from 13.

The organization said Iran’s tiered internet system had made access to the global internet difficult and expensive, leaving much of the population restricted to a domestic network controlled by the authorities.

All global social media platforms, from X and Telegram to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, are banned in Iran.

Several readers also accused operators of “stealing data,” saying their allowances were depleted far faster than their usage would explain.

“I topped up my data package two days ago. Today, only 600 megabytes of my six gigabytes are left, even though we don’t have a decent connection,” one reader said.

Another said a six-gigabyte package bought for 570,000 rials ($0.21) had run out within two days despite limited use, and now cost 730,000 rials ($0.27) to replace.

For families, the increases have also raised concerns about the cost of education if gas shortages force schools to move classes online.

One reader said a one-gigabyte Hamrah-e Aval package cost 330,000 rials ($0.12), including tax. “With things like this, how are we supposed to buy data for online classes?”

Another said repeated price increases had left them unable to afford internet access at all.

“We live in a country with vast oil and gas resources,” another reader said, “but we earn in rials and spend in dollars.”

Iran still has the knowhow, middlemen and shadow-fleet infrastructure it spent years developing to sell sanctioned oil to China. But it has now run out of oil outside Iran to put through that system.

The US naval blockade has exposed a limitation in Tehran’s sanctions-evasion machinery: ship-to-ship transfers, false paperwork and steep discounts can disguise and sell crude once it is at sea, but they cannot get fresh cargoes out of Iranian ports.

For months, Iran was able to keep selling oil to China because millions of barrels had already left the country on tankers and were sitting in Asian waters. That reserve is now effectively exhausted.

Kpler analysts cited by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday estimated Iran had about 135 million barrels in overseas storage when the war began in February. By October 5, that had fallen below one million barrels.

Vortexa gave a different figure, estimating Iranian stocks off Singapore at roughly six million barrels on October 9. The difference reflects varying tracking methods and locations, but both show that the offshore stocks that sustained Iranian exports have been largely depleted.

Malaysia sits at the heart of how Iranian oil has reached China, serving mainly as a transfer point rather than the true source of much of the crude.

The Wall Street Journal reported in May on ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian crude off the Malaysian coast.

A sharp drop in China’s purchases recorded as Malaysian crude could therefore provide another indication that the flow of Iranian oil through the system has dried up.

But the figures are not a one-for-one measure of Iranian exports. Chinese customs data record the declared origin of cargoes, while ship tracking can miss transfers or vessels operating without transponders.

The timing nevertheless coincides with the depletion of the offshore stocks that had fed the trade. If no new Iranian crude is available for transfer near Malaysia, fewer cargoes would be expected to appear in Chinese data under a Malaysian origin.

China remains Iran’s most important potential buyer, but its independent refineries are already lining up alternatives.

Reuters reported on October 6 that Chinese “teapot” refineries had purchased at least 12 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari crude for delivery in October and November. Traders suggested the total could reach 15 million to 20 million barrels.

Iranian oil had been attractive largely because of its steep discount. Iraqi and Qatari cargoes may cost more, but they arrive through normal channels and carry less risk of sanctions trouble or sudden interruptions.

Iran could offer deeper discounts or rely more heavily on intermediaries to retain Chinese customers. Neither solves the central obstacle: the oil still has to be loaded and shipped.

Reuters reported in August that offers of Iranian oil to Chinese buyers had already fallen as stored cargoes were sold.

Jask, on the Gulf of Oman, is often cited as Iran’s alternative export outlet. The Goreh–Jask pipeline and terminal were built so oil could reach the sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

So far, however, the facility has not shown it can replace Iran’s main export system.

The International Energy Agency’s February 2026 factsheet described Jask as effectively out of regular service. S&P Global later reported tanker activity there between March and July, indicating occasional use.

That suggests the route can handle some cargoes, not that it can support exports on the scale Iran needs. A port outside Hormuz is also not necessarily beyond the reach of a blockade aimed at Iranian ports.

Rail and trucking through neighboring countries offer still less capacity. They face high costs, limited infrastructure, border procedures and sanctions risks.

If crude cannot be exported, Iran’s problem moves from the sea back to its oil fields.

Tehran can send more crude to domestic refineries, use available storage or cut production. Kpler estimated earlier in the blockade that Iran had already begun reducing output as inventories rose and usable storage space tightened.

Usable storage is not the same as total tank capacity: some tanks hold condensate, and not all can simply be switched to crude.

Further production cuts would mean less revenue and could make restarting output more difficult. But continuing to pump oil with nowhere to send it risks filling remaining storage and eventually forcing deeper cuts.

The financial impact will also emerge gradually because payments for cargoes already delivered can arrive weeks later.

The United States says the blockade has denied Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, a CENTCOM estimate cited by the Journal rather than an independently verified measure of Tehran’s net losses.

Iran has not forgotten how to evade sanctions or lost the network it built to sell oil despite them. But before Tehran can disguise a cargo, transfer it between ships or sell it at a discount, it first has to get the oil out of Iran.

China's imports of oil recorded as Malaysian have plunged alongside the collapse of Iranian exports under the US naval blockade, suggesting how heavily Iran relied on relabeling its crude for its biggest customer.

In September, China imported just 276,000 barrels per day of oil recorded as Malaysian, down from an average of nearly 1.3 million barrels per day in 2025.

In some previous months, the figure had reached 2 million barrels per day. That is roughly four times Malaysia's total oil production.

Much of the discrepancy may reflect oil coming from Iran but recorded by China's customs as originating in Malaysia, alongside sanctioned oil from other producers and genuine Malaysian exports.

Chinese customs authorities have consistently reported zero monthly imports of Iranian oil since 2020. Yet tanker-tracking companies estimate that Iran delivered an average of around 1.5 million barrels per day to China last year.

Kpler previously told Iran International that most Iranian oil exports to China are recorded as Malaysian, while some cargoes are declared as originating from Iraq, Oman and even the United Arab Emirates. TankerTrackers has also documented the practice.

The decline in China's recorded Malaysian imports has accelerated as US sanctions have tightened and the naval blockade has choked off Iranian exports.

Kpler data obtained by Iran International show that Iran delivered more than 1.55 million barrels per day of oil to China between January and May this year. From June through September, the average fell to less than half that level.

By mid-October, the volume of Iranian oil afloat outside the US blockade line had fallen to zero.

If current trends persist, China's imports of oil recorded as Malaysian could fall to their lowest level in years, potentially approaching the 2017 level of just 130,000 barrels per day as early as this month or next.

While Iranian oil exports have collapsed, tanker-tracking data show that overall oil exports from the Middle East have recovered to prewar levels and even surpassed them.

The Wall Street Journal, citing Kpler data, reported that the region's exports of oil and petroleum products have reached 24 million barrels per day, above the level recorded before the war.

Before the war, more than 80% of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz was destined for Asian markets, with China the largest buyer.

Chinese customs data show that in September, China imported an average of 2.9 million barrels per day from Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Iraq, up from less than 2 million barrels per day in May.

The figure nevertheless remained below February's prewar level, when China's combined imports from those five countries exceeded 3.8 million barrels per day.

The numbers also reflect a broader shift in Chinese oil buying after the outbreak of war. As global prices surged, China at one point cut overall crude imports by around 30% and drew instead on its strategic petroleum reserves.

In that sense, China acted as a significant shock absorber, helping limit an even sharper increase in global oil prices.

Before the war, China imported around 11.5 million barrels per day of crude. Following the US-Israeli war on Iran and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, imports fell to around 8 million barrels per day before recovering more recently to above 9 million.

The shift suggests that China is increasingly replacing lost Iranian barrels with oil from other Middle Eastern producers. The disappearance of China's “Malaysian” imports is yet another measure of how sharply the blockade has curtailed Iran's access to its most important oil market.

#35689. James Packer agrees to testify in Netanyahu’s corruption case

Australian billionaire James Packer has agreed to testify in the explosive corruption trial of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but has refused to return to Israel to give his evidence.

This masthead revealed on Monday that Packer had paid at least $US1.25 million ($1.78 million) to the Tel Aviv law firm also defending Netanyahu against allegations that he corruptly received benefits from the reclusive businessman and other wealthy supporters a decade ago.

Monthly wire transfers of $US50,000 have been made for the past two years from a bank account controlled by Packer’s company to the account of Netanyahu’s legal defence firm, Hadad Roth Shenhar.

The revelations have been seized upon by Israeli news outlets and Netanyahu’s political enemies one day before citizens vote in crucial national elections.

A source aware of the payments, but not authorised to speak publicly, said they should be urgently investigated to determine whether Netanyahu was receiving an undisclosed benefit as the law firm defends allegations the Israeli leader unlawfully accepted large volumes of champagne and cigars from Packer between 2014 and 2016. This masthead has not confirmed that Netanyahu benefited from the payments.

Netanyahu’s primary defence attorney is Hadad Roth Shenhar’s most senior lawyer, Amit Hadad. Further links between Packer and Hadad emerged on Monday night (AEDT), including a formal request by the defence team for Packer to return to Israel to give evidence.

Hadad also wants two other Australians close to Packer, his one-time “right-hand man” Ben Tilley and the former Consolidated Press Holdings chief executive officer Guy Jalland, to provide evidence. Neither is accused of wrongdoing but travelled frequently to Israel between 2013 and 2016 and are likely to be familiar with Packer and Netanyahu’s friendship.

Hadad’s request for Packer to give evidence risks sparking further questions over whether it is appropriate for the billionaire to pay the firm given its deep involvement in the Netanyahu case, despite Hadad saying the work for Packer is unrelated to the trial.

Netanyahu’s legal team believes Packer, Tilley and Jalland can be assets to their argument that the charges laid against the prime minister are flawed and baseless.

However, the trio refused to return to Israel for the case, claiming the “outrageous behaviour of the Israeli authorities has caused significant damage to Mr Packer”.

Writing on behalf of Packer, Jalland said the trio would not travel to Israel to testify because they wanted to ensure further proceedings in the case are “handled in a way that assures that our rights will be fully protected, according to the laws of our respective places of residence”.

“Mr Packer was very fond of Israel,” Jalland wrote in a letter filed in the court. “As is well known, he intended to spend a good part of his time there. Mr Packer is deeply disappointed by the treatment he has received from the Israeli authorities.

“He was shocked to learn that the Israeli investigators violated his privacy and took his private documents and private information without his knowledge or consent, with no due process procedure.”

However, Packer, Jalland and Tilley have agreed to appear remotely – likely via audiovisual link – because they were “law-abiding citizens” who would respect any order given to them by a court in the country in which they live.

“If such an order were given requiring us to testify under oath and to answer questions put by counsel for both the defence and the prosecution, we would comply.”

While Netanyahu’s team believes Packer’s evidence could support the prime minister’s view that he has done nothing wrong, testifying would also open the door for the prosecution to cross-examine the businessman.

It is unknown where Packer’s evidence would be given; he is currently in Argentina, but spends a significant amount of time in the United States, and visits Sydney often.

Israeli authorities have repeatedly blocked Netanyahu from receiving funds from wealthy backers to pay for his defence in the long-running corruption case.

If it were found that Packer’s monthly $US50,000 payments directly or indirectly benefited Netanyahu, it could involve fresh breaches of Israeli laws governing how politicians can accept support.

When contacted by this masthead on Friday night, Packer did not deny the rolling $US50,000 payments but declined to comment.

A source close to the businessman later insisted the wire transfers to Netanyahu’s lawyers were for work done for Packer – including “deal finding” in Israel where Packer has business interests – and unrelated to the prime minister’s court case.

Hadad was peppered with questions about the payments from Packer on Monday night AEDT as he entered court in Israel.

He smiled, asked reporters if they were “serious” and kept walking.

In his formal written request for Packer to give evidence at Netanyahu’s trial, Hadad noted that he and his firm represent companies controlled by Packer “on issues that have no connection to the ongoing trial”. He did not say what these matters involved.

Asked about the allegations on Monday morning, a spokesperson for Netanyahu told The Age and the Herald: “I couldn’t give a monkey’s about your questions.”

Packer found himself entangled in Netanyahu’s corruption case after gifting the prime minister champagne and cigars more than a decade ago, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing.

Packer and Netanyahu at the time lived in neighbouring villas in the exclusive township of Caesarea and were regular guests at each other’s homes.

The Israeli leader and Packer became estranged after the corruption allegations first emerged in 2016 and did not talk for up to eight years. However, the pair reconnected around the time Netanyahu addressed the US Congress in July 2024, when Packer sat in the viewing gallery as a special guest. They later shared a Shabbat dinner.

The first payment by Packer to the prime minister’s law firm was made eight weeks after the two rekindled their friendship.

Australian Federal Police officers interviewed Packer on behalf of their Israeli counterparts in late 2017 but stressed he was a witness in the case – not a suspect – and that he co-operated fully.

Consolidated Press International (CPI), the company which had made the $US50,000 payments to Netanyahu’s law firm, is one of several private investment arms operated by Packer.

Packer’s Australian-based company Consolidated Press Holdings is now run by Sydney business identity Lawrence Myers. Myers and CPI did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

Jalland, the company’s former chief executive, worked for both James Packer and his late father, Kerry Packer, for decades.

Jalland resigned as a director of casino company Crown Resorts after the Bergin inquiry found the company should no longer hold a gaming licence.

Although he was found to be a credible witness, the inquiry report concluded he shared responsibility for Crown’s governance failures.

#35691. Teen arrested in Florida shooting will be tried as adult, US officials say

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

The shooting took place in Perry Street near Florida A&M University.

Tallahassee, Florida – A 15-year-old boy who was arrested in the shooting of 11 people after a college football game in Tallahassee, Florida, will stand trial as an adult, a Florida prosecutor said on Oct 26.

The teenager, Anthony Rivers III, was ordered to remain in custody at a juvenile court hearing on Oct 26 after his arrest the day before. The shooting took place in a crowded, closed-off street on Oct 24 about an hour after Florida A&M University’s (FAMU) homecoming game. A crowd of just over 20,000 attended the event.

The shooting left six people hospitalised as of Oct 25, one of whom was in critical condition. A spokesperson for Leon County School District said four of its students were wounded, including the one in critical condition.

Six of the 11 people shot were minors, the Tallahassee Police Department said. A 12th person was injured but not shot, officials said.

Lawrence Revell, chief of the Tallahassee Police, said at a news conference on Oct 26 that the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a physical altercation among people who knew one another and that none of the victims appeared to be intended targets. He said more arrests were possible.

Judge Andrew Sheeran, who presided over the hearing on Oct 26, said he would grant the request of the top prosecutor in Tallahassee to try Rivers as an adult, which Florida law allows in certain cases. He will be charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, officials said.

“It’s our discretion because of the severity of the offence,” said prosecutor Jack Campbell.

In a phone interview, he added that he had discussed the decision with juvenile-case prosecutors before asking his prosecutors to review the case. “Ultimately, it was my decision,” he said.

Rivers, dressed in a white T-shirt, grey gym shorts and sandals and his hair pulled up into a bun, stood quietly at the hearing on Oct 26 with his hands clasped behind his back as the public defender who was representing him addressed the court.

The public defender said she had previously represented Rivers. Her office did not reply to a request for comment. Efforts to reach relatives of Rivers were not immediately successful.

According to court records, Rivers has been arrested previously on charges including burglary and theft of a gun, but it was unclear what the outcome was. He was arrested on Sept 6 for violating his probation and had been sentenced to a juvenile home.

According to a police affidavit, Rivers was arrested after surveillance cameras and an ankle monitor he was wearing identified him at a Tallahassee mall where gunfire had erupted in an underground carpark.

The police identified another 15-year-old who was with Rivers as the shooter, according to the affidavit. Nobody was injured in the shooting, which occurred after an altercation in the mall.

Campbell declined to discuss anything about Rivers’ criminal record. But he said if someone was a repeat offender, “that’s something we consider” when determining whether to charge a juvenile as an adult.

The shooting echoed others in Tallahassee in recent years. Nine people were shot – one fatally – outside a liquor store in 2022 that Campbell said was connected to a homecoming event at Florida A&M.

In 2025, two people were killed and six others were wounded in a shooting at Florida State University, which is near Florida A&M.

Campbell is seeking the death penalty against the shooter in that case, Phoenix Ikner, who has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

The shooting on Oct 24 could have been much worse, Campbell said.

It happened in Perry Street, a residential street that runs alongside Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the football team plays. The street was blocked off for vendors selling food and T-shirts, and is a popular place before and after games.

“If you go to FAMU, you’ve spent time in Perry Street,” Campbell said. NYTIMES

#35697. Two Iran Air retirees died after forgoing treatment over cost

Two retired employees of Iran's national airline died after being forced to abandon medical treatment they could not afford, the semi-official ILNA news agency reported on Monday, citing the head of the airline's retirees' association.

Jalal Hashemi, chairman of the Iran Air Retirees Association, said the deaths occurred over the past two to three weeks amid worsening financial and healthcare problems affecting around 13,000 retirees and pensioners of the airline, also known as Homa.

"The situation has become so catastrophic that in just the past two or three weeks, two of our retired colleagues were forced to abandon treatment because they could not afford hospital expenses, and unfortunately lost their lives," Hashemi told ILNA.

Iranian households face mounting economic hardship after years of inflation, sanctions and economic mismanagement, compounded by two rounds of war with the United States and Israel.

Iran Air retirees have staged repeated protests over pension payments, healthcare coverage and the management of their retirement fund.

In August, retirees gathered outside the airline's headquarters in Tehran to demand improvements to healthcare services and the reinstatement of suspended welfare payments.

Hashemi said Iran Air had paid only two of 12 installments owed to Iran Insurance Company under its insurance contract for the Iranian year ending in March 2026, prompting the insurer to suspend inpatient hospital coverage for retirees.

According to Hashemi, Iran Air retirees receive an average monthly pension of around 270 million rials (about $100), while approximately 5,600 receive minimum pensions of just over 180 million rials (about $66).

He estimated the shortfall in the airline's healthcare insurance fund at 4 trillion rials (about $1.5 million), saying no institution had accepted responsibility for covering the deficit.

Recent reductions in government-subsidized foreign currency for medicine imports, drug price increases and rising out-of-pocket healthcare costs have further strained the fund.

Hashemi also said Iran Air management had suspended a monthly welfare allowance of 60 million rials (about $22), citing financial losses from the war and reduced flights.

Flour shortages have forced bakeries to close in several Iranian cities and pushed up bread prices, with residents and bakers reporting disrupted supplies, falling purchasing power and growing uncertainty over their businesses.

Residents in Tabriz, Karaj, Kerman and Hamedan told Iran International that interruptions and delays in flour deliveries had disrupted independent bakeries and producers of various types of bread.

Several bakeries on a street in Tabriz have shut down, a resident said.

“I asked why, and they told me they weren't receiving flour. They keep promising that the flour quotas will be replenished today or tomorrow, but nothing happens.”

The sender said suppliers had attributed the suspension to the government's failure to announce new flour prices, leaving bakeries uncertain about when deliveries would resume.

The resident also said certain flour mills were selling supplies on the black market without issuing invoices specifying prices.

Comments by provincial grain officials about flour allocations have added to questions over the distribution system and the availability of supplies.

Iran's judiciary has indicted comedian Saeed Shakiba on charges including supporting Israel and the Pahlavi dynasty, state media reported on Sunday, days after authorities opened a case against him over a video impersonating former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

The judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency said Tehran prosecutors had issued the indictment following an investigation into what authorities described as insulting and offensive content published by the comedian on Instagram.

According to Mizan, the charges include knowingly expressing support for Israel on social media, insult and engaging in propaganda against the Islamic Republic through negative portrayals of the country and support for the Pahlavi dynasty, which ruled Iran until the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Mizan said the case had been referred to court for further proceedings.

Shakiba came under scrutiny after publishing a satirical video on October 13 in which he imitated Khamenei's voice, parodying his meetings with poets.

On October 14, Mizan announced that Tehran prosecutors had opened a case against a social media personality identified only by the initials S.Sh., accusing him of publishing insulting and offensive content.

The agency said action had been taken against the individual but provided no details about the measures, the specific charges or his whereabouts.

US-based rights group Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRANA) reported on October 14 that authorities had opened a case against Shakiba following the satirical video, saying the judiciary had not disclosed details about the proceedings or his situation.

Shakiba is known for posting comedy videos and voice impressions of prominent figures on Instagram, where he had around one million followers.

Following the announcement of legal proceedings, posts on his Instagram account were removed. A notice bearing the emblem of Iran's police said the account had been restricted by judicial order over what authorities called criminal content.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-affiliated Fars news agency also criticized the video, accusing Shakiba of insulting Khamenei and his family.

Shakiba had previously published satirical impressions of other Islamic Republic officials and expressed support for protestors killed during the January uprising.

Previous arrests and prosecutions of Iranian comedians

Iranian authorities have previously arrested and sentenced comedians and satirists over their work, drawing criticism from human rights groups.

Last month, Shaker Bori, a comedian and social media personality from the southwestern city of Abadan, was sentenced to 13 months and 20 days in prison for disseminating false information with the intent to harm others, according to the rights group HRANA.

Bori was also fined 45 million rials (approximately $17) for insulting a member of parliament. The case followed a complaint by lawmaker Mousa Ghazanfarabadi over a video Bori had published.

Bori had previously been arrested on July 31, 2023, after reporting to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence office in Abadan to seek the return of his confiscated mobile phone, according to the Norway-based rights group Hengaw.

He was released on bail on August 10, 2023, after spending 10 days in detention.

Another comedian, Zeinab Mousavi, known for her online character Empress Kuzco, was sentenced to six months in prison in November 2025 over a satirical video about Ferdowsi, the celebrated Persian poet.

In February 2026, a Tehran appeals court upheld the sentence, which also included a fine of 160 million rials (approximately $59) and an order to write a research paper about Ferdowsi, according to HRANA.

Mousavi had previously been arrested in October 2022 in the central city of Qom during nationwide protests sparked by the death of Mahsa Amini in morality police custody. She was released on bail in November that year and subsequently sentenced to two years in prison.

Mousavi said she had spent 25 days in solitary confinement during her detention.

She was arrested again in 2023 and released several days later, according to HRANA.

In another case, satirical writer Kioomars Marzban was arrested at his home on August 26, 2018, by Revolutionary Guard intelligence agents.

Marzban was sentenced in August 2019 to 23 years and nine months in prison on charges including insulting the supreme leader, propaganda against the Islamic Republic and cooperating with a hostile state, according to HRANA.

The sentence, of which 11 years were enforceable under Iranian law, was upheld on appeal in October 2019.

Marzban was released from Tehran's Evin prison in February 2021 after serving approximately two and a half years. His lawyer, Mohammad Hossein Aghasi, said six years of his sentence had been pardoned and the remainder suspended, according to freedom of expression organization ARTICLE 19.

Following his release, ARTICLE 19 condemned his prosecution, saying he should never have been imprisoned for his writing.

"His case is emblematic of the Iranian authorities' zero tolerance for freedom of expression and the Judiciary's lack of independence," said Saloua Ghazouani, then director of ARTICLE 19's Middle East and North Africa program.

PEN America has also criticized Iran's treatment of satirical artists. In June 2023, the organization condemned the arrest of cartoonist Atena Farghadani following the publication of a satirical drawing on Instagram.

"Cartoonists should not be persecuted for their creative expression," said Julie Trébault, then director of PEN America's Artists at Risk Connection.

PEN America said the arrest reflected broader efforts by Iranian authorities to intimidate artists, journalists and activists.

Iran may be approaching a mental-health emergency as prolonged uncertainty over war, economic pressure and the future takes a growing toll on the public, the head of the country’s Psychology and Counseling Organization said on Sunday.

Asked by ILNA how far Iranian society was from a mental-health emergency, Alireza Agha-Yousefi said: “I don’t think we are very far from it.”

He pointed to marriage, divorce and birth rates as areas of concern and said authorities needed to act before psychological and social problems became more severe.

Agha-Yousefi said the prolonged state of neither full-scale war nor peace was itself becoming a major source of pressure.

“The overall condition of society in a situation of neither war nor peace can create significant psychological strain,” he said.

He said people normally try to meet their needs while also responding to threats, but when both are present at the same time, threats tend to dominate.

“Uncertainty about the future is one of the most difficult situations,” he said, adding that it deprives people of the ability to plan their lives.

Agha-Yousefi said prolonged uncertainty could produce severe anxiety and, over time, lead to both physical and psychological exhaustion.

He cautioned that the consequences of intense stress do not always appear immediately.

“The effects may show themselves one or two years later,” he said, citing depression, marital conflict and physical health problems as possible outcomes.

He also pointed to prolonged muscle tension, joint and spinal pain and gastrointestinal problems as conditions that can be associated with chronic stress.

President Masoud Pezeshkian last week also described the current “no war, no peace” situation as the worst position Iran could be in, as tensions with Washington remained unresolved.

Agha-Yousefi said the same economic conditions contributing to psychological strain were also making treatment less accessible.

He said demand for counselling had risen, but inflation and declining purchasing power meant many people could no longer afford psychological services.

“Psychological services are not covered by basic insurance,” he said, adding that official figures on the number of people seeking treatment could therefore give a misleading picture.

He said some people who need help simply do not seek it because of the cost.

A proposal to bring psychological services under insurance coverage had been submitted to the organization’s central council around four months ago but had yet to be approved, he said.

Pressure on families and social stability

Agha-Yousefi also said Iran appeared to be moving toward greater social dislocation.

“It seems our social situation is, to some extent, moving toward anomie or social normlessness,” he said.

He warned that as social stress rises, the effects can spread into family life and wider social behavior, including later marriage, addiction and greater instability within households.

“When problems enter the family, they can be a sign of deeper social damage,” he said.

He added that severe family pressures could, in some cases, contribute to extreme violence, including killings within families.

Agha-Yousefi said delaying preventive measures would make the psychological, physical and social consequences much harder and more expensive to address later.

His comments come as speculation grows over possible renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran.

Recent reports have said the US military has prepared options for further strikes after the November 3 midterm elections if President Donald Trump authorizes them.

That uncertainty has added another layer of pressure to an economy already strained by inflation, a weakening currency and declining purchasing power.

The war with Iran raises a familiar question for Israel: Can battlefield gains produce lasting peace? Its military history offers mixed answers, from unresolved victories to withdrawals and ceasefires that left adversaries armed.

Destroying Iran’s military capabilities and preventing their reconstruction are different objectives, requiring different measures of success.

Since 1948, Israel has fought conventional Arab armies and armed organizations such as Hezbollah and Hamas, and has increasingly confronted Iran directly through missile, drone and air attacks far beyond its borders. These forms of warfare have overlapped, posing different challenges for bringing the fighting to an end.

Their endings show how battlefield outcomes interact with diplomacy, outside pressure and arrangements for security after the fighting.

Fighting between Jewish and Arab communities followed the UN’s 1947 partition plan. After Israel declared independence in May 1948, neighboring Arab armies entered the conflict. Israel survived and gained territory beyond the boundaries proposed for the Jewish state.

In 1949, it signed separate armistice agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. These established lines separating the forces, rather than permanent political settlements. The Egyptian agreement explicitly envisaged a subsequent peaceful settlement.

Israel’s survival did not resolve the territorial dispute or the displacement of Palestinians. The fighting ended without peace between Israel and its neighbors.

1956: Military gains, withdrawal under pressure

During the Suez crisis, Israel attacked Egypt in coordination with Britain and France, rapidly advancing across Sinai.

Pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Nations forced a withdrawal, completed in March 1957. Israel could not retain the territory it had captured, despite its battlefield success.

The outcome nevertheless brought security gains: Israel regained access to the Straits of Tiran, while a UN emergency force deployed in Sinai. The US State Department’s historical account distinguishes those gains from the territorial withdrawal.

The episode illustrates why withdrawal is not automatically evidence of military defeat, and why military superiority alone does not determine a war’s political outcome.

1967: Six days of fighting, decades of consequences

Israel’s opening airstrikes devastated Egypt’s air force. Within six days, Israeli forces had captured Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.The war ended through ceasefires, without a formal surrender by the defeated Arab states. Israel’s decisive battlefield victory transformed the territorial balance but did not settle the conflict.

UN Security Council Resolution 242 subsequently established a framework linking Israeli withdrawal from occupied territory with an end to belligerency and recognition of states’ right to live within secure, recognized boundaries.

The military result was immediate. Disputes over occupation, borders and Palestinian rights lasted far beyond the fighting.

1973: From surprise attack to a peace treaty

Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli forces in Sinai and the Golan Heights in October 1973, initially making substantial gains. Israel counterattacked and crossed the Suez Canal before US-Soviet diplomacy and UN ceasefire resolutions helped stop the fighting.

The US State Department’s history describes the war as opening the way for Henry Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy and, ultimately, the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty. Egypt did not recover all Sinai through military action, but the war helped break the diplomatic stalemate.

The 1978 Camp David accords provided the framework for the 1979 treaty. Israel agreed to withdraw from Sinai in exchange for peace with Egypt. The main withdrawal was completed in 1982; the disputed Taba area was returned in 1989 following arbitration.

Egypt recovered territory through a combination of war and diplomacy. Israel exchanged territorial control for a political agreement with a major adversary.

Lebanon, 1982–2000: Initial success, prolonged conflict

Israel’s 1982 invasion drove into Beirut, where US-mediated arrangements secured the departure of Palestine Liberation Organization leaders and fighters. This was an evacuation from Beirut, not the elimination of every Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon.

Israel withdrew much of its force in 1985 but retained a southern security zone alongside the allied South Lebanon Army. Its remaining troops left in May 2000, following years of conflict with Hezbollah. UNIFIL’s historical account records both withdrawals.

The withdrawal was unilateral, without a peace treaty or formal Israeli surrender. Hezbollah portrayed it as a victory; Israel ended a prolonged deployment without resolving the underlying confrontation.

The departure of one armed organization’s leadership in 1982 had not produced a lasting end to fighting.

The 2006 war followed Hezbollah’s cross-border attack and capture of two Israeli soldiers. Israel launched extensive air and ground operations, but Hezbollah remained armed and continued firing rockets during the conflict.

Neither side’s survival or military performance alone explains the settlement. The operative mechanism was UN Security Council Resolution 1701, adopted on August 11, followed by a cessation of hostilities on August 14.

It called for Hezbollah to stop attacks, Israel to stop offensive operations, and Israeli forces to withdraw as Lebanese troops and an expanded UNIFIL deployed. It envisaged an area between the Blue Line and Litani River free of armed personnel and weapons other than those of the Lebanese government and UNIFIL.

Hezbollah was not disarmed. Nevertheless, UNIFIL says the arrangements helped sustain almost 17 years of relative calm before the escalation beginning in 2023. An incomplete settlement still had significant practical effects.

The Gaza wars of 2008–09, 2012, 2014 and 2021 ended without Hamas surrendering or losing all its military capabilities.

Scholars Efraim Inbar and Eitan Shamir described Israel’s approach as “mowing the grass”: periodically degrading an adversary’s capabilities and restoring deterrence rather than expecting a permanent political resolution through force. Their study appeared online in 2013 and in the Journal of Strategic Studies in 2014.

After Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, Israel set broader objectives, including dismantling its military and governing capabilities and recovering the hostages. Shamir argued that the attack marked a departure from the previous limited-campaign approach. That was his strategic assessment, rather than proof that eliminating Hamas was achievable.

The ensuing war devastated Gaza. The October 2025 ceasefire did not settle its future: a year later, the UN human rights office was still reporting killings despite the agreement.

Lebanon after 2023: Military damage and state authority

Israel’s 2024 campaign killed Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and other senior commanders, severely damaging its leadership. The fighting nevertheless moved toward a negotiated cessation of hostilities rather than formal surrender.

The US-French-brokered arrangement took effect on November 27, 2024, and again rested on implementing Resolution 1701, Lebanese state authority and Israeli withdrawal.

Disarmament remained contested. In October 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that Hezbollah demanded the return of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities, illustrating the continuing struggle over weapons outside state control.

Iran: Ending operations or preventing reconstruction?

The June 2025 war involved Israeli attacks on Iranian military and nuclear targets and direct US strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. US involvement therefore preceded the broader war of 2026.

Israel’s Foreign Ministry described the nuclear threat as “existential and imminent” in its account of the operation. That characterization was Israel’s stated justification, not an independently established finding that Iran possessed nuclear weapons. The same document records Israel’s acceptance of a US-proposed ceasefire on June 24.The broader confrontation in 2026 extended to shipping and energy supplies. By October, the US naval blockade and the standoff over reopening the Strait of Hormuz remained unresolved.

Netanyahu has explicitly advocated moving beyond containment. Addressing military cadets in February 2026, he declared there would be “no more containment of threats” and emphasized preemptive action. This supports describing a shift in his stated approach, without assuming a uniform doctrine across every Israeli institution.

Destroying launchers or facilities has measurable immediate effects. Preventing their reconstruction depends on industrial capacity, supply networks, political decisions and whatever monitoring or enforcement follows.

Within the approach of seeking to prevent Iran from rebuilding its military threat, two scenarios can be considered. Neither is a prediction or an exhaustive account of how the conflict might end.

The first is a military defeat sufficiently extensive to destroy much of Iran’s offensive capability and substantially constrain its reconstruction. Lasting results would depend on measures that prevent replenishment, rather than destruction alone.The second combines military defeat with the end of the Islamic Republic and its replacement by a political system that abandons hostility toward Israel and support for armed proxies.

That scenario depends on more than a change of leadership. It assumes a successor government both chooses and can enforce a different policy, including ending financial, military and operational support for allied armed groups. A government’s collapse would not itself establish those conditions.

The scenarios may overlap, but neither guarantees stability. Their outcomes would depend on political authority, security arrangements and the capacity to enforce commitments after combat ends.

Other possible outcomes include a negotiated agreement that constrains Iran’s capabilities without changing its government, or a prolonged armed standoff sustained by deterrence. Neither would necessarily eliminate the underlying hostility, though either could bring the current fighting to an end.

Israel’s earlier wars provide different benchmarks: territorial withdrawal under international pressure in 1956, land exchanged for peace with Egypt, unilateral withdrawal from Lebanon, and ceasefire arrangements that reduced fighting without disarming Hezbollah. Each ended a particular phase of conflict; only some produced a broader political settlement.

Iranians say they are paying more for slow, unreliable and heavily restricted internet after mobile operators raised data prices by up to 40%, with some reporting that their allowances run out unusually quickly.

Messages sent to Iran International described mounting frustration over the cost of staying connected, from families worried about paying for online classes to users struggling to send even a text message.

“All we have left of life in Iran is passing the time on our phones, and they are taking that away too,” one reader from Baharestan said.

Mobile operators Hamrah-e Aval and Irancell increased their data package prices by up to 40% early on Friday, October 23, according to state media.

One reader said a weekly four-gigabyte package had risen from 330,000 rials ($0.12) to 450,000 rials ($0.17). Another said a monthly six-gigabyte package that cost 530,000 rials ($0.20) three days earlier now cost 740,000 rials ($0.28).

The pressure comes as Iran’s official minimum wage stands at about 166.3 million rials per month, equivalent to roughly $62 at the unofficial-market exchange rate.

Others questioned why prices were rising again after earlier increases before and during the war.

“Didn’t they raise internet prices two months before the 40-day war? Didn’t they raise package prices again during the war, taking advantage of the blackout?” one reader asked, referring to the US-led war that began on February 28. “So what is this latest increase for?”

The higher charges have brought no improvement in service, according to accounts from users across the country.

A reader in the northern province of Mazandaran described Hamrah-e Aval’s connection as moving “at a snail’s pace,” saying Wi-Fi connections in many areas also cut out, even when accessing domestic messaging apps.

In Iranshahr, in southeastern Iran, another reader reported severely degraded ADSL service followed by a complete outage from 8 p.m. on Friday. Another said sending a text message on Telegram was difficult, let alone a photograph or video.

Iran International reported on Friday that users in Semnan, Shiraz, Tabriz, Kerman, Tehran and Tonekabon had complained of sharply slower connections, malfunctioning tools used to bypass internet filtering and difficulty accessing social media.

The Telecommunications Company of Iran has previously attributed some disruptions to “upgrading and optimizing technical infrastructure.”

The complaints come against a backdrop of extensive restrictions on internet access. Freedom House’s 2026 report gave Iran an internet freedom score of nine out of 100, down from 13.

The organization said Iran’s tiered internet system had made access to the global internet difficult and expensive, leaving much of the population restricted to a domestic network controlled by the authorities.

All global social media platforms, from X and Telegram to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, are banned in Iran.

Several readers also accused operators of “stealing data,” saying their allowances were depleted far faster than their usage would explain.

“I topped up my data package two days ago. Today, only 600 megabytes of my six gigabytes are left, even though we don’t have a decent connection,” one reader said.

Another said a six-gigabyte package bought for 570,000 rials ($0.21) had run out within two days despite limited use, and now cost 730,000 rials ($0.27) to replace.

For families, the increases have also raised concerns about the cost of education if gas shortages force schools to move classes online.

One reader said a one-gigabyte Hamrah-e Aval package cost 330,000 rials ($0.12), including tax. “With things like this, how are we supposed to buy data for online classes?”

Another said repeated price increases had left them unable to afford internet access at all.

“We live in a country with vast oil and gas resources,” another reader said, “but we earn in rials and spend in dollars.”
