#35783. Iran sends conflicting signals on US deal as Trump raises prospect of strikes

Tehran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, Iran’s envoy to Pakistan said Saturday, while an IRGC-affiliated outlet rejected such an exchange and President Donald Trump raised the possibility of strikes as soon as “tomorrow.”

Iran’s ambassador to Islamabad, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran had conveyed through Pakistani mediators that it was prepared to reopen the strait if Washington ended its blockade of Iranian ports, the Associated Press reported.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, Moghadam said Iranian officials had communicated that position during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir. He accused Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade would continue.

Moghadam said Iran remained open to negotiations under a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in June, according to AP’s readout of his remarks.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker that framework, which envisaged restoring shipping through the strait, lifting the blockade and beginning negotiations on a broader deal covering Iran’s nuclear program.

Al Arabiya separately reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources, that Iran had informed Pakistan it was willing to resume negotiations with Washington and reopen the strait in exchange for the blockade being lifted.

But the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an informed source rejecting Al Arabiya’s account as “lies and fantasy” and saying Tehran had made no new proposal to Pakistani mediators.

“Iran fundamentally does not accept any equation of the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the blockade,” the source said, adding that Iran would find ways around the blockade and ultimately break it.

The source said Tehran stood by seven conditions already formally conveyed through mediators. An earlier “seven-day plan” setting out its demands for reopening the strait had been passed to Washington, the source said, adding that insecurity would persist until all Iranian demands were met, including an end to disruption of its ports and shipping.

Tasnim’s denial explicitly targeted Al Arabiya’s report, rather than the ambassador’s remarks reported by AP.

Trump, meanwhile, kept open the possibility of both military action and an agreement, saying he wanted a permanent solution to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” Trump told reporters Saturday. “There’s a possibility I will. There’s also a possibility we’ll have a nice big beautiful agreement.”

He said Iranian leaders wanted a deal but questioned whether they would abide by it.

“They want to make a deal. But the problem is, will they hold the deal?”

Trump argued that ending the military campaign after B-2 bomber strikes in 2025 would have allowed Iran to rebuild its nuclear capabilities and eventually develop a bomb.

“I’ve got to make it permanent. That’s the only reason I’m doing it as long as I’m doing,” he said.

The Hill reported Saturday, citing two sources familiar with the planning, that the US military had prepared options for renewed strikes on Iran after November’s midterm elections.

One source said US Central Command had follow-up strike plans ready pending White House authorization. Another said multiple options were being presented to War Secretary Pete Hegseth and that Trump would keep his options open until a final decision was required.

A Pentagon official told The Hill the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that US naval forces are preparing for possible renewed strikes against Iran, with sailors loading munitions and readying aircraft aboard American warships.

The preparations include the USS George Washington aircraft carrier strike group, as Washington considers further military action against the Islamic Republic.

Armed Baluch groups in Iran’s southeast are adding one more strain on the Islamic Republic’s security forces just as war has stretched them thinnest, with 18 attacks in the 18 days to October 10, more than in any full month this year.

At least 63 armed incidents were documented across Sistan and Baluchestan and neighboring Kerman province between March 31 and October 10, leaving at least 94 people dead and 33 injured, according to the rights group HRANA. The attacks have grown more complex as well as more frequent: coordinated ambushes, roadside bombs and heavier weapons.

The question is whether a decades-old insurgency, long contained by force, can become a wider problem for a state fighting on other fronts.

Several Baluch armed organizations joined forces in December 2025 under the People’s Fighters Front. The coalition includes Jaish al-Adl, which Iran and the United States both list as a terrorist organization.

The front has increasingly framed its goal as ending the Islamic Republic’s rule rather than winning concessions for the Baluch. Whether it can draw support beyond the southeast is unproven.

Its timing is not accidental. Iran’s security services are absorbing the consequences of war with the United States and Israel while still needing the forces they rely on to suppress dissent at home.

Rahim Bandoui, an Iranian-Baluch human rights activist and senior member of the Balochistan People’s Party, said the conflict itself is nothing new.

Speaking on Iran International’s Eye for Iran podcast, he traced it to decades of repression, arguing that Tehran has long treated peaceful political activity and armed resistance in the province as the same security threat.

What has changed, he said, is the state’s position. A government weakened by war presents armed groups with an opening they did not have before.

If the attacks keep growing, Tehran will have to send more personnel and resources to the southeast at a time when its security forces are already stretched. Those forces have contained unrest there before through military operations, mass arrests and lethal force. A sustained insurgency adds a cost on top of the war.

That cost could be felt elsewhere. Every unit tied down in Sistan and Baluchestan is one not available against protests or other opposition in the rest of the country.

The limits are real, though. There is no evidence the coalition can take and hold territory or threaten the central government’s control. Its political ambitions face a further obstacle across the border: Baluch armed groups in Pakistan differ considerably from their Iranian counterparts in ideology and aims, so a unified cross-border movement is unlikely without substantial change on both sides.

The insurgency sits on grievances that successive crackdowns have failed to address.

Sistan and Baluchestan, home to a mostly Sunni Baluch population, is among Iran’s poorest provinces despite its position on the Pakistani and Afghan borders and its natural resources. Residents face discrimination, few jobs and poor access to schools, clinics and other basic services.

Tens of thousands of people in the province have no official identity documents, Sabah Baluch, a human rights advocate with Iran House, told the podcast, which shuts them out of basic services and legal rights. For some families that has meant generations without formal schooling or work.

Hardship pushes residents into dangerous informal work, above all carrying fuel across the border, where they risk being shot by security forces or burning to death in vehicle fires.

The province has also seen some of the Islamic Republic’s deadliest violence against dissent. On September 30, 2022, during the nationwide protests that followed the death of Mahsa Amini, security forces killed at least 87 people in Zahedan, the provincial capital, most of them Baluch worshippers, in what became known as Bloody Friday.

Baluch prisoners are also executed out of all proportion to their numbers. According to Iran Human Rights, they accounted for 20 percent of recorded executions in 2023, 11 percent in 2024 and 9 percent in 2025, from a group that is a small fraction of Iran’s population.

For now the Islamic Republic retains the military and security capacity to hold the southeast, and nothing suggests the insurgency can change the balance of power on its own.

The larger question is not whether armed groups can defeat government forces in Sistan and Baluchestan. It is whether a state that has relied on lethal force against its opponents for decades can go on containing several challenges at once while war makes new demands on the forces it uses to do so.

For Iran’s wider opposition, the answer will matter well beyond the southeast.

You can watch Eye for Iran on YouTube or listen on any podcast platform.

Pakistan is mediating between Iran and the United States even as it sends troops to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Tehran’s allies, placing Islamabad in the conflicting roles of peace broker and military partner to Iran’s rivals.

On Tuesday, Pakistan's military chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran.

Munir has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, including meetings at the White House.

Islamabad helped broker the June agreement between Washington and Tehran. The truce did not last, but Pakistan has kept its mediation channel open.

Pakistan has taken a direct military role in Saudi Arabia's defense.

Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed approximately 8,000 troops, a squadron of fighter jets and air-defense systems to the kingdom under a bilateral agreement. Saudi Arabia financed the deployment, according to Pakistani officials cited by Reuters.

Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security deepened in August when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, treating an attack against one member as an attack against all.

This week, Islamabad announced that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed ratification, while Turkey's remained pending. The partners have also discussed further military mobilization following attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi territory.

On Wednesday, Pakistan signed another defense agreement, this time with Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia. The Badr agreement, signed in Doha, offers opportunities for industrial cooperation and defense production.

Together with Makkah, the agreements deepen Pakistan's military, diplomatic and economic ties across countries pursuing different regional agendas.

That tension was evident during Munir's Tehran visit. Pakistani government sources told Turkey's state-run Anadolu news agency that the talks focused more on stopping Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia than on reviving US-Iran negotiations.

Munir pressed Iranian leaders to use their influence over the Houthis, citing Pakistan's commitment to defend the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states supply much of Pakistan’s energy, while millions of Pakistani workers live in the region. Defense cooperation brings financial support and industrial opportunities, while diplomacy helps protect relations with competing partners.

Pakistan appears to be carving out an unusual role: mediating between Iran and the United States, helping defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, and joining new regional defense ventures while retaining direct access to Iranian leaders.

But the same network could become harder to manage if regional tensions escalate. The more security commitments Pakistan assumes, the greater the chance that relationships which currently give Islamabad leverage could eventually force it to choose between them.

China regards its relationship with Iran as largely transactional and is not firmly committed to defending the current Iranian government, according to Tong Zhao, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Speaking to Iran International, Zhao said Beijing shares Iran’s “common displeasure” with the United States and Western systems and values Iran’s geographic position for the Belt and Road Initiative.

Yet he described the partnership as driven by energy security, economic interests and longer-term geopolitical calculations rather than ideological solidarity.

“There is some long-term interest in there for sure,” Zhao said. “But it is a transactional relationship.”

China has become Iran's main economic lifeline under US sanctions, buying nearly all of its exported oil, while Tehran has increasingly looked to Beijing alongside Moscow for diplomatic support in the face of Western pressure.

Energy security has provided one of the clearest illustrations of the limits of that partnership.

In a recent meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, both sides publicly underscored that the Strait of Hormuz should remain open without any toll system.

“China is protecting its own economic and energy interest first and foremost,” Zhao said. “We do see China’s position evolving when its own domestic calculations about energy and overall supply chain security change over time.”

The 25-year comprehensive strategic partnership signed by China and Iran in 2021 has also under-delivered. Reports at the time suggested Chinese investment of roughly $400 billion, or about $20 billion annually.

Actual flows have been “at least one order of magnitude smaller,” Zhao said, as Chinese banks and companies have sought to avoid US secondary sanctions.

Zhao said Beijing has come to value nuclear non-proliferation more as its global influence has grown, in part because of its experience with North Korea.

“China doesn’t want Iran to have nuclear weapons, but China eventually is sympathetic to Iran’s cause,” he said. “It thinks that Iran’s need for deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is ultimately driven by American hostile policy.”

Beijing does not see its role as changing Iran’s calculations and has been reluctant to threaten economic or military cutoffs, Zhao said. Instead, it has emphasized that the US and Israel should alter their policies to reduce Tehran’s incentives for nuclear deterrence.

Opposition to externally imposed regime change is a higher priority for Beijing than the nuclear file itself, he said.

“China’s primary security concern is its own regime security, so it doesn’t want to see the norm of allowing foreign countries interfering in other countries’ internal affairs and toppling governments that they don’t like.”

Beijing’s initial criticism of the US-Israeli war against Iran focused heavily on the killing of the supreme leader, which China viewed as a violation of international norms.

But Zhao suggested Beijing's opposition had limits and would depend in part on whether efforts to remove Iran's government violated what China regarded as established international norms.

Beijing has cultivated ties with Saudi Arabia, including joint military exercises and involvement in its missile and nuclear programs, partly as a hedge against uncertainty elsewhere in the region.

China and Russia have meanwhile provided Tehran with diplomatic cover at the UN Security Council, disputing the reimposition of UN sanctions on Iran and most recently opposing efforts to restore international monitoring of their implementation.

Yet China has shown little appetite for becoming a security guarantor for Iran or other regional partners, Zhao said, including through proposals that Iran transfer enriched uranium to Chinese custody.

“China is keenly aware of the potential risks and burdens to play a greater security role,” he said. “Its approach is to develop relations, increasing Chinese influence at the lowest cost.”

That calculation could change as the conflict develops. Zhao said China and Russia could influence its trajectory by supplying air-defense systems or missile-related materials that would help Iran deter or survive future strikes.

But he declined to predict how the confrontation over Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz would ultimately end.

“I generally don’t have good answers about how this war will end in the long run,” Zhao said.

Iranian leaders raised the conditions for negotiations with the United States and issued fresh warnings of a wider military response on Wednesday, even as signs persisted that Tehran was leaving room for diplomacy.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said threats and sanctions must be lifted in practice before conditions for negotiations could be established, while Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said Iran would launch offensive operations against any country that attacked it as part of a shift toward asymmetric warfare.

An unnamed senior security official also told state-run Press TV that Iran was prepared for an all-out war and would respond “without restraint” to renewed attacks or assassinations.

The rhetoric coincided with high-level discussions in Tehran. Iranian media reported Wednesday that Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf had met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss the latest military and economic developments in the confrontation with the United States and Israel.

The meeting also addressed strengthening Iran's national capabilities, maintaining social cohesion, tackling economic difficulties and “advancing relations with strategic partners,” according to the reports.

Yet diplomatic channels remain active. Russian President Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that there was still room for diplomacy over Iran and that an agreement with Tehran was needed, according to the Kremlin.

The competing signals leave open whether Tehran is raising the price of a negotiated pause or preparing for another phase of confrontation.

The conservative daily Jomhouri Eslami reported, citing “informed sources,” that discussions mediated by Qatar and Pakistan could take place this week around a framework for halting military clashes and securing reciprocal concessions.

The report followed Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir's visit to Tehran on Tuesday and came amid a flurry of diplomatic activity involving Russia and other regional powers.

According to Jomhouri Eslami, the framework would seek to halt military clashes, address outstanding disputes and sequence concessions in a way that reduced the risk of fighting resuming.

The newspaper said it expected that “the region will not see an escalation of tensions under current conditions.”

The prominence given to the prospect of an agreement by a conservative establishment newspaper is notable at a time when Iranian officials publicly deny that substantive nuclear negotiations with Washington are under way.

Sobh-e No, a newspaper aligned with Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, also linked renewed discussion of talks to diplomatic contacts involving Pakistan and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who visited Tehran on Tuesday.

The newspaper reported on a Russian proposal for a joint Iranian-Russian-Chinese initiative concerning the Strait of Hormuz, although Tehran has continued to insist on maintaining its authority over the waterway.

The Pezeshkian administration's Iran newspaper argued that the country's security depended on exercising sovereignty over the strait rather than sharing responsibility with outside powers.

“To preserve our security, we have no option but to exercise sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz,” it wrote.

That position points to one of the difficulties facing any potential agreement: Tehran wants the Strait of Hormuz and broader maritime security addressed alongside the conflict, while Washington has continued to prioritize Iran's nuclear program.

Hardline lawmaker Hassan Nataj called for Supreme Leader Khamenei to reconsider the religious prohibition on nuclear weapons in response to the conflict.

“We should ask the Supreme Leader to revise the fatwa prohibiting nuclear weapons in light of the current situation,” he told the Didban Iran website.

The comments come amid a wider debate among Iranian politicians and commentators over whether the country's nuclear posture still provides sufficient deterrence against further US or Israeli attacks.

The simultaneous emphasis on diplomacy and escalation does not establish which course Tehran ultimately intends to pursue.

But the pattern has become clearer: diplomatic channels remain open while Iranian officials publicly raise the conditions for negotiations and stress that renewed attacks could bring a broader military response.

Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed Iran with US envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday and offered Moscow’s help, shortly after Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran as Russia seeks a role in efforts to end the Iran-US conflict.

The meeting adds to signs that Moscow is positioning itself as both an ally of Tehran and a potential intermediary with Washington as diplomatic efforts remain deadlocked over Iran’s nuclear program and the sequencing of commitments.

Earlier this month, Putin said Russia was prepared to do everything it could to help resolve the crisis and subsequently conveyed Tehran’s position to US President Donald Trump. Neither the contents of the message nor Washington’s response was made public.

In Tehran on Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the two countries had “never” worked as closely as they do now, while Lavrov described Iran’s cause as “just” and said Russian specialists who left the Bushehr nuclear power plant during the war were gradually returning.

Yet Iranian media and commentators questioned how much Moscow could achieve as an intermediary given the fundamental differences between Tehran and Washington.

Tabnak, a news website considered close to Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, said Moscow could help by conveying messages, consulting with both capitals and supporting a political solution, but cautioned that no mediator could overcome the underlying disagreements on its own.

“As long as fundamental disagreements over the terms of an agreement persist, no mediator can guarantee success,” it wrote, citing differences over the sequencing of negotiations and the scope of commitments.

The reformist outlet Rouydad24 said there was little evidence Moscow had brought a comprehensive plan capable of breaking the deadlock.

“What has so far been presented by official Iranian and Russian sources points less to a ‘grand peace plan’ than to the continuation of Russia’s traditional role as a facilitator of dialogue,” it wrote.

A central obstacle in the diplomatic impasse is Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60%.

Russian officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, have indicated that Moscow is prepared to receive the stockpile, a move that could address one of the central concerns surrounding Iran’s nuclear program.

Tehran, however, has rejected the idea of transferring its enriched uranium abroad and denied that nuclear negotiations with Washington are under way.

The position was reiterated during Pakistani army chief Asim Munir’s visit to Tehran on Tuesday. Rezaei told Munir that none of Iran’s enriched material would leave the country, describing it as a national asset intended for domestic use.

Before Lavrov’s arrival, conservative political activist Ali Gholhaki claimed Russia had been partly persuaded by an Iranian proposal, advanced when Ali Larijani was secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to establish a framework for transferring uranium enriched to 60%.

But following the visit, Gholhaki said Lavrov had produced no tangible result and had left “without any particular achievement.”

The conservative newspaper Khorasan argued that negotiating over Iran’s enriched uranium could increase rather than reduce the danger of another attack.

It argued that while Iran did not possess a nuclear deterrent, its stockpile of highly enriched uranium itself acted as a form of deterrence by raising the risks of further US escalation.

Mohammad-Sadegh Alizadeh, a journalist interviewed by the conservative Farhikhtegan newspaper, said Tehran’s immediate priority should instead be ending the war on terms acceptable to Iran.

“Whether the Russians have agreed to accept Iran’s 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% is a secondary issue to be addressed later,” he said. “First, the question of ending the war must be settled.”

Doubts about Russia’s intentions extend beyond whether it can bridge the divide between Tehran and Washington.

Reformist journalist Ahmad Zeidabadi argued that Iranian decision-makers should nevertheless welcome any Russian initiative capable of stopping another war.

“Russian interference is an evil, of course, but compared with the prospect of another war, it is the lesser evil,” he wrote on Telegram.

Commentator Mehran Tabatabaei argued that Moscow’s approach to Iran remained subordinate to its negotiations with Washington over Ukraine.

“Russia will not take any positive steps until it resolves the Ukraine issue and obtains the concessions it wants from the United States over Ukraine,” he wrote.

Journalist Mohammad Aghazadeh offered a starker assessment, saying failure by Lavrov to make progress would suggest diplomacy itself was approaching a dead end.

“Either the current state of uncertainty will continue, or an intense war will begin,” he wrote, “one that will probably not be as easy to end as it is to start.”

#35785. NYT Smashed Beef Kofta with Cucumber Yogurt Sauce

This Smashed Beef Kofta is a streamlined take on koftas where spiced beef mince is cooked in raggedy chunks rather than threading on skewers. Based on a wildly popular New York Times Cooking recipe, it’s impressively fast, incredibly delicious, and there’s so many ways to serve it!

Every year the New York Times publishes its most popular recipes and last year, Smashed Beef Kebab recipe by Zaynab Issa took the top spot. It’s a streamlined take on Persian kebabs where turmeric spiced beef is dropped in a hot pan in rough chunks, hard seared on one side then served on a bed of cucumber yogurt sauce.

Like traditional Persian koobideh kebabs, grated onion is mixed through the beef, along with walnuts and raisins that would usually be sprinkled over Persian yogurt sauce.

I love the technique and how you can make it your own. I wanted more kofta flavour (the original recipe only uses turmeric), so I used my lamb kofta spice mix. It all gets piled over cooling cucumber mint yogurt sauce and finished with a drizzle of pomegranate molasses – don’t skip this, it’s *chef’s kiss*! (Balsamic is a perfect substitute). Then you serve with warm pita for scooping or stuffing.

Beef – This recipe uses beef mince but lamb would be equally as delicious. Chicken or turkey could also be used but just be aware they are leaner so the meat won’t be quite as juicy.

Kofta spices – As mentioned above, the original recipe on New York Times Cooking only uses turmeric. I made it as written, but wanted more kofta spices so I used the spice mix from my lamb koftas. Feel free to omit the cayenne for zero spiciness, but whatever you do, don’t skip the cinnamon! This is what makes it special. 🙂

Cranberries – or raisins. Raisins is actually traditional but I liked the extra tartness that cranberries brings to this.

Walnuts – Or almonds or pecans roughly chopped.

Whole onion – This is grated using a box grater. If you wear contacts like me, lucky you. If you don’t, look, nobody will laugh if you wear onion goggles. It’s worth it, trust me! Grating onion is a fabulous flavour-adding secret I regularly deploy, and the Persians have been doing it for centuries! 🙂

Yogurt – Just any plain, unsweetened yogurt. Full fat is better, but low fat will work. 🙂

Large cucumber – One large Lebanese cucumber (Persian cucumber), about 25cm / 10″ long, or two medium ones. There is no salting and sweating or squeezing liquids out, the grated cucumber is just mixed straight into the yogurt and the water loosens it into a sauce.

Mint – The recipe calls for fresh mint which really does add a beautiful hit of freshness into the sauce. Coriander/cilantro makes a great alternative for a different flavour that goes with the spices in the beef. Otherwise, dried mint can be used.

Salt – This gets added in right at the end, just before spreading on the plate. If you add it at the beginning then the cucumber will sweat which will make the sauce more watery.

Don’t try to be neat and roll balls when dropping lumps of meat into the pan. The whole point is raggedy lumps of meat so you get lovely texture when those jaggedy edges crisp up!

Yogurt Sauce – Make the yogurt sauce first, to give it a bit of time for the flavours to meld. Grate the cucumber in a bowl using a standard box grater. Add the mint and yogurt, mix, then set aside on the counter while you make the smashed koftas. We will mix salt in just before serving – if you do it now, it makes the cucumber sweat and go watery.

Grate the onion using a standard box grater straight into a bowl.

Make kofta mix – Add remaining kofta ingredients into the bowl and mix well with your hands.

Drop chunks – Heat the oil in a large non-stick pan over medium high heat (or if using a very well seasoned cast iron pan, you won’t need oil). Then drop 2.5cm / 1″ chunks of meat into the pan – no rolling, no precision here, just raggedy chunks of meat. Move at a solid pace and just eyeball the size.

Hard sear one side – It’s fine if your pan is full, the meat shrinks. Leave it undisturbed for 5 to 7 minutes until the underside is dark golden brown. If your heat source is patchy, rotate and shuffle the pan as needed to make the pieces brown as evenly as you can.

Add fruit and nuts – Once the underside is really well browned, flip the beef as best you can to get a bit of colour on the other side. Add the cranberries and walnuts (I crumble whole walnuts in with my hands) then after 1 minute, stir gently and make sure all the beef is cooked through.

Serve – To serve, mix salt into the yogurt then spread it on a large-ish plate. Pile the beef over. Drizzle with pomegranate molasses (about 1 tablespoon), extra virgin olive oil, sprinkle with remaining mint and pile warm pita bread on the side. And it’s ready to serve!

This dish is fabulously versatile! Here are some options (I’m sure there are more):

Pita for scooping – use pita bread to scoop the yogurt and pile some beef on.

Stuff – split the pita bread pockets open and stuff the yogurt and beef inside!

Wraps – make gyros-like wraps by using flatbreads and adding shredded lettuce, tomato slices and chopped red onion.

Bowls – Make bowls with basmati rice, and a pile of diced tomato and cucumbers on the side. There’s plenty of yogurt sauce that you won’t need to make a separate dressing for the salad.

To be honest though, I think you’ll even find it enjoyable just eating spoonfuls of the yogurt sauce and beef. It’s such a lovely combination – the warmly spiced beef with the refreshing yogurt sauce.

Any other suggestions for how to serve these smashed koftas?? Share your thoughts to inspire others! – Nagi x

#35786. Sopa de carne, legumes e macarrão.

Se fez frio, por aqui tem sopa de carne na mesma hora! A verdade é que aqui em casa nem precisa fazer frio pra rolar sopinha porque o Marcelo adora. A Lis desde pequena come que é uma beleza e eu sempre estou querendo. Então para vocês “sopa nem é janta” ou é?

Aqui é sempre bem vinda, mas não importa quanto eu faça, nunca sobra!

Ou o brasileiro ama sopa, ou odeia. Não tem como encontrar alguém que fique no meio-termo, mas garanto que a maioria não fica de fora dessa paixão. Absolutamente em todos os cantos do país existem receitas únicas! Daquelas que conquistam paladares com sabores da região, porém se tem uma coisa que é comum a qualquer receita é como ela carrega um “ar de conforto”!

Isto é, você sempre se sente como se estivesse comendo na casa da sua avó de tanto carinho que um prato de sopa carrega. E olha que isso não tem nenhuma relação com a temperatura ou ambiente! Isso porque seja no calor do nordeste ou no frio do sul, uma boa sopa é sempre bem-vinda.

As sopas favoritas dos brasileiros são muitas e refletem a rica mistura cultural do país, então temos a tradicional canja de galinha, por exemplo, que é sempre uma escolha clássica. Feita com arroz, frango, legumes e temperos, essa sopa é conhecida por suas propriedades nutritivas e por ser um verdadeiro “remédio caseiro” para resfriados e gripes.

Outra queridinha é o caldo verde, originário de Portugal, mas que ganhou o coração dos brasileiros. Com linguiça, batatas e couve, essa sopa é especialmente popular nas noites frias do sul e sudeste do Brasil.

Para quem aprecia sabores mais intensos, o caldinho de feijão é uma ótima pedida. Simples, porém delicioso, ele é feito com feijão preto ou carioca e temperado com alho, cebola e bacon. É comum encontrá-lo como entrada em bares e restaurantes, acompanhado de torradas ou pão.

No nordeste, não podemos esquecer do caldo de sururu, uma iguaria feita com mexilhões, leite de coco, coentro e azeite de dendê. É uma explosão de sabores que remete às praias e à cultura praiana da região.

E, claro, não podemos deixar de mencionar a versátil sopa de legumes ou com o seu nome chique, o Minestrone, que varia de acordo com a disponibilidade de ingredientes e o gosto de quem a prepara. É uma opção saudável e saborosa que aquece o corpo e a alma.

Independentemente da receita, as sopas são um verdadeiro conforto em forma de comida, trazendo calor e satisfação e por aqui amamos tanto que tem “Especial de Sopa” por aqui e no Youtube, afinal nada melhor do que uma boa sopa para aquecer o coração e reunir a família ao redor da mesa.

Chega de papo furado e bora pra receitinha porque é para isso que estamos aqui, então se prepara para uma sopa simples porém muito saborosa e que agrada todo tipo de paladar.

🔸1 cebola pequena picada;🔸2 dentes de alho;🔸1 col. (sopa) de shoyu;🔸1 col. (sopa) de extrato de tomates;🔸Suco de 1/2 limão;🔸250g de carne bovina picada (usei músculo);🔸2 xíc. (chá) de legumes picados (usei batata, cenoura, vagem e chuchu);🔸2/3 xíc. (chá) de macarrão para sopa;🔸Azeite, sal, pimenta-do-reino e ervas a gosto.

Na panela de pressão refogue a cebola no azeite, junte a carne e quando perder o aspecto de crua, junte o alho e mexa mais um minuto, acrescente então os legumes, o shoyu, o extrato e o limão.

Acrescente o macarrão e cubra com agua quente (dois dedos acima do nível dos ingredientes).

Tempere com um pouco com sal, pimenta-do-reino e ervas.

Tampe a panela e após pegar pressão conte 5 minutos e desligue o fogo. Deixe a pressão sai e corrija os temperos se necessário.

Me conta o que achou e o que se você tem outra receita de sucesso ai na sua casa!

#35787. Massa de Pizza para Forno Caseiro

Eu já falei há anos aqui no blog sobre a massa de pizza. Disse que é impossível conseguir um resultado igual ao de pizzarias com forno à lenha. Isso porque nossos fornos caseiros não atingem os mais de 400ºC necessários. Então aquela borda queimadinha, aquelas bolhas na massa que você adora saiba que isso é impossível! Mas dá para fazer massa gostosa usando o máximo de calor que conseguirmos.

Para conseguir melhorar o forno, usei a frigideira de ferro porque ela aquece bem e retém o calor. Você também pode usar uma pedra especial para pizzas ou assadeiras comuns. Mas neste caso por conta da espessura ser mais fina fique de olho para a massa não queimar por baixo.

1 xícara (chá) de farinha de trigo sem fermento;1/2 col. (chá) de sal;1/2 col. (chá) de fermento biológico seco granulado;aproximadamente 100ml de água.

Coloquei a farinha de trigo numa tigela, juntei o sal e misturei (mas atenção porque isso é necessário porque se o fermento entrar em contato direto com o sal ele pode “morrer”ok?).

Juntei aos poucos a água e fui misturando porém só no meio desse processo que acrescentei o fermento. Coloquei água até dar ponto de desgrudar das mãos e então sovei alucinadamente a massa. Isso porque precisamos desenvolver ao máximo o glúten para conseguir uma textura boa para massa de pizza.

Dica: Se você tiver uma panificadora (máquina de fazer pão) ou batedeira planetária com gancho, sugiro que use, porque tem que sovar uns 10 a 15 minutos.

Com a massa sovada é só cobrir com plástico filme e deixar em local abafado até dobrar de tamanhom, mas antes que me pergunte, não existe um tempo certo para isso, pode ser 1h, 2h, enfim, depende de quão quente e abafado esteja aí, pois é esse calor que ativa o fermento.

Atenção: Só prossiga quando a massa dobrar de volume.

Agora você liga seu forno na temperatura máxima, que no meu caso são 250ºC. Eu usei a frigideira de ferro, que coloquei para aquecer dentro do forno, então enquanto esquentava, separei os ingredientes que ia usar na cobertura. Pode usar os que você quiser, mas cuidado com excesso de queijo, porque pode encharcar a massa de gordura.

Abri a massa em uma superfície polvilhada com farinha e dei uma enroladinha na borda pra ficar mais grossa (mas ja adianto que é frescurinha minha, nem precisa).

Passados 20 minutos que a frigideira estava no forno, tirei, untei com azeite e coloquei a massa (com muito cuidado pois a frigideira estava muuuuito quente). Então pré assei a massa por 5 minutos em temperatura máxima.

Tirei, coloquei a cobertura e voltei pro forno, foram mais 10 minutos e o resultado foi excelente. Já te adianto que não ficou igual de pizzaria, mas muito bom para um forno caseiro.

Se você esta procurando mais idéias, aqui eu te ensino em vídeo como fazer sua pizza na Airfryer e aqui te apresento minha playlist de pizza no Youtube com todo tipo de pizza que você possa imaginar.

Então se quer fugir do convencional deixo a minha receita de Pizza de Carne Moída e a maravilhosa Pizza de Batata pra você não ter como escapar dessa delícia

Sabe o dia que sua receita começa com o pé esquerdo? Joguei os ingredientes na minha panificadora, e ela estava quebrada, aí tirei tudo e sovei na mão, mas acho que não sovei direito porque a massa não cresceu muito, esperei 2 horas e nada. Aí acendi o forno coloquei a minha forma de ferro lá dentro e fui abrir a massa, o forno se apagou sozinho. Ou seja, não pré-aqueceu a forma. Aí desisti de pré-aquecer a forma pois estávamos morrendo de fome, e fui montando a pizza, aí me lembrei que deveria pré-assar a massa antes de colocar a cobertura. No final das contas ficou gostoso, mas a massa ficou meio dura. Fiz duas receitas pois minha forma é de 35 cm de diâmetro. Agora que minha panificadora está arrumada, quero tentar novamente!

#35790. Pavê de Torta de Morango

Esse pavê de Torta de Morango é uma delícia e já te adianto que eu amo essa receita e é muito fácil de fazer então não vamos perder tempo!

Você precisa entender que nele, tem todas as camadas de uma torta (se você preferir pode chamar de bolo) tradicional de morangos, mas é feita diretamente no refratário o que facilita muito para quem não tem grandes habilidades para confeitar. Ou então, é como eu que prefere receitas mais práticas. Já te aviso que você pode trocar morango por outra fruta ou então misturar mais de uma.

Primeiro fazemos um pão-de-ló assado no próprio refratário em que ficará o doce. A receita é facílima! Os ingredientes são apenas:

5 ovos;5 colheres (sopa) farinha de trigo;1 colher (sopa) de fermento em pó químico.5 colheres (sopa) de açúcar;

Bata as claras em neve, então quando estiverem bem firmes junte as gemas e bata em velocidade mais baixa só para misturar. Desligue a batedeira e misture manualmente a farinha, o açúcar e o fermento, mas mexa com cuidado!

Preaqueça o forno em 180ºC por 5 minutos e unte um refratário grande (aproximadamente 45cm x 25cm) com óleo ou manteiga e polvilhe farinha, coloque então a massa e leve para assar (eu uso um spray de untar).

Atenção: pão-de-ló assa bem rápido e não se deve deixar corar demais. Quando começar a dourar por cima faça o teste do palito. Espete um palitinho no centro, se sair limpo está pronto, deixe esfriar.

Espalhe uma camada generosa de geleia de morango sobre o pão-de-ló, eu usei a geleia comprada mesmo mas se quiser fazer tem ensinei uma receita maravilhosa que você não pode perder.

Bata um chantilly, que pode ser aqueles de caixinha (ja antecipo que 1 caixinha basta) ou então 300ml creme de leite fresco batido até formar o chantilly. Lave e pique 1 caixinha de morangos e misture os tudo com 2 colheres (de sopa) de açúcar, porém se o morango estiver azedo vc pode colocar mais, siga seu institnto!

Espalhe o chantilly com morangos sobre a geleia e por cima coloque suspiros despedaçados (esse eu também compro pronto), te garanto que fica uma delícia e vai fazer muito sucesso!!!

IMPORTANTE: Mantenha na geladeira coberta com plástico filme ou em recipiente com tampa.Essa sobremesa fica mais gostosa depois de 24 horas porque o pão-de-ló vai ficando mais úmido. Se quiser fazer para servir um dia depois não coloque o suspiro, deixe para colocar na hora de servir porque ele perde a crocância.

#35791. Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang

On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post fromÂ SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure.Â This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

GLM is a text generation model from Z.aiÂ that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many modelsÂ available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3Â on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. Â

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context.Â We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe.Â Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMsÂ andÂ smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence.Â We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Hereâs what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated modeÂ such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233Â on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

GLM 5.3 launched on Workers AI with a prefill KV pool smaller than its context window. The exposure was present from launch.

Cloudflare begins verifying the HackerOne report.

Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.

After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was setÂ to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.

Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.

All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.

Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.

Meeting with the SGLang maintainers (RadixArk CTO and core engineers) to agree on upstream fixes.

Additional hardening rolled to all production SGLang deployments (details below).

Upstream SGLang merges the admission fix, per-transfer checksums, abort-ACK preservation, and turns deferred KV release on by default.

Coordinated publication with the researcher and RadixArk.

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.Â

Retires aborted prefill requests before their result reaches decode. This stops the exposure in this incident.

Rejects these requests at admission, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer. Follows the approach in Cloudflare's draft patch, #38704.

sgl-routerÂ cancels both halves of a request on client disconnect or prefill failure.

Enables deferred KV release only on backends that support it, then turns it on by default.

Fixes cases where the drain confirmation was lost, so releases happen on confirmation instead of waiting out the timeout.

Holds pages on every transfer failure, not only decode-initiated aborts.

Fixes a regression in the abort notification path.

A failed Mooncake send no longer reports its writes as drained.

Tags abort messages per request so a reused ID cannot consume a stale confirmation. Adds MORI support.

Shares the prefill-to-decode failure notification across Mooncake, NIXL, and MORI.

Optional cap on Mooncake transfer batch size, so one timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded number of writes in flight.

Decode waits for an in-progress offload to host memory before retracting a request and freeing its pages. Authored by Cloudflare.

Keeps tensor-parallel ranks in agreement when a host-memory cache restore fails.

Adds --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum: decode verifies a checksum of the transferred KV before generating. Cleanup in #39729, merged and awaiting release.

Fixes for SGLang's KV canary, which detects and logs potential corruption.

Metrics for deferred release: count, duration, and whether each hold ended on drain confirmation or timeout.

These follow-ups are still works in progress:

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500Â is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

RDMA copies data directly from one nodeâs memory to anotherâs. Itâs vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when itâs finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. TopazÂ enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of MeerkatâsÂ QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLangâs distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove â as far as possible â that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.
