#35807. Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale

Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves outThe timeline of an investigationSo how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hoursIn our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.The disagreement underneathThe instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.The OntologyThis agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application .api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" .api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident .INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway .INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" .In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:Creating determinism from non-determinismBuilding this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:category IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"]sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"]# Result — a deterministic triple:thread:123 slack:category "incident" .thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:The five layers to create determinism from non-determinismEnrichers: Agents as entropy reducersWe use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:every entity carries an rdf:type,every URI follows a single naming scheme, andthe catalog gates every ops:Application.Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chainsThe correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

#35809. Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification

For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtainedÂ South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.

For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.

A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:

The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).

Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.

Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.

We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflareâs sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.

The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountryÂ headerÂ at the origin and as request.cf.countryÂ inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:

What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.

It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.

ISMSÂ is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.

Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.

The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.

Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.

The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.

The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.

KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:

If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.

That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.

For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a teamâs own compliance assessments.

Cloudflareâs entry can be found onÂ KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the CloudflareÂ Trust Hub.

The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.

For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.

ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.

Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.

That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.

To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

#35810. GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary

GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history.

GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal.

GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels.

Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases:

Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields:

1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026.

Pre-trained multimodal models read each ad, product, and page, including its text and images, and encode the items into an embedding that carries world knowledge. The tokenizer combines that content signal with representations learned from how people engage with the items, then quantizes the result into a short sequence of discrete tokens. Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. For example, there’s overlap between two running shoe ads from the previous season to the current season, so the new campaign immediately benefits from everything the model has already learned about the previous season’s products.

At the heart of GenRecs Tokenization is a three-stage pipeline that:

Maximizing ads recommendation quality requires diverse combinations of these stages depending on entity and feature semantics. For example, for many ad representations, GenRecs Tokenization uses prefix n-grams that combine a learned encoder, residual decomposition,  learned vector codebooks, and token parametrization.

Independently of downstream ranking gain, tokenizer model quality can be evaluated against intrinsic measures like:

Across the eight tokenizer versions we tested, we see a strong correlation between these intrinsic quality metrics and downstream ranking prediction accuracy. Tokenizer versions that scored better on these metrics also had better CTR prediction accuracy for ads models.

Tokenization maximizes the efficiency of high-volume campaigns by uncovering deeper semantic patterns across their vast product catalogs. For tail ads that accumulate fewer impressions, tokenization enables ads recommendation models to generalize across them via shared content structure, recovering cold-start performance and enabling cross-entity transfer. When a sportswear brand launches next season’s trail shoe, tokenization lets the new product and its ads build on what the model learned from last season’s shoe, even before anyone sees the new ad.

By improving tail ad prediction quality, tokenization not only lets tail ads be ranked accurately, but also improves the training data, which then improves prediction quality for all ads. Each pass through this self-reinforcing flywheel improves the quality of model predictions.

Tokenizer improvements are not confined to the model they were tuned for. Optimizing codebook quality through diversity loss, dead code resets, and contrastive objectives produces measurably better downstream performance when the resulting tokens train generative recommenders. Our work on LLM-native retrieval shows how far this can go. A two-tower architecture built on a shared LLM encoder reaches state-of-the-art retrieval quality while remaining efficiently servable, matching classic two-tower performance on a fraction of the training data. Building on this, we are now extending reasoning-aware ranking on top of the same vocabulary.

We are continuing to push GenRecs Tokenization toward the ROI-optimal frontier along three directions:

Deepening cold-start generalization: Tail ad inventory is where semantic tokens contribute most and where advertiser impact is largest. We are scaling the coverage of tokenization across all items to deliver better performance to advertisers.

Treating tokenizer quality as a first-class objective: Engagement-aligned training, unified cross-entity vocabulary, and codebook improvements are active areas of investment. Because intrinsic quality measures predict downstream ranking gains, we can iterate on the tokenizer without waiting on a full model training cycle.

Serving LLM-native architectures efficiently: Fully verbalized tokenization gives a model the richest view of an ad, but requires context windows that are impractical at ads scale. We are combining compacted verbalized tokens with semantic IDs to retain reasoning quality while maintaining acceptable latency.

Looking further out, we are exploring whether the same vocabulary that improves ads ranking today could unify representation across surfaces. A shared token space spanning ads content across text, image, audio, and video, would let models reason about what a person is interested in and what an advertiser has to offer with one representation, rather than stitching together separately learned embeddings.

As recommendation systems evolve from discriminative scoring to include generative reasoning, the data foundation benefits from evolving from ephemeral IDs to stable semantic representations. GenRecs Tokenization provides the foundation, translating the complexity of Meta’s ads ecosystem into a vocabulary that generative models can learn, reason about, and generate from.

We would like to thank Weifeng Cui, Ling Leng, Luke Simon, Hadar Ohana, Jimmy Chen, Minghai Chen, Chiyu Zhang, Dinesh Ramasamy, Debajyoti Roy, Shawn Shi, Gajanan Golegaonkar, Xiao Yang, Ashkan Aleali, Anuj Gargava, Xizhou Feng, Liquan Huang, Frank Shyu, Xiaoyu Chen, Kungang Li, Chonglin Sun, Matt Steiner, Sandeep Pandey,  Santanu Kolay, Anuj Madan, Tak Yan, and the entire team behind the development and productionization of the first large scale semantic tokenization effort in Meta’s ad recommendation system.

#35811. Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications

Authors: Divya Gadde, Ko-Jen Hsiao, Dhaval Patel and Moumita BhattacharyaThe motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models.The previous two blog posts(1, 2) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model.In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches.Embeddings from Foundation modelTransformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings.Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store.An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique (paper). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features.This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online.Embedding Store integrationThis approach is often the initial and most straightforward way for applications to interact with the Foundation Model. Embeddings can serve as powerful features for other models or for candidate generation, helping to retrieve appealing titles for a user or facilitate title-to-title recommendations. Integrating embeddings as features into existing pipelines is generally well-supported and offers a low barrier to entry. Compared to other integration approaches, using embeddings from the Embedding Store is expected to have a relatively smaller impact on training and inference costs.However, this approach also has some cons. The time gap between embedding computation and downstream model inference can lead to staleness, impacting the freshness of recommendations. This may prevent applications from fully unlocking the benefit of the Foundation Model, especially for use cases requiring real-time adaptability.Overall, the default starting point for leveraging the Foundation Model is through its profile and item embeddings via the Embedding Store, provided that the embeddings’ freshness and stability meet application-specific needs. While embeddings may not leverage the full power of the Foundation Model, they offer a good initial step.Our biggest learning from working on this approach is that embeddings are a low cost and high leverage way of using the Foundation Model. A resilient embedding generation framework and embedding store are essential for updating the embeddings daily and serving them to application models. We found this infrastructure to be so valuable that we stepped up our investment here to build a near-realtime embedding generation framework. This new framework also enables us to update the embeddings based on user actions during the session, making the embeddings and our downstream models more adaptive. Although the near-real time framework cannot be used for very large models, it represents an important direction for addressing embedding staleness and adaptiveness of recommendations.Foundation Model as a SubgraphThis approach involves using the Foundation Model as an input to the downstream model i.e. the Foundation Model decoder stack is a subgraph of the application model’s full model graph and hence the name “subgraph integration”. The Foundation Model subgraph processes raw user interaction sequences and outputs representations that are then fed into the downstream model graph.Foundation Model Subgraph integrationApplications can fine-tune the Foundation Model subgraph as part of their own training process, potentially leading to better performance than just using static embeddings. In this approach, there is no time gap or staleness between the Foundation Model inference and the application model’s inference, ensuring that the most up-to-date learnings are used. This approach also allows applications to leverage specific layers from the Foundation Model that may not be exposed through the Embedding Store, uncovering more application-specific value.However, the subgraph approach comes with some complexities and trade-offs. To use the Foundation Model as a subgraph, application models need to generate all the features necessary for the subgraph as part of their feature generation process. This can add time, compute and complexity to their feature gen jobs. Merging the Foundation Model as a subgraph also increases the application model size and inference time. To alleviate some of these complexities, the Foundation Model team provides some reusable code and jobs that make the feature generation more compute efficient. To optimize the inference performance, we split the subgraph and ensure it only runs once per profile per request and is shared by all items in the request.Overall, the subgraph approach allows for a deeper integration and enables the applications to harness the full power of the Foundation Model. But it can also make the application’s training code more complex, requiring a trade-off between metric improvement, compute cost, and time. Therefore, we would reserve this approach for high impact use cases where the increase in metric wins compensate for the cost and complexity.Fine-tuning Foundation Model and use directlyThis approach is similar to fine-tuning LLMs with domain specific data. In the previous blog post, we described how the Foundation Model is trained on a next-token prediction objective, with the tokens being different user interactions. Different interactions are of different importance to various surfaces on the Netflix website. For example, for the ‘Trending now’ row, recent interactions on trending titles might be more important than old interactions. Hence, the Foundation Model can be fine-tuned on more product specific data and then the fine-tuned model can be used to directly power the product. During fine-tuning, application teams can choose to do full parameter fine-tuning or freeze some layers. They can also choose to add a different output head with a different objective. We built a fine-tuning framework to make it easy for application teams to develop their own custom fine-tuned versions of the Foundation Model.Fine-tuned Foundation Model IntegrationThis approach offers the ability to adapt the Foundation Model to application’s specific data and objectives, making it optimized for their use case. A side benefit of this integration approach is that it provides a de facto baseline for new models/applications. Instead of coming up with a new model stack and spending months on feature engineering, new applications can directly utilize fine-tuned foundation models. However, this approach can lead to more models and pipelines to maintain across the organization.The latency and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of the fine-tuned model must be carefully optimized for the specific application use case.ConclusionWe are continuing to innovate on these integration approaches over time. For example, the Machine Learning Platform team is working on near-real time embedding inference capabilities to address the staleness issues with the embedding approach. We are also working on a smaller distilled version of the Foundation Model to reduce the inference latency of the subgraph approach. We also provide a fine-tuning framework to make it easy to fine-tune and leverage the Foundation Model. We also continue to refine and standardize the APIs used in these approaches to make it easy for application teams to use them. Overall, these three integration patterns provide a comprehensive framework for how Netflix applications can interact with and extract value from the Foundation Model.AcknowledgementsWe thank our stunning colleagues in the Foundation Model team for developing and continuing to innovate on the Foundation Model. We thank our colleagues in the AIMS applications teams for driving the integrations and their valuable feedback and discussions. We also thank our Machine Learning Platform team for building and supporting the infra components to get these approaches up and running in production.Contributors to this work (name in alphabetical order): Davis Shepherd Inbar Naor Jin Wang Jonathan Indig Kevin Zielnicki Luke Wang Mario Garcia-Armas Maryam Esmaeli Michael Tu Nicholas Hortiguera Qiuling Xu Robbie Greuner Roger Menezes Sejoon Oh Trung Nguyen Vito Ostuni Yesu Feng.Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

#35813. DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack

by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian ShangIntroOur Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets.Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values.Initial ProblemScattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required:extensive business knowledgefamiliarity with experimentation conventionsand complex engineering practicesThis led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform.Enter DataJunctionTo address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case.DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform.Architecture DecisionsA critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention.API First, UI and Other Interfaces LaterA metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request.Consistent Graph First, Other Features LaterA complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them:semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoringmetric and dimension query / definition generationmetric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine)data visualization and data trackingperformance optimization (aka caching or materialization)integration layer with other tools andany / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more.Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core.Cube as The Perfect Consumption ProtocolAnalytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects.In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below.We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters.One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset.Experimentation at NetflixMetrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions.At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation.This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models.ConclusionsWith experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both:find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ)easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stackThat will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix.Related resources:2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck)2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video)2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog)DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

#35814. The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do

We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point.

When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything.

It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating.

The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists.

Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives.

Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources.

The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem.

Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge.

We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one.

The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request:

Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded.

One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space:

Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability.

Each subagent follows a standardized structure:

This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first.

Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent.

Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour.

For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists.

The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems.

The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries:

This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit:

The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained.

We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes.

The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable.

This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include:  Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin.

#35815. Tortinha de Atum

Eu cansei de fazer essa torta em tamanho grande, mas depois que fiz miudinha, nessas forminhas que são maiores que de empada (mais ou menos o dobro do tamanho) nunca mais fiz a grande.

Gente que delícia!!! Ficou tão macia, não sei dizer porque a massa feita nas forminhas menores fica muito mais macia, acho que porque fica menos tempo no forno, não sei mesmo, só sei que se eu fosse vocês tentaria fazer essa versão também porque ficou incrível!!!

A torta é a mesma que fiz neste post AQUI (tanto a massa quanto a cobertura). Coloquei massa até a metade das forminhas, coloquei a cobertura de atum e levei para assar.

Foram uns 25 minutos de forno em 200°. Nossa que delícia!!! Olha como fica por dentro:

As tortinhas de atum são uma excelente opção para quem busca refeições práticas, saborosas e ricas em nutrientes.

O atum, principal ingrediente, é conhecido por seu alto teor de proteínas, essenciais para a manutenção muscular e para a recuperação do organismo.

Além disso, é uma fonte natural de ômega-3, gordura boa que promove a saúde do coração, reduzindo os níveis de colesterol ruim e prevenindo doenças cardiovasculares.

Outro benefício é o aporte de vitaminas como B12 e D, fundamentais para a saúde óssea e para o sistema nervoso.

A combinação de ingredientes da tortinha, como vegetais e massas integrais, pode ser ajustada para incrementar fibras, ajudando na digestão e prolongando a sensação de saciedade.

Para tornar a receita ainda mais versátil, é possível explorar uma variedade de ingredientes que atendam diferentes preferências e restrições alimentares.

Assim, você pode adaptar a tortinha ao seu paladar ou necessidade específica, sem perder sabor ou qualidade nutricional.

Se você deseja variar a receita ou atender restrições alimentares, há diversas alternativas de massas. Para uma versão mais leve, experimente fazer a massa com farinha de aveia, que é rica em fibras e ajuda no controle da glicemia.

Para uma textura mais macia, por outro lado, opte por massa de liquidificador, que é rápida e fácil de preparar. Já para um toque mais rústico, a farinha integral traz um sabor diferenciado e mantém a crocância.

Embora o atum seja o protagonista, é possível diversificar o recheio da tortinha. Para quem busca reduzir o consumo de carne, uma excelente alternativa são os vegetais refogados, como, por exemplo:

Outra opção é o frango desfiado temperado, que combina muito bem com ervas frescas. Caso prefira sabores mais sofisticados, os cogumelos são uma adição deliciosa.

Preparar e armazenar tortinhas de atum pode ser ainda mais eficiente com algumas estratégias simples que garantem sabor, textura e frescor por mais tempo.

O segredo para uma massa crocante está no uso de manteiga gelada e na técnica de não trabalhar demais a massa com as mãos, evitando que ela aqueça.

Outra dica, aliás, é pré-assar a base por alguns minutos antes de adicionar o recheio. Isso garante uma tortinha bem assada e com textura impecável.

Para quem gosta de praticidade, as tortinhas de atum podem ser congeladas com facilidade. Após o preparo, espere esfriar completamente, embale em plástico filme ou em recipientes herméticos e congele por até 3 meses.

Para aquecer, utilize o forno para preservar a crocância, evitando o micro-ondas, que pode deixar a massa borrachuda.

A tortinha de atum é versátil e combina com diferentes acompanhamentos. Pensar nos pratos e bebidas que complementam seu sabor pode transformar uma refeição simples em uma experiência completa.

Para uma refeição leve, opte por uma salada verde com vinagrete, que traz frescor e leveza. Se desejar algo mais robusto, sirva com um creme de milho ou sopa de legumes.

Como bebida, o suco natural de limão ou laranja equilibra os sabores e enriquece a experiência com toques cítricos.

Uma salada verde com um molho leve de mostarda e mel pode ser o acompanhamento perfeito para as tortinhas de atum. Portanto, o molho suave e levemente adocicado contrasta com o sabor do atum, criando um equilíbrio agradável no paladar.

Um arroz de coco ou um arroz integral pode ser uma excelente escolha para acompanhar as tortinhas. Então, o arroz de coco traz um sabor sutil e cremoso, enquanto o arroz integral adiciona uma textura mais firme e nutrição extra ao prato.

Batatas assadas com alecrim, tomilho e azeite são outro ótimo acompanhamento. Desse modo, a crocância das batatas assadas complementa a suavidade das tortinhas, criando uma refeição completa e saborosa.

A tortinha de atum apresenta diferentes versões ao redor do Brasil, adaptando-se aos ingredientes locais e preferências regionais.

No Nordeste, é comum substituir a farinha de trigo por farinha de mandioca ou milho. Além disso, o atum pode ser misturado com queijo coalho e temperado com coentro.

Já no Sul do Brasil, a receita recebe toques mais cremosos, incluindo requeijão caseiro e ervas frescas, como salsinha e cebolinha.

Para quem busca uma alternativa mais saudável, a massa pode ser feita com farinha de amêndoas ou aveia, e o recheio pode incluir atum natural, iogurte e chia.

A qualidade do atum influencia diretamente no sabor e na textura da tortinha. Veja algumas dicas para escolher a melhor opção:

O atum fresco tem um sabor mais intenso e pode ser grelhado antes de ir para a receita. Já o enlatado, prático e acessível, deve ser drenado corretamente para evitar excesso de líquido no recheio.

Opte por marcas que utilizam pesca sustentável e evite produtos que contenham excesso de conservantes.

Os molhos podem dar um toque especial à tortinha de atum, tornando-a ainda mais saborosa.

A escolha da bebida pode realçar o sabor da tortinha de atum. Aqui estão algumas sugestões:

Opções como Sauvignon Blanc e Chardonnay combinam bem devido à sua acidez e frescor.

Sucos cítricos, como limão e laranja, equilibram o sabor do atum.

Chás de hortelã e camomila trazem leveza e refrescância para a refeição.

Agora, então, veja algumas dúvidas comuns sobre o assunto.

Para uma versão mais saudável, substitua a massa tradicional por opções integrais e adicione vegetais no recheio. Além disso, reduza o uso de queijos gordurosos e opte por queijos magros, como ricota ou cottage.

O atum fresco pode ser usado. Para isso, portanto, cozinhe ou grelhe o atum, temperando com sal, azeite e limão antes de desfiar e incorporar ao recheio.

Queijos com sabor suave, como muçarela, bem como, parmesão ou queijo minas, são ideais para equilibrar os sabores sem sobrecarregar o recheio.

Você pode fazer uma torta grande utilizando formas de fundo removível. Assim, apenas ajuste o tempo de forno para garantir que a massa asse de maneira uniforme.

Inclua temperos diferentes, como curry ou páprica, para dar novos sabores ao recheio. Além disso, ervas frescas, como manjericão ou coentro, trazem aromas especiais e sofisticação à receita.

A sardinha e salmão são boas opções para substituir o atum, desse modo, mantendo o sabor e a textura da receita.

O segredo está em não assar a tortinha por tempo excessivo e assim, garantir que o recheio esteja cremoso antes de ir ao forno.

Basta substituir a farinha de trigo por alternativas como, por exemplo, farinha de amêndoas, aveia ou arroz.

Na geladeira, pode durar até 3 dias em um recipiente fechado. No congelador, por outro lado, pode ser armazenada por até 1 mês.

O ideal é utilizar o forno a 180 °C por cerca de 10 minutos, a fim de preservar a textura crocante da massa.
