#35824. Receita simples para jantar: veja as melhores e os seus benefícios

Conhecer receitas simples para jantar é essencial para que você tenha uma digestão mais rápida, o que fará com que você e sua família tenham uma ótima noite de sono.

As receitas simples para jantar são soluções ideais para quem quer uma refeição prática e, ao mesmo tempo, deliciosa. Por isso, o artigo a seguir explora vários pratos irresistíveis que farão da hora da ceia um momento mais do que especial.

Para preparar um cardápio com receitas simples para jantar, antes de tudo, é crucial definir um período de planejamento.

Ou seja, decidir se deseja planejar para uma semana inteira, alguns dias ou, então, apenas para uma noite. Depois, você só precisa:

Vale ressaltar que o objetivo é criar refeições para um jantar simples e rápido, portanto, evite as mais complexas ou que exijam muitos passos de preparo.

A simplicidade não só tornará a refeição mais prática, mas também permitirá que o processo de preparo seja mais prazeroso.

A melhor forma de preparar um jantar com poucos ingredientes é optar pelas receitas para jantar em família que podem ser feitas em apenas uma panela, como, por exemplo, sopas, ensopados, refogados ou macarrão primavera.

Use, além disso, itens básicos e versáteis, como arroz, massas, ovos e legumes, já que eles podem ajudar a criar refeições deliciosas com poucos complementos.

As receitas simples para jantar são macarrão cremoso na panela de pressão e arroz de forno. Isso porque, elas não exigem muito tempo de preparo, além disso, são saborosas e nutritivas.

Elas oferecem, acima de tudo, uma combinação perfeita entre facilidade na cozinha e mais prazer ao sentar-se à mesa para comer.

O macarrão cremoso na panela de pressão é um prato super prático para fazer em casa e, assim, incrementar o cardápio no dia a dia. Para prepará-la, aliás, você vai precisar dos ingredientes abaixo:

Separe todos os ingredientes em porções para facilitar na preparação. Em seguida, coloque o macarrão, molho de tomate, água, sal, cebola e alho em uma panela de pressão.

Depois, tampe-a e leve ao fogo médio até obter a consistência do seu agrado. Enquanto a massa cozinha, doure o bacon em uma frigideira com pouco óleo para não ficar muito gorduroso.

Por fim, adicione-o à panela do macarrão junto ao presunto, a mussarela e o creme de leite. Misture tudo em fogo baixo, até que o queijo derreta e sirva-se à vontade.

Essa é uma das receitas salgadas para jantar simples que surpreende, pois fica pronta em apenas 30 minutos, pois tem um preparo prático e saboroso. Veja os ingredientes necessários:

Você também pode fazer um arroz de forno cremoso com atum ou frango desfiado com uma salada de acompanhamento. Não existe um preparo mais simples e saboroso.

Lave e escorra o arroz, depois frite com óleo até cobrir os grãos. Logo após, junte com o sal e cozinhe em água fervente sem tampa até secar. Em seguida, transfira para uma tigela e reserve.

Por último, adicione cebola, presunto em cubos, queijo, creme de leite, ervilha, leite e cheiro verde e misture com o arroz. Depois é só levar ao forno por 30 minutos e, assim, servir quando estiver pronto.

Essa é uma das melhores receitas rápidas para jantares. Assim, em apenas 15 minutos, você pode preparar um delicioso macarrão alho e óleo com tomate-cereja. Portanto, para incrementar ainda mais o sabor, adicione um pouco de queijo parmesão ralado por cima.

As carnes e aves são ótimas opções de receitas simples para jantar. Isso porque, há vários modos de preparar essas proteínas com rapidez e garantir uma refeição deliciosa, veja algumas opções a seguir.

Essa é uma das opções de receitas simples para jantar romântico, já que envolve uma elaboração a mais e combina muito bem com vinho.

Assim, para o seu preparo será preciso separar os seguintes itens:

O primeiro passo é temperar a carne ao seu gosto e fritá-la em seguida. Depois, bata as batatas, o leite e o queijo no liquidificador, com uma pitada de sal, até virar um creme consistente.

Refogue a cebola com a carne e adicione o creme batido e as duas fatias de muçarela na mesma panela.

Por fim, adicione o cheiro verde a gosto e misture bem, para que tudo fique homogêneo e temperado. Dessa forma, essa é uma das receitas fáceis para jantar mais gostosas.

Outro prato de proteína que se destaca entre as receitas simples para jantar é a isca de frango crocante com legumes.

Isso porque, além do frango, ela pode ser feita com bovinos, suínos, caprinos e granjeiros, veja os ingredientes a seguir:

O primeiro passo é temperar o frango, alho, sal, pimenta e o que mais preferir e reservar. Assim, aqueça 1 colher de óleo e refogue a abobrinha.

Junte a cebola, o pimentão e a cenoura na panela e deixe dourar devagar. Em seguida, reserve. Então, na mesma panela, refogue o frango, coloque a maionese e misture. Por fim, adicione os legumes e misture com leveza para servir.

Uma receita simples e rápida, ideal para o jantar, é o frango grelhado com legumes salteados. Assim, o frango é uma fonte excelente de proteína e, combinado com legumes frescos como abobrinha, cenoura e pimentão, cria um prato equilibrado e saboroso.

Optar por receitas simples para jantar traz uma série de benefícios, por exemplo, facilita na digestão.

Além disso, você pode economizar tempo, bem como reduzir o estresse no momento de preparar as refeições.

Outras vantagens que isso pode oferecer são:

Isso também ajuda a evitar desperdícios, o que é bom para o meio ambiente e para o seu bolso. Por fim, o mais importante, que é passar mais tempo com a família e amigos, em vez de ficar preso na cozinha.

Aqui estão alguns ingredientes que podem ser usados em uma variedade de pratos e facilitam o preparo do jantar.

Os ovos são super rápidos de preparar e podem ser usados de várias formas: fritos, cozidos, mexidos ou em uma omelete. Então, eles são uma ótima fonte de proteína e podem ser combinados com quase qualquer ingrediente, como queijos, vegetais e até arroz.

Uma simples omelete pode se transformar em um prato sofisticado com a adição de ervas ou vegetais frescos.

O arroz é um dos ingredientes mais versáteis em um jantar. Desse modo, em apenas 20 minutos, você pode preparar um arroz simples e, a partir daí, criar pratos como arroz com legumes, arroz de frango ou até um arroz de forno.

Para tornar o prato ainda mais rápido, use arroz pré-cozido ou arroz de micro-ondas.

Os legumes congelados são uma excelente opção para quem tem pouco tempo para cozinhar. Portanto, eles são práticos, nutritivos e, em alguns casos, já vêm cortados e prontos para o preparo.

Você pode salteá-los em azeite, adicionar a um molho ou até mesmo incluí-los em sopas e caldos.

#35826. How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering

Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type.

That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review.

Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step.

With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it.

With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration.

When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t.

So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change.

With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible:

Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike.

Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers.

Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously.

Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action.

That ownership model needs machinery with five key components:

The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts.

Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next.

Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from.

Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture.

The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect.

Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause.

One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions.

While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness.

We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places:

Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself.

Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off.

What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it.

Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile:

The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework.

We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions.

#35827. Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino: ricetta cremosa alla romana

Quando ho letto in questo modo si scioglierà creando una crema perfetta senza stracciare ho avuto un sussulto. Da quando in qua gli spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino, quelli che chiudevano un qualsiasi party giovanile, sono diventati cremosi? L’era internet pare li voglia cremosi almeno a giudicare dai follower che Marco Meschini, chef social, esibisce su Instagram.

Quindi correggete il titolo della ricetta in Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino con mentuccia e pecorino. E non sono una boutade perché la ricetta che leggete di seguito è pubblicata nel libro Pasta per tutti i gusti edito da Mondadori Electa. Una ricetta, ci avvertono, che reinterpreta la semplicità della tradizione. Arricchendola con il tocco erbaceo e fresco della mentuccia e la sapida cremosità del pecorino romano.

Modestamente Marco Meschini propone questi spaghetti che sono – copio incollo – la sua versione iconica, migliore e definitiva (sic) di uno dei classici più amati di sempre.

Però poi questa idea del pecorino è nelle corde del giovane food creator che ha i suoi natali nel quartiere tiburtino. Nel libro raccoglie 80 ricette che rappresentano la sua idea di cucina immediata e profondamente legata alla tradizione romanesca. Quindi, se avete intenzione di regalarvi o regalare il libro, sappiate che dentro ci trovate il sacro quartetto: carbonara, amatriciana, gricia, cacio e pepe. Ma anche variazioni come l’amatrigialla e la gricia alle pere, quella da non dire al contadino.

E quindi che formaggio sia in questa versione degli spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino visto che Marco Meschini usa la salsa cacio e pepe anche nella ricetta con la porchetta. La cacio e pepe è proposta anche con scampi e lime (qui la crema deve essere più fluida per un piatto leggero), con le cozze e il lime e pure con il gambero rosso. Il pecorino, insomma, lo ama senza dubbi.

Pasta per tutti i gusti. Mondadori Electa. 224 pp. 22,90 €

Dal mondo della moda a quello del cibo ma sempre con stile

#35828. Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II

By Yogesh NagarurIntroductionIn Part 1 of this series, we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII.If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it.Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime.Let’s dive in.A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata RegistryWhen an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two.In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry, a Key-Value store:When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry.It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small.Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event.This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth.The ad server writes per-impression metadata to the globally replicated registry on the serving path, and the Ads Event Publisher reads it back to enrich each client event.But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear.Why we needed to evolveThe forcing function was Live. Netflix’s live slate has grown rapidly, from NFL games to blockbuster fight nights to the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027, and viewership keeps growing. That traffic looks nothing like Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD): a single event can surge toward tens of millions of concurrent viewers within minutes, then drain just as fast when it ends. Building the ad pipeline for Live meant building for that trajectory.To see why the old design could not get there, let’s put some numbers on it. When Netflix streamed the Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson fight to more than 100 million viewers, a single ad break at that scale would generate an enormous volume of ad events. Serving those ads in the old design would have meant writing metadata for each of them to the Metadata Registry and waiting for acknowledgment before the ads could serve: millions of must-succeed database writes per second on the ad-serving critical path. That pattern created three core problems at Live scale:It was a scaling bottleneck. Every ad and every ad break is a write. Multiply that by tens of millions of concurrent viewers, keep it non-lossy (a dropped write is a dropped ad, and lost revenue), add Live’s spiky on/off pattern, and the write load becomes enormous. But you cannot safely scale the registry up once the event starts. Adding nodes reshuffles data across the cluster to rebalance it, and doing that in the middle of a live event could slow or even fail the very writes you are adding capacity for. That leaves one safe option: pre-scaling for the peak in advance and hoping the forecast is accurate.Fewer dependencies on the critical path. Serving an ad meant a synchronous, must-succeed write to the registry, followed by a wait for its acknowledgment. Every system on the critical path is one more thing that can stop an ad from serving, and the metadata registry had no fallback, so an unhealthy registry meant serving stopped. Taking hard dependencies off that path was the goal, and the registry was the biggest one we could remove.It put event freshness at risk. If writing slowed down under load, or lookups timed out, events spilled into retries and dead-letter queues, and enriched ad events were delivered late. Some systems might be fine, but others, such as frequency capping, cannot. It needs events under a strict SLA to decide whether the next selected ad can run without breaking policies.So we asked a simple question: the ad server already knows and logs everything about the ad it served. Does it really need to write that to a database on the hot path? Can we match that against the downstream Kafka stream of client events, which is always there, after the fact?The write leaves the critical path entirely; no shared datastore outage can stop serving, and enrichment becomes something we scale elastically with Live rather than a cluster we babysit.Matching two streams after the fact is a streaming join, and that is where Flink comes in.Why FlinkWe chose Apache Flink because near-real-time, stateful stream processing is exactly what it is built for, and because it has deep, production-tested platform support at Netflix. Just as important, we already knew how to run it. As Part 1 noted, our Ads Sessionizer is a large stateful Flink job, so operating one at scale, tuning state, checkpoints, and recovery under production load, was familiar ground for the team. Enrichment on Flink was built on that experience rather than starting from scratch.The new architectureAt its core, the new Ads Event Publisher is built as an Apache Flink streaming job. Each event moves through a handful of stages:Normalize. Client events arrive from several sources, including SVOD, live, playback, and embedded ad breaks, each with a slightly different shape. We first normalize them into a common form.Re-route. Client events and response events may appear in different regions; we inspect and reroute them to the correct job-processing region for a successful join.Join. The heart of the job: we match each client event to the ad-serving response for the same impression, enriching it with the full serving context using a KeyedCoProcessFunctionDeduplicate. Revenue-bearing events are de-duplicated, so nothing is counted twice.Publish. We extract measurement beacons for our partners and route the enriched ad event to its downstream consumers.The ad server logs responses to Kafka rather than writing to a registry; the Flink job joins responses with client events in real time and routes enriched ad events downstream.The join is the interesting part. Client events and ad serving responses arrive on separate streams at different times, so the job holds recent responses in memory and matches events against them over a 60-minute window. Three things can happen:The response is already there when an event arrives → we enrich it on the spot.The event arrives first → we hold it for a configuration duration (currently set to 60 minutes) until the matching response shows up, then enrich it.No response arrives within the window → we mark the event as unmatched for later recovery.We built the join as a custom Flink operator (a KeyedCoProcessFunction) rather than a built-in windowed join. We do not need a windowed join ordering and time-window semantics, since downstream consumers handle ordering; we simply match each client event to its response by key. Owning the operator at its lowest API form lets us control the matching state directly, including how long we hold it and what we do with an event that never matches. This allows us to tune retention per stream or persist unmatched events to a durable store later without rewriting the join. Our goal is always to build a strong base to reap the benefits later as we scale.To make that concrete, picture a member watching a live game. When the ad server decides which ad to show, it logs its response, and a few seconds later, the member’s device fires a “first quartile” event carrying the opaque token. Both arrive at the job keyed to the same impression, and because the response is already waiting, the event is enriched on the spot with its campaign, creative, price, and tracking URLs, then published downstream in near real-time.Why 60 minutes? Almost all events, roughly 99.999% of them, reach the job well before that, so extending the window further would only grow the state store and lengthen checkpoints for a vanishingly small gain. The remaining 0.001% still matters for precise billing and reporting, and we recover those events via a separate path described later on.Cross-region: matching events where their data livesThe Metadata Registry handled cross-region enrichment for us because it was built on a globally replicated key-value store: a client event could land in any region and still find its ad’s metadata. Global replication was a feature the platform provided (see Netflix’s Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer), so serving an ad in one region and enriching its events in another was simply not something we had to think about.A streaming join does not come with that convenience, and here the two sides of the join live in different places. The ad serving response stays in the region where the ad was served. The client event, though, is fired by the device, and the device can be anywhere: a member might start an ad on home wifi and switch to mobile data partway through, and that network change can route the event to a different region than the one that served the ad. So a client event is routed to a region that does not have the matching serving response.The tempting fix is to stream every region’s serving responses into every other region so that each region can match any client event locally. We rejected it: that would mean every region storing every serving response worldwide, the vast majority of which will never be used in the join, which is wasteful in both cost and compute.Instead, we treat this as a routing problem and route the client event rather than replicating the response. We encode the serving region into the ad token, so when a client event arrives in the wrong region, we forward it to the region that owns its response. For example, an ad is served in us-east-2, the member’s device switches from wifi to mobile data mid-ad, and the resulting event arrives in us-east-1. That region reads the token, sees the ad belongs to eu-west-1, and forwards the event back there, where its serving response is waiting. Only the small trickle of genuinely cross-region events pays for the extra hop.Catching the long tail of late-arriving eventsSixty minutes covers the vast majority of events, but not all of them. A device may have been offline, an ad paused, or an engagement event delayed by hours. Rather than drop these stragglers, we set them aside and recover them through a companion path: an hourly Spark batch job, orchestrated by Maestro, Netflix’s workflow orchestrator, re-pairs each straggler with its serving response from our data warehouse (which has a far longer retention than our in-stream window) and publishes it through the same downstream sinks. This keeps the streaming job’s memory bounded while still catching the long tail.This also lets us support event types that arrive well after the 60-minute window, including certain tracking-related events, while keeping the door open to extending the system to additional event types down the line and improving our match rate as needed. We also designed this offline job with reuse in mind: it can replay dead-letter queues and backfill historical data, giving us a single mechanism for both long-tail recovery and operational recovery.What was hardBeyond the architecture itself, three things took real work, and together they are what made the pipeline stable, correct, and safe to switch on.Keeping the core lean.Operating a stateful streaming join at live-event scale took real tuning, and most of our hard-won lessons come back to one idea: the job’s only job is matching events. Anything else we were tempted to bolt on, such as external lookups or incidental side-processing, was better moved off the hot path, or it eventually showed up as instability under load. Getting this right was the difference between a job that comfortably kept pace with live traffic and one that fell behind. It is unglamorous work, and it is most of the work.De-duplicating EventsDuplicates are a fact of life here in an event processing pipeline. A client may retry an event, and our upstream delivery is at-least-once so that the same event can arrive more than once. For revenue-bearing events, the ones that feed billing, nothing should be counted twice.The solution here is a simple and idempotent key. For each event, we compute a stable ID by hashing a few fields that uniquely identify it, such as the ad ID, the event type, and, for repeatable events, an offset or timestamp. The same underlying event always hashes to the same ID, so if we have seen an ID before, we drop the repeat.What changed with Flink is where we remember those IDs. The previous design kept them in an external key-value store and did a check-and-write over the network for every event; Flink lets us keep that state local to the job instead. We key the stream by event ID, which routes every copy of a given event to the same place, and a local state store with a short time-to-live remembers the IDs we have recently seen. Keying by ID also removes the race the external store had to guard against, since a given ID is handled in only one place at a time, with no network hop on the hot path. Multiple improvements here alone.We are deliberate about the guarantee: at-least-once delivery with best-effort de-duplication, not exactly-once. In-stream dedup removes the vast majority of duplicates within its window. However, a few can still slip past, for instance, through a cross-region reroute, a late-arriving recovery, or a restart that replays recent events. So we also carry the event ID through to the enriched ad event itself, which lets consumers who need exact counts, such as billing, run their own idempotent de-duplication over their own, longer windows.Production RolloutThis was the most challenging part of the project. For a system that feeds billing and frequency capping, “trust me, the new one is correct” is not good enough, so we ran the Flink pipeline alongside the legacy one and made it earn its traffic.Both pipelines continuously processed the full event stream, allowing us to compare them in real time: we published their outputs side by side. We ran automated audits that alerted us when the two drifted apart. Those audits earned their keep, surfacing subtle discrepancies we would never have caught from dashboards alone.How do we know the enrichment logic between the two systems was equal for the audits to make sense? Early in development, we extracted that logic into a shared module that both the legacy service and the Flink job depend on, so any change to how an event is enriched is applied to both at the same time. A failure in the audits, therefore, pointed to a real difference in the pipeline mechanics.Cutover was a separate question from comparison, and this is the part that warrants precision. We could not simply send a random percentage of events to each pipeline, because the same event landing in both would be double-counted downstream. Instead, the split was deterministic: a stable key on each event decided which pipeline was responsible for publishing it, so every event was published exactly once, even though both pipelines saw all of them. Raising the threshold moved events from the legacy pipeline to Flink a slice at a time, and we could dial it back instantly if anything looked off.Both pipelines process the same events behind a gradual traffic dial; an audit compares their outputs until we trust them; then the legacy service and registry are retired.By the time we fully cut over, the two pipelines agreed on well over 99.99% of events, and we rolled it out region by region rather than all at once. Then came the satisfying part: we turned off the ad server’s writes to the Metadata Registry, and decommissioned the legacy service and the registry itself. The single point of failure on the ad-serving critical path is simply gone. One of the oldest ad serving components at Netflix was deleted.Operating the Flink platformOperating a large stateful streaming job in production is its own job, and we did not build that muscle alone. We leaned heavily on Netflix’s Flink platform team. Early on, the job’s checkpoints were slow and heavy. The first checkpoint in particular took a long time, and we were holding more state in memory than we needed. Working with the platform team, we trimmed the state, reduced checkpoint durations, and validated the gains in load tests. That is what keeps the job from stalling during Live bursts.The same team also gave us operational scaffolding we did not have to invest in, including continuous delivery and canary deployments, so we could ship and roll out the Flink job with the same guardrails and confidence as the rest of our production systems. Netflix operates more than 25,000 Flink jobs (see Building a Scalable Flink Platform at Netflix), and that maturity is what we have to build on. We layered on custom canary metrics that catch issues before a release, CI/CD that lets us stagger rollouts, and a deploy flow that keeps the old job running until the new one has detected healthy checkpoints, so we never destroy a working job before the new job gives us the green light.The resultsEnrichment is off the critical path for ad serving. The ad server no longer performs a synchronous, must-succeed database write to serve an ad. It logs and moves on, and an entire class of “the lookup store is down, so ad serving is down” failures no longer exists.Fewer systems, fewer schemas, fewer hops. We retired both the legacy service and the Metadata Registry.Built for Live, and continuously tested for it. An ad break is what this service is designed to handle, so during our journey, we also ran large-scale load tests to simulate real-life traffic. In our latest load test, a single AWS region handled one ad break for a large concurrent audience, processing hundreds of thousands of events per second, joining the large majority of them against their serving responses in real time, and outputting enriched ad events at a comparable rate, all with negligible timeouts and errors. We test this throughout development and keep doing so as live audiences grow, and we are not at the ceiling yet.We delivered the Part 1 roadmap. Live-stream ad events, in-stream de-duplication, and richer real-time enrichment all shipped on this foundation.Key takeawaysTake the database off the hot path when you can. Our biggest win wasn’t raw performance — it was blast radius. Trading a synchronous write-and-wait for a fire-and-forget log plus a downstream join removed an entire failure mode from ad serving.Match events where their data lives. Real-time joins beat global replication by routing events to their data rather than copying the data everywhere.Earn the cutover. Running both systems in parallel and diffing their output on live traffic was slower than a flag-day switch — and it’s the only reason we trust the result.What’s nextWe have an exciting list of projects on the horizon: scaling the live path for the next tier of concurrent audiences, bringing the remaining delayed engagement events fully into the streaming world, reducing the Flink state size we need to manage, working on bringing even more resilience to the eventing processing pipeline, and continuing to add new event types and richer signals for our downstream consumers.Re-architecting the engine of a running, revenue-critical pipeline in place was a real multi-team effort. If building real-time systems at this kind of scale sounds like your thing, Ads Engineering is hiring.AcknowledgementsThis was a multi-team effort across Netflix. Thank you to everyone who designed, built, validated, and operated the new pipeline:Ads Engineering: Yogesh Nagarur, Kinesh Satiya, Jeet Mehta, Nitin Saini, Persis Shah, Guangyu Chen, Jimmy Liu, Riley Berton, Simon Spencer, Aadesh PatelAds Data Engineering: Eugene Yusim, Brandon Nicklas, Indu NarayanAds SRE: Max Michaels, Kevin Chung, Carlos Avalos, Brian ChristieData Movement: Mark Cho, Herbert Wang, Shraddha Ladda, Nikhil Sulegaon, James Lubin, Daniel TragerBehind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

#35830. How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents

Jenny Lea,Â Max Brosnahan,Â andÂ Matthew Conroy

AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online.

Thatâs because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a siteâs HTML â they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it.

Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, itâs currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf.

In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCPÂ in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code.

Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once?

Hereâs why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way.

Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts:

âMerchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesnât have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchantâs site, and the merchant keeps the relationship.

We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. Thatâs where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly.

WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP, and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopperâs browser. Itâs the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants donât have to choose between the two or manage them separately.â

Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.comâs backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic.

When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP.

Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart."

With WebMCP: The agent detects the store's tools on document.modelContextÂ and makes two clean calls:

Because the agent runs inside your active browser session on the store's domain, your cart updates in real time. Commerce.comâs backend MCP server determines the commerce flow:Â when youâre ready to complete the purchase, you click checkout yourselfÂ â keeping your payment details secure and leaving you in complete control of the final buy.

When Commerce.com asked to turn on WebMCP across almost 100000 storefronts, we ran into a practical challenge: WebMCP was originally designed as a single on-or-off switch for an entire domain zone.

Commerce wanted to enable our mcp-server-client toolpack, which acts as an edge bridge â proxying tool definitions and requests directly from Commerce.comâs backend MCP server to the visitor's browser. Because Commerce.com uses Cloudflare for SaaS to host thousands of merchant vanity domains on shared zones, we needed a way to deliver this platform-wide while giving individual store owners an easy way to opt out.

Instead of building a complex custom allowlist, we hooked WebMCP into the existing Cloudflare concepts of Configuration RulesÂ and custom hostname metadata.

Commerce.com turns WebMCP on for their main zone, then adds a rule at the edge that checks merchant metadata. If a merchant flips the "opt-out" switch in their Commerce.com dashboard, Cloudflare bypasses WebMCP for that specific storefront automatically:

Because Cloudflare evaluates these rules at the edge before serving the page, an opted-out store gets zero extra latency, no remote lookups, and no injected scripts.

As with any preview release, working with a partner in the real world revealed a few practical details we hadn't accounted for:

Custom MCP paths:Â When the mcp-server-client toolpack was enabled, our bridge originally expected to find every site's MCP server at /mcp. Commerce.comâs server lives at /api/mcp. To handle this, we added a configurable MCP URL setting at the zone level. When this is set, we pass the custom path into the injected script tag:

Seamless fallbacks:Â If a store's MCP server is offline or a customer's browser doesn't support WebMCP, the script exits. The storefront loads normally and human shoppers aren't affected.

We'll keep investing in WebMCP as the standard evolves, starting with helping agents find a site's tools more easily. Cloudflare and Commerce.comÂ will continue to work together to make shopping with agents fast, reliable and safe for both merchants and shoppers.

#35831. 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale

Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record!

There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time.

Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle.

But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament.

It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel.

Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern.

Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand.

Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament.

For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience.

During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours.

Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final.

All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics.

Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption.

That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed.

We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms.

We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself.

Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one.

Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.

Meta believes in building community through open source technology. Explore our latest projects in Artificial Intelligence, Data Infrastructure, Development Tools, Front End, Languages, Platforms, Security, Virtual Reality, and more.

Engineering at Meta is a technical news resource for engineers interested in how we solve large-scale technical challenges at Meta.

#35832. A Deep Dive into Salesforce’s Agent Tech Stack

Datadog’s free eBook covers what actually separates the agents that ship from the pilots that stall. Spoiler: it’s not the model. It’s durable execution, memory management, evaluation pipelines, and observability.

Identify the four failure modes that kill agent programs before they ship

Build evaluation pipelines that let you trust and govern agents at production scale

Instrument agent workflows with the observability needed to debug non-deterministic behavior in production

Measure the leading indicators that prove agent ROI to your team and leadership

Salesforce agents have completed 7 billion Agentic Work Units (AWUs), the unit the company uses to count work done by AI agents, across Agentforce and Slack. Of those, 3.2 billion came in its second quarter alone.

But getting agents to follow instructions consistently was a real challenge. The first version of Agentforce, Salesforce’s platform for building and running agents, put all instructions into one large prompt. As the rules piled up, the model began skipping some important ones. For customers using agents to interview job candidates or handle patient data, that was unacceptable.

Salesforce moved to a new design, a multi-layer system that combines deterministic code with reasoning models for maximum reliability. To understand how this works, we met two of the leaders behind it at Dreamforce 2026: Muralidhar Krishnaprasad (MK), President and CTO at Salesforce, and Khushwant Singh, SVP of Product Management for the AI application development platform. Thanks to MK and Khushwant for sharing the details with us.

Why a naive design that relies on prompting is not reliable

How to combine deterministic code with probabilistic reasoners to increase reliability

How to build a data layer that supports identity resolution and links records from many systems into one unified profile

How Agent Identity gives an agent its own permissions

How AIforce and the Headless Toolkit let agents in tools such as Slack and Claude reach Salesforce data and actions

The simplest way to build an agent is to write everything into a single prompt. That is how most teams build their first agent. Imagine you are building a support agent for a healthcare company. You can write the business rules as natural language instructions (e.g., only discuss the patient’s own records). Then add a description of available tools (e.g., “get scheduled appointments”). You also include other relevant info like patient data. The agent then includes all of this in the LLM’s context window. That’s the whole design. We just hope that the LLM does the right thing.

In this naive design, the model is expected to handle four things at once: 1) enforce the rules, 2) find who the customer is across different systems, 3) include the data the model may need, and 4) ensure the agent does what it is allowed to do.

The first version of Agentforce handled everything this way. According to MK, the team kept adding instructions such as only do this, only do that, and first get all the appointments. An interesting observation from the team was that this worked fine for up to eight instructions. But beyond eight, the model would discard instructions.

But why would a model discard an instruction? To a model, an instruction is not necessarily a rule. It is just some text in the context. There is no guarantee that an instruction will actually be followed. Besides that, instruction following will also get worse as we add more instructions to the context. This is not specific to Salesforce. A benchmark called IFScale tested 20 models with up to 500 simple instructions in one prompt to measure instruction following, and even the best model followed only 68% of them at the full 500.

So a prompt only tries to shape the behavior of the LLM. It cannot enforce that behavior. Let’s see what Salesforce built around the model to fix this.

Salesforce’s new design handles reliability by taking the four jobs out of the prompt and having dedicated systems to handle each. To see where these systems are, let’s review the current Salesforce platform stack. The four main layers in the stack, from bottom to top, are:

Data layer: Turns a company’s data sources into one consistent view. Salesforce calls this Data 360.

Application layer: The business applications for sales, service, and marketing, which supply the actions an agent can take. Salesforce calls this Customer 360.

Agent layer: Where agents are defined and run. Salesforce calls this Agentforce.

Surface layer: The places where a person talks to the agent, such as a Claude chat or Slack.

Instead of putting everything in a prompt and expecting the model to handle every job, each job is handled separately by a system in one of these layers. For example, in the Agentforce layer, a scripting language called Agent Script ensures to enforce the rules. In the data layer, identity resolution is responsible for finding a unified profile of the customer. Agent Context Engine is a separate system that decides which data reaches the model. The model just handles steps that require reasoning.

In the rest of this section, we go through the four systems built to handle each job one by one. To make it concrete, we follow the demo MK shared with us. The company is a simulated healthcare provider called Cumulus and the patient is Harper Clark, but according to MK everything behind it runs in production.

The first job that should be handled outside of the prompt is to enforce the rules. Many checks have to happen in every session turn, and they can be enforced deterministically. It is neither efficient nor reliable to expect the model to handle them. Another system can enforce them more reliably by just running code. That is the job of Agent Script, the language Salesforce built for describing agent behavior. According to MK, the team started working on it last year, after the first version of Agentforce ran into the instruction limit. It is open source and looks almost like Python [x].

How does it work? You just write the agent’s behavior in an Agent Script file. That file is compiled into a structured specification called the Agent Graph, and the Agent Graph is executed by the Atlas Reasoning Engine, the runtime behind Agentforce [x]. The engine runs the code parts and calls the model when reasoning is needed.

To better understand, compare this with SQL triggers. A trigger is code that the database runs automatically before or after updating a row. The application that issues the update cannot skip it. Agent Script follows a similar pattern.

Let’s compare the naive design with Agent Script using a concrete example. Imagine Harper asks a question like “When is my upcoming appointment with Dr. Perl?” In the naive design, the prompt says “always fetch the appointments first” and we hope the model would follow. In Agent Script, the lookup is a line of code in the before_reasoning block of the medical appointments subagent. Because of that, it always runs reliably.

Putting the pieces together, here is what happens when Harper asks her question:

The model picks the medical appointments subagent.

The before_reasoning block runs (the appointment lookup executes as code)

The model receives the prompt and writes the answer.

Lastly, the after_reasoning block executes. It may also send the conversation to a different subagent if needed.

This separation between deterministic tasks and reasoning parts allows the system to stay reliable. The model only focuses on reasoning over the context prepared by the code, not things like fetching appointments or what should happen after the reply.

While deterministic instructions improve reliability, they should not be used everywhere. The best practice is to use code for the parts we want predictable behavior, such as conditions, and use natural language for the parts that need actual reasoning.

The second system handles “who the customer is.” Harper’s appointment question may look like a simple lookup, but the appointment data may not be in the CRM (customer relationship management) system at all. It may be in Snowflake, a cloud data warehouse. Harper may also exist many times, as shown below.

One approach is to hand the model different lists of records and ask which ones are the same person. But that becomes a source of unreliability. Instead, a data layer, in three steps, can handle this.

Step 1: Reach the data. The data an agent needs is usually not in one place. The data layer connects to various sources and reads from them directly. This way, the agent has an updated view of the records. To show this, MK changed the insurance plan on Harper’s record in Snowflake and the change was reflected immediately.

Step 2: Harmonize. Different sources may have inconsistent views of the same record. For example, one system may store a full name in a single field while another splits it into two columns. The data layer maps each source onto a shared data model with common objects such as person, lead, and maybe account. According to MK, this mapping is automatic and works across thousands of sources.

Step 3: Resolve identities. This step handles situations where records from different sources describe the same person. In Data 360, this is done by match rules that an admin can configure. A rule can be an exact match (such as the same email address), a fuzzy rule that allows small differences, or a normalized rule, which cleans up a field before comparing it. This way, two phone numbers written in different formats will match. Note that the source records are never changed, and the output is a unified profile that links back to each of them.

With these steps, when Harper’s appointments are needed, it is obtained from the unified profile, instead of the model figuring out who Harper Clark is.

The third job is to decide what data should go into the prompt. If we put everything into a prompt, it adds to the latency and may bury the relevant facts. A context management system has to sit between the data and the prompt and decide what a question needs. That is the job of the Agent Context Engine (ACE), a new component of Data 360.

The context engine handles a request in six steps:

Resolve: Identify the user, the agent, the purpose, and the entities the question is about.

Plan: Choose where to look for that information (e.g., relational queries, the profile, search indexes)

Reconcile: Rank findings by some metric (e.g., relevance, authority, freshness)

Govern: Apply rules (e.g., access, masking, consent)

Compile: Create the context that includes working state, memory, etc.

Learn: Decide what from this interaction should be remembered or updated.

MK compared this with the naive design of an insurance support agent. In the naive version, with no context management, the question “show me details of my insurance plan” made the agent pull data from various sources, leading to 124,000 tokens. With the context engine, the same question ended up with 9,000 tokens. After a follow-up about moving to Florida, the naive session had used about 300,000 tokens in two questions, while the session with the context engine used 65,000 after a third step to process an enrollment. The gap between the two designs grows as the conversation continues, which shows the importance of having context management in place.

So how does the context engine pick what to send?

There are different implementations in practice. One is to hold the customer’s profile as a graph in memory, where the nodes are things like the person or the plan. Then we select only the nodes that relate to the question. Documents can be filtered in a similar way. When Harper asks “What lifestyle is best for me?” three indexes that match exact words, meaning, and linked entities (an approach known as GraphRAG) select relevant passages out of hundreds of documents.

The context engine can also handle memory. For example, after the Florida question, it can store a note that this customer may be moving to Florida. MK pointed out that this is a memory, not yet a fact. It became a fact only when the customer went ahead with the enrollment, and only approved facts like this are promoted into long-term memory. Either way, the model only ever sees a small, current slice of what the company knows about the customer.

The last job is to ensure the agent does what it is allowed to do. In most agent setups today, the agent acts as the user. Imagine Alex is a sales rep who connects an agent to Salesforce. The agent gets Alex’s credentials and can do everything Alex can do.

This setup is not ideal because with Alex’s full credentials, any mistake it makes becomes a real problem. A human with broad permissions is at least limited by how fast they can work. An agent is not. It can make a mistake and repeat it many times. According to Khushwant, what customers want is: “This agent is working on behalf of Alex, but I don’t want the agent to have the same rights as Alex.”

The fix is to give the agent an identity of its own. Salesforce already controls what users can do with permission sets. A new system, Agent Identity, lets an admin attach rules and permissions to an agent too, so each agent ends up having a unique identity with unique permissions.

With Agent Identity, when an agent authenticates, there are two tokens, one for the agent and one for the user it is acting for. Before an operation runs, Salesforce checks the user’s permissions, the agent’s permissions, and the data policies. The operation runs only if none of them deny it.

So far, we have looked at what happens inside a reliable agent platform. But users using an agent may work from somewhere else, like Slack or Claude. Some companies build their agents on other platforms entirely. Customers generally want Salesforce to meet their users where they are.

The way to do this is to separate the platform from its own interface. Software built this way is called headless. Instead of running on its own user interface, it exposes its functions through APIs to make it available to other surfaces. To make this happen, Salesforce developed a live interface layer, called AIforce, that brings the platform’s data, workflows, and logic to wherever people and agents already work.

For an outside agent to use a headless platform, it needs a few things. The first is APIs, the functions the platform exposes. The second is skills. An API tells an agent what it can call, but not which calls a task needs or in what order. A skill fills this gap by listing the APIs, their parameters, and the order of the steps. The third is MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard where a server publishes a list of tools and agents can call them.

Salesforce developed the set of building blocks behind AIforce, named Headless Toolkit, that provides all of the above. Salesforce’s APIs already serve 9.6 billion calls a day, and its skills are published in a public GitHub repository called sf-skills.

A separate challenge is tool count. MCP makes it easy to expose tools to an agent, but every tool the agent can call is typically loaded into its context window as a definition. It may contain things like a name, a description, and a parameter schema. Those definitions are sent each time a request is sent to the model, which is costly. When there are hundreds of tools, they will consume a large share of the context with definitions the agent will rarely use.

A common solution is to create a small index of tools instead of all tools. The agent first searches for what it needs, then reads the details of what it found, and finally runs it. The Salesforce MCP Server works this way with just four tools.

Suppose you are in Claude with the Salesforce plugin, and you ask for the 20 best opportunities from the last 100 days. The request goes through three steps:

Claude calls “discover” with its interpretation of your request. The server runs a semantic search over an index of available API and skill, and returns a short ranked list.

Claude calls “describe” on the best match. The server returns the skill’s contract, which lists the APIs, the parameters, the dependencies, and the order of the steps.

Claude calls dispatch. The server routes the call to the right endpoint, checks the user’s access, and returns the result.

This way, the agent’s context holds only four tool definitions instead of containing tool definitions for all available tools.

Everything in this article is a piece of scaffolding around the model. Today those pieces live in different products. The next step, according to both MK and Khushwant, is to make them one system. That is Enterprise AI Harness. A single place that enterprises can flexibly use. They plug in their agents and their data, and get eval, tracing, and other functionalities, applied to all of them at once, whether the agents run on Agentforce or somewhere else.

With discover, describe, dispatch, a wrong answer can start with search ranking a near-duplicate skill first, and the final transcript hides that. Logging the ranked list from discover and scoring top-1 hits against a labeled set of requests catches it when someone adds a new skill with a similar description.

Agents dropping rules after about eight instructions matches what I've seen. Prompts give an agent intent, but rules that always have to hold belong in code and permissions. I start my agents read-only and widen access once I've seen how they behave.

#35833. Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award

Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta.

Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes.

Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality.

Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp.

We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true.

As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start.
