#35836. Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI

Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions.

The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for.

GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers.

GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas:

Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions.

Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun, co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results.

Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI.

Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM, a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation (Solaris) to harvest the gains from the upstream model.

Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously.

Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and across every key advertiser objective from off-site conversions to mobile app installs. The generalizable representations learned on data-rich click tasks transfer into data-sparse conversion tasks. A new training recipe with cost-free data mixing and the domain expert framework makes this heterogeneous, large-scale learning tractable, with predictable scale and enhanced reliability.

Challenge: Training a RecSys foundation model across thousands of GPUs at this scale requires careful orchestration of compute, parallelism, communication, and memory. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization while scale.

Solution: We developed custom kernels with low precision and new 5D parallelism strategies co-designed with the latest GPU hardware and Meta’s training cluster, and optimized model architecture with infrastructure together to scale efficiently across thousands of GPUs. End-to-end training efficiency is doubled to 20-25% model FLOPS utilization (MFU) with 4x total training FLOPs, enabling GEM to train at LLM-scale at Meta (see full technical story in our companion blog on Training GEM at LLM Scale).

GEM introduces a new LLM-style model architecture — Kunlun. Compared to the previous version (Interformer), Kunlun delivers 2x performance gains with the same computation scaling. Kunlun is designed around the following innovations:

GEM’s Kunlun architecture effectively bends the recommender system scaling curve at frontier training scales by empowering ultra-long user sequences and massive user-item interaction features. For the following technical discussion, we define two types of features: non-sequence features (such as user demographics, ad content representations), and sequence features with a sequence of events, each composed of a set of features.

This architecture introduces three fundamental advancements:

We advanced the LLM-style architecture to better capture the unique characteristics of recommender system models — specifically, heterogeneous features and data dynamics.

We co-designed the architecture with the latest generation of hardware to allow it to grow deeper and wider efficiently:

We introduced specialized component designs to make ultra-long sequences computationally tractable:

Component Skip Connection (CompSkip): The computational skip mechanism selectively activates sequence modules in each layer, and only routes outputs through residual connections. By selectively deactivating the specific components, which is based on the assumption that the network can recover quickly after re-activating, we reduce FLOPS by 43% with negligible quality loss.

Sequence Unification (OneSeq): We selectively unify user sequences chronologically after the event feature aggregation. This allows a single, unified sequence layer to process long sequences, even when individual events possess heterogeneous structures and features. In the system, we have different user sequence sources, some of which have different events features. For example, an event in a purchase sequence can be described by ad ID and account ID, while the event in a post sequence is described by actors and object ID. They cannot simply be unified from the data source level due to the different set of event features. It requires the flexible sequence unification approach to maximize GPU efficiency because of large-size tensor operations and minimizing operator fragmentation.

The new architecture makes ultra-long sequences feasible. GEM scaled the long engagement context length by 2x in production, and further enabled the capability of scaling long context to 25x, demonstrating infrastructure capability at frontier scale. Along the way, we discovered:

The value of the foundation model depends on how effectively its intelligence transfers to the hundreds of vertical models that serve ads in real time. GEM revolutionizes post training for recommendation systems through the structure representation with the deep historical memory from the central brain, achieving 2x of transfer effectiveness beyond knowledge distillation. Furthermore, async computation is introduced to a few domain-specific foundation models to transfer the knowledge to vertical models.

Knowledge distillation is effective but limited in bandwidth: downstream models only receive a compressed view of GEM’s intelligence at each training process. To address the limitation, we introduce the precomputed structure representation, such as LoopFM, to understand and compress the central brain from the foundation model into a compact representation, and then structure it with deep historical memory. It enables the downstream models to learn the long context from our central brain. It consists of the following major components across the system:

The representation generation process is precomputed and shared with the computation to generate soft labels of the foundation model for knowledge distillation without additional foundation model cost.

Solaris keeps knowledge transfer fresher, precomputing the user-ad representation from GEM just before vertical model inference needs it. Evaluating the large-scale model inside a live ad request is not affordable, Solaris moves it in time: It speculatively precomputes foundation model embeddings for the user-ad pairs a future request is likely to need, and delivers them just-in-time on the serving hot path. Downstream models gain access to near-real-time foundation model intelligence without being constrained by the latency. Borrowing the idea of speculative decoding from LLM serving, Solaris works through the following major components across the system:

We further trained GEM with the ads data at Meta scale, including all-surface data (e.g., Facebook and Instagram Feed and Reels/video) and deep funnel optimization (e.g., off-site conversion, mobile app install). GEM powers the first optimized model that jointly predicts both CTR  across all the surfaces and conversion rate (CVR) across the major optimization goals. Previously, each surface and each prediction objective had its own system. This means learnings from engagement patterns across platforms can more directly be used to understand its conversion behavior (e.g., purchase) across ad surfaces. This positions GEM as the central model and compute engine for ads recommendation across Meta’s advertising surfaces.

Unlike LLMs with the static data, RecSys models need to deal with data dynamics and freshness as well as the diverse distribution across surfaces and traffic. To overcome the challenge, GEM built the first training recipe for the large-scale cross-surface, cross-domain unification through:

A Cost-Free Data Mixing Strategy: It introduced virtual data loading from different combinations of data pipelines without physically merging data together and incurring additional storage cost. It can flexibly adapt to the current ads ecosystem where the downstream models still train with the specific surface or traffic data. We also design a data mixture mechanism to control the mixture proportions during offline and online training close to the real datastream order received in real time, mitigating instability for domain switch and overmemorization for the recent domain data.

A Domain Expert Framework: A shared expert learns a unified representation across all domains, while domain-specific experts capture surface-specific patterns. Each domain expert benefits from both: the shared cross-domain knowledge and its own specialized knowledge. Experts are built on top of the Kunlun architecture framework.

GEM now trains at LLM scale on several thousand of the latest-generation GPUs. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics and rich user & ads signal interaction patterns that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization for training a foundational recommendation model of GEM’s size.

We measure training efficiency through E2E MFU, which decomposes into two factors: E2E MFU = Local MFU (compute efficiency) × Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency). Local MFU (compute efficiency) measures how well a single GPU’s compute units are utilized — how close the workload runs to the hardware roofline. Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency) measures how much single-GPU performance is retained when distributing across thousands of GPUs. This decomposition matters because it lets us treat compute efficiency and scaling efficiency as related but distinct optimization problems, each with its own dedicated set of techniques. Both must be addressed to maximize end-to-end MFU.

We tackled these challenges through complementary compute efficiency and scaling efficiency innovations:

The result: We doubled GEM’s E2E training efficiency to 20-25% MFU over the past 12 months while scaling total training FLOPs by 4x. Training a foundation model at the intersection of LLMs and recommendation systems is a co-design problem, not a software problem or a hardware problem alone. This 2x efficiency gain came from carefully considering every layer of the stack for optimization — kernels, precision, parallelism, networking, and memory all had to move together.

For the full technical story, see our companion blog: GEM Training: Train Meta’s LLM-Scale Ads Recommendation Model Efficiently.

Looking forward, we are excited to extend GEM to learn from all of Meta’s platform data, capturing behavior across organic and ads engagements spanning text, images, and video. We’re building toward LLM-scale long context, giving the model the ability to reason over longer spans of engagement context. This will unlock better ad relevance and help advertisers connect with the right audiences more efficiently.

We will continue to scale GEM on even larger compute clusters, opening new scaling opportunities. We are introducing AI-driven optimizations, such as ecosystem enhancement and architecture co-design, to accelerate future evolutions. These optimizations will iteratively refine model architecture in lockstep with hardware advancements, so that each new generation delivers more intelligence per dollar of compute. We will evolve the post-training paradigm with reasoning capability to transfer more of this intelligence to downstream models, further improving advertiser performance and user experience.

#35837. 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know

Christopher Patton,Â Bas Westerbaan,Â Trishna,Â andÂ Jeremy Hartman

OnÂ October 19, 2026, at approximatelyÂ 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a linkÂ to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLSâs encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers.Â The recommended actions are summarized below.

Cloudflare One Client: Upgrade to: v2.5.7 (Android), v1.12.7 (iOS), Windows Desktop (2026.8.2115.0), macOS (2026.8.2115.0), Linux (2026.8.2115.0)

1.1.1.1 app: Upgrade to: v6.38.11 (Android), v6.31.8 (iOS), Windows Desktop (2026.8.2115.0), macOS (2026.8.2115.0), Linux (2026.8.2115.0)

Customers using Cloudflare Containers, including Sandboxes, should review their container images and application dependencies for affected certificate trust stores and apply updates based on your deployed image.

Customers can also enable HTTPS egress interceptionÂ to route outbound HTTPS requests through Cloudflare, moving remote-server certificate validation from the application to Cloudflare-managed infrastructure. This allows Cloudflareâs trust-store mitigations to protect intercepted connections. Containers that have this enabled are already protected.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozillaâs Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packagesÂ that have been patched.Â We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jacksonâs test siteÂ providesÂ browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the applicationâs actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just oneÂ application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, weâre excited about projects like upkiÂ that understand a trust store canât be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

#35838. EP230: RAG vs Agentic RAG

They must endure waiting for users, and weather tool failures. They must take each new jump in model intelligence in stride.

Inngest makes long-running agents durable, observable and improvable over time.

Check out their generous free tier and a sleek local dev server for testing your workflows.

Top 5 AI Building Blocks Every Engineer Should Know (Youtube Video)

OAuth (authorization) + OIDC (authentication layer)

Understanding the Linux Directory Structure

RAG is a technique that combines information retrieval with an LLM to generate answers. Here is how RAG works at a high level:

A user asks a question to the application.

The retrieval system fetches the relevant information from a knowledge base.

The application adds that information to the prompt.

The LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

RAG usually follows a predefined retrieval process. The quality of its results depends on the accuracy of the retrieved context.

Agentic RAG follows a different approach. Instead of retrieving once, an agent can repeatedly fetch and evaluate information until it has enough evidence to generate an answer. Here is how it typically works:

An agent selects the right tools based on the task.

Those tools can search documents, APIs, databases, or the web.

The fetched evidence is then checked if it is sufficient for the task.

If it is not, the agent can adjust its search or choose a different tool.

Once sufficient evidence is achieved, LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

Open source is the foundation of nearly everything we build, and the maintainers behind it make it possible. The good news: the movement to support them is growing.

If you want to show Google Calendar events inside your Slack channel, it will require permission to read your calendar. How would you let Slack access your calendar without giving Slack your Google password?

This is where OAuth 2.0 comes into the picture. Slack basically never sees your Google password. It lets an app access a protected resource on your behalf without knowing your credentials.

Basically OAuth 2.0 handles authorization. In Slack’s case, it will send you to Google’s authorization server, where you will login and give Slack permission to access your calendar. Google gives you the authorization code, and Slack will exchange that code for access_token.

If Slack also wants to authenticate the identity of the person requesting the access to Google Calendar, you will need OIDC for that. The OIDC handles authentication and sits on top of OAuth 2.0.

OAuth answers what you’re allowed to touch, while OIDC answers who you are. In addition to the access_token returned by the authorization server, this time, it will also send an id_token, a signed JWT which basically tells Slack who just signed in.

The linux directory structure starts with the root directory "/". Let’s navigate to the directory structure of linux.

The kernel image and bootloader files are stored in the "boot" directory. Your hard disk partitions and device related files are located in the “dev” directory.

All your programs and libraries are stored in "bin", "sbin", "usr", and "lib" directories. Like, your installed software is located in the "usr" directory. Ever wondered where ls, cp, and cat commands are? "bin" is the directory that holds those essential commands.

System-wide configuration goes in "etc", and "var" holds data that changes as the system runs, which is where you'll find your logs.

If you have a USB drive, it gets mounted in “bin” folder. For any external drive that you want to mount temporarily on your linux machine, "media" is the directory for it. If you have multiple user accounts, "home" is the directory for each user in your linux system.

What's a "RAG"? It'd be helpful if you would spell out your acronyms the first time you use them. thanks!

Small correction to the Linux directory section: a USB drive isn't normally mounted under /bin. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard assigns /media to removable-media mount points and /mnt to temporary filesystem mounts; /bin holds essential executable programs. It would help beginners to distinguish where a utility is installed from the directory where an attached drive becomes accessible.

#35839. Pizzoccheri originali della Valtellina: ricetta per farli cremosi

Grano Saraceno e formaggio Valtellina Casera Dop sono le caratteristiche dei pizzoccheri originali, quelli veri, della Valtellina. Diffidate dalle imitazioni e ricordate che una quota del 20% o poco più è riservata alla farina di grano tenero 00. Eliminarla significa fare una pasta gluten free e dunque adatta ai celiaci.

Non possono mancare altri ingredienti nella composizione del piatto tipico valtellinese. Sono patate, verze, burro d’alpe. Non ve ne priverete in alcuna stagione: al posto della verza sono ammessi coste o fagiolini.

Dove sono nati i pizzoccheri? L’ingrediente principale, cioè la farina di grano saraceno, arriva da lontano. Nel tardo Medioevo il grano saraceno arriva attraverso l’Europa Centrale e il Mar Nero dalla Manciuria e dalla Siberia. E trova residenza stabile nei campi terrazzati della Valtellina. La sua farina scura è il protagonista dei pizzoccheri. La nascita si vuole nel piccolo borgo di Teglio – nel cuore della Valtellina – dove nel 2002 è nata l’Accademia del Pizzocchero. A lei è affidata conservazione e diffusione della ricetta originale dei pizzoccheri.

Che prevede anche l’impiego del Valtellina Casera Dop, formaggio da latte vaccino parzialmente scremato. Perché questo formaggio nella ricetta dei pizzoccheri originali? Perché ha una naturale capacità di fondere e amalgamarsi con la pasta e gli altri ingredienti. Con il Casera, la cremosità è assicurata.

E poi c’è il burro da panna del latte delle vacche al pascolo di alta quota. Ancora morbidezza, ancora sapore inconfondibile per i pizzoccheri originali.

E qui ci affidiamo alla leggenda perché di sicuro c’è poco. Se non che Dante e Boccaccio usassero “pinzochera” per indicare povertà e semplicità. Caratteristiche proprie dei pizzoccheri della Valtellina.

Derivazione da questo significato o, come sostengono alcuni studiosi, parola legata alle beghine. Cioè alle suore talmente povere che vivevano al di fuori dei chiostri da nullatenenti. Tranne il loro abito che era un mantello grezzo che ricorda appunto i pizzoccheri. E il nome di pizzocchere era dato a queste suore povere nell’Italia centrale dove erano considerate eretiche.

Leggerete comunque di una ricetta semplice. Ma attenzione: l’Accademia di Teglio non è lì per spargere ciclostili nel mondo. Perché dovreste frequentarla per imparare la scarellatura che non è una fregatura della ricetta. Ma l’arte di lavorare e stendere la sfoglia con il matterello nello spessore ideale delle listarelle da cui ricavare i veri pizzoccheri.

Tocca quindi imparare partendo dalla ricetta dei pizzoccheri.

Sappiate solo che esistono anche i pizzoccheri “bianchi” ma sono della Valchiavenna e che a Milano trovate da Crotto Quartino. Mentre a Teglio avete più di un ristorante che propone i pizzoccheri originali della Valtellina: Ai Tigli, La Galeda, Al Castello (che è anche pizzeria). E li trovate anche negli hotel dove potete soggiornare: Combolo, Bellavista e La Rosa

#35843. Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust

Boshen Chen,Â Dimitri Mitropoulos,Â andÂ Christoph Nakazawa

Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max SchwenkÂ of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain.

Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.

To be clear, we are notÂ forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the languageâs design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScriptâs adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.

The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation â and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.

Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrsÂ is up to 8xÂ faster and uses ~70%Â less memoryÂ compared to TypeScript 7.0Â when using the same number of type check workers:

As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and weâre hoping to find more.

You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScriptâs defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarksÂ are comparing the same configuration.

By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:

TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrsÂ package from npm:

Weâve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript teamâs port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.

However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.

You might be thinking: âTypeScriptâs Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isnât that enough?â

However, itâs not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rustâs language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Goâs garbage collectorÂ along with it. But Rustâs memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.

CloudflareÂ Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in WorkersÂ with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that itâs now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldnât have been run before.

This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.

First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rsÂ and tsrsÂ into a single package that supports all of TypeScriptâs features including Language Server ProtocolÂ (LSP) and content mappers. Second, weâve seen a lot of success with how we maintain VinextÂ in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post:

We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we donât introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, weâll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.

Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.

Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrsÂ integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.

Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrsÂ as a well-maintained healthy open source project â without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously â they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

#35844. OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks

At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011.

Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative.

This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone.

As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack.

IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface).

This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers.

As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible.

We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric.

With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages:

Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings.

This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure.

Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit.

That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale.

At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches.

The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work.

The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space.

At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement.

Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff.

We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG.

The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors.

We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI.

A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies.

We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology.

Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS.

We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack.

The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for:

This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it.

Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases.

With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future.

Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols.

SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable.

To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer.

OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for:

Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware.

Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository.

As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics.

At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack.

The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone.

We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands.

Meta believes in building community through open source technology. Explore our latest projects in Artificial Intelligence, Data Infrastructure, Development Tools, Front End, Languages, Platforms, Security, Virtual Reality, and more.

Engineering at Meta is a technical news resource for engineers interested in how we solve large-scale technical challenges at Meta.

#35845. Nike CEO Elliott Hill knew he’d always miss breakfast with his kids. He made another part of the day nonnegotiable.

Nike CEO Elliott Hill said he protects family time by scheduling them like work commitments.

Hill, who came out of retirement to lead Nike in 2024, said he follows a structured routine when he is not traveling.

"What time I try to get to sleep, what time I try to wake up. I get a workout in every morning, too. That helps keep me grounded and keeps me balanced," Hill told host Greg Byrne on the "You Got Byrned" podcast.

He said he makes a point of identifying what matters most to him and scheduling time for those priorities.

"I sat down, and I actually listed what was important to me: family, friends, my own personal — and then work — growth, and I put commitments underneath each one of those, and then I built them into my calendar," Hill said.

For example, he said he knew his work schedule meant he would miss his two kids before they headed to school, so he found other ways to show up for them.

"I knew I wasn't ever going to be there for breakfast with the kids because I was an early bird, and I was going to be in the office," Hill said. "But I did say I'm going to be home for dinner, and I had my admin build it into my calendar so that I would leave in time to be home for dinner."

He also blocks off parent-teacher conferences and other school events on his schedule, and said he would shift work trips when they overlap with those commitments.

"It all comes down to being very deliberate about what's important to us. Writing it on a piece of paper was very, very helpful, and then being planful enough to build it into your calendar. That's how I've always managed the balance," Hill said.

#35847. Why Distributed Systems Prefer Independence over Coordination

In a distributed system, you have components running in separate processes or machines. These components could be application services, database replicas, or even background workers.

Since in distributed systems, we divide the system into so many components, it’s pretty common that one component may need to talk to another component to get something done. It may also have to wait for the other component’s response. You can think of coordination as this talking between components. For example, you may have one service waiting for another service to approve a request. Or a database waits for acknowledgment from its replicas. Or a worker waits for a lock.

In this article, we’ll look at why coordination is a challenge for distributed systems. Here’s what we will cover.

Inizio schioppettante con i benvenuti divertenti e saporiti. Ottimi e anche belli esteticamente. I lievitati di Carlo Gabbiano e Carlo Carandente Coscia lasciano sempre un segno positivo. Il problema diventa fermarsi. Pane grissini e un Danubio al top. In abbinamento l’olio dell’azienda agricola Russo di Vico Equense e il burro.

La Merenda di Ciccio – Katsu-sando di coniglio all’ischitana, gambero rosso e rafano (25 €) – è un omaggio all’amicizia tra lo chef e il vecchio amico pescatore che portava i gamberi. Qui creano un connubio incredibile con il coniglio che farcisce il lievitato. Bella idea e ottimo sapore

Il Baccalà con fagioli butirri, alghe, zuppa forte (25 €) è piatto molto ben realizzato e gradevole. Baccalà in versione elegante senza rinunciare al sapore.

La Linguina con zuppetta di murena, emulsione ai ricci, lattuga di mare (30 €) è un piatto molto saporito. La murena è ottima protagonista unitamente ai ricci e la cottura della linguina è impeccabile.

Anche il Raviolo con verza, riso e parmigiano (25 €) è gustoso. Una versione originale del classico verza e riso racchiusa in un raviolo molto ben realizzato.

La Ricciola con friarielli, mandarino ed escabeche (35 €) è visivamente bello da vedere, ma soprattutto buono da mangiare. Il sapore per lo chef ischitano, cresciuto alla corte di Gaetano Trovato in Toscana, resta giustamente un caposaldo imprenscindibile.

Il Pollo bianco di Laura Peri con funghi autunnali, patate e spinaci (40 €) è una delizia. Petto cotto alla perfezione e farcito benissimo. Poi la chips di pelle farcita ad accompagnare con gusto una grande materia prima. Il pollo di Laura Perì non tradisce.

Dopo un fresco predessert arriva una buonissima Tarte au citron: lemon curd al limone sfusato amalfitano, meringa, vaniglia di Tahiti (20 €). Siamo felici per l’esecuzione del pastry chef.

Chiusura affidata al Cioccolato al latte con lamponi, noci e miso (20 €).

Maxi del Capo la Gala. Via Luigi Serio, 8, 80069 Vico Equense NA. Telefono: 081 801 5757. Instagram

Il Capo La Gala a Vico Equense è sempre un felicissimo approdo in Costiera Sorrentina con i due ristoranti Maxi e Nerea. La bellezza e l’eccellenza sono di casa grazie alle cure ed alla capacità imprenditoriale di Enzo Acampora e famiglia che hanno fatto di questo luogo una delizia per occhi, palato ed ospitalità.

Le redini sono ora in mano a Mario Acampora, figlio di Enzo.

20 tra camere e suite iper panoramiche, Nerea, la trattoria di mare praticamente quasi nell’acqua, il Maxi che è il ristorante gastronomico. In breve questo è il mondo del Capo La Gala.

Il ristorante Maxi, segnalato in guida Michelin, è guidato dall’anno scorso da Emmanuel Scotti che è allievo di Gaetano Trovato, 2 stelle Michelin storiche in Toscana. Può contare sul sous chef Carlo Carandente, sul pastrychef e panificatore Carlo Gabbiano che ci ha deliziato con lievitati e dessert. Completano la squadra, Marianna Ciufo, Michele Langella, Valerio Montuori e Yesenia Montes Guzman.

La sala è il regno di Giulia Tavolaro, figura storica e riferimento assoluto, vicana doc coadiuvata dal giovane e bravo Mariano Fiorentino.

Inizio scoppiettante con il Ponte con alici, caffè Guatemala di Gianni Frasi e limone bio di Sorrento. La presentazione è molto bella e il sapore non è da meno. Bei contrasti tra i vari elementi con un risultato molto gradevole. Ottimo inizio per collegarsi con quello che arriverà dopo.

È tutta una bufala è un antipasto in grande equilibrio con grandi prodotti. Oltre alla carne di bufalo magistralmente cotta, completano il piatto la ricotta in salvietta di Costanzo e un cremoso di carciofi con brunoise di carciofi arrostiti. Realizzazione da wow.

Scalo di Procida sono le linguine alla brace con insalata di limoni in conserva, ricci di mare, polvere di limoni e le sue foglie. Un primo piatto interessante con sentori di brace che si abbinano benissimo con il resto degli elementi dai sapori decisi per un risultato veramente molto saporito.

Intramontabile è il bottone alla genovese di coda stufata, ostriche perle noir e zuppa di prosciutto e basilico. Gran bel piatto del Maxi Capo La Gala, complesso e gustoso. Volutamente sapido ma buono nel complesso. Il livello resta comunque alto .

Quando arrivi manda un messaggio cioè il risotto alla pizzaiola al nero di seppia che provo in versione ufficiale al Maxi. Bello a vedersi e ottimo da mangiare. Wow.

Benedetta primavera è un rombo cucinato ottimamente e che, come gli altri piatti, si presenta anche molto bene. Si presenta come una rollatina di rombo con verdure primaverili, fiori eduli e salsa Beurre blanc. Direi che qui al Maxi Capo La Gala se esiste una difficoltà in più per lo chef è riuscire a colpire i commensali spesso distratti da uno scenario fantastico che li circonda. Emmanuel Scotti fino ad ora ci riesce.

Con Cambio d’identità arriva in tavola l’agnello Laticauda alla brace, carciofo violetto di Castellammare, salsa aiolì e bernese montata con estrazione di grasso d’agnello. Continua la giostra di sapori molto intensi e identitari. Il bravo chef ischitano si fa forza delle sue esperienze segnanti e soprattutto quella con Gaetano Trovato. Cotture giuste di carne e carciofo e anche quest’ultimo recita la sua parte da protagonista.

Dulcis in fundo assaggiamo le Fragole buone buone, una mousse al lime con inserto al cetriolo, sorbetto al finocchietto, burro d’arachidi e salsa di fragole.

Ottima realizzazione come anche Tu vuo’ fa l’americano. La mousse è alla banana accompagnata da cremoso fondente 55%, biscuit alle mandorle, caramello passion fruit, cioccolato bollato fermentato in bucce di banana, gelato arachidi. Entrambi dolci di spessore che dimostrano le ottime doti di Carlo Gabbiano già a me note per aver assaggiato un eccellente panettone ad un evento. Il pastry chef del Maxi Capo La Gala è da tenere d’occhio.

La cena è una prova superata dallo chef Emmanuel Scotti e dal suo team e spero che il Maxi torni nell’empireo delle stelle dove ha già meritato di stare.

Ci sono solo menu degustazioni con formule interessanti e soprattutto c’è un degustazione open “A 4 mani “ dove due portate le sceglie lo chef e le altre due i commensali. Il costo è di 90 € .

Il degustazione Contemporaneo da 6 portate costa 110 €.

Ancora il degustazione Ci pensa Emmanuel, 6 portare a sorpresa al costo di 110 €

Infine, il degustazione “Artigianato gastronomico “ di 8 portate a 130 €.

#35850. Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization

When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.

Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them â aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.

About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.

The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data.

The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) â $1.44 (June) â $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tierÂ (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe thereâs a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our âfull reviewâ tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though.

At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models.

Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself.

The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost.

One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCodeÂ v2, which is a ground-up rewriteÂ from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. Weâre also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. Weâre hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!

Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, Â cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that Â most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.

That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language modelÂ (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.

Itâs worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cacheÂ works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from whatâs been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so theyâre a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.

That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.

Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.

The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.

The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.

On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.

The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.

Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.

The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.

Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use

Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.

One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request

In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.

Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB

About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.

On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%.

OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw.

Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider

A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit.

Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none

GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished.

Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled

The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it.

A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer.

The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked.

When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving.

Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment.

The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings.

Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%.

The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5.

On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below.

To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that.

We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers.

The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30.

By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been.

A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened.

With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions.

First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence.

Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews.

Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low.

Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical.

So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next.

Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems.

Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%.

An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each sessionâs first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside.

Lower cost reviews didnât automatically mean worse quality, but it didnât automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things weâd check first are whether each sessionâs first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level youâre paying for.

If youâre at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, Iâm talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, Itâs time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. Iâll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.
